blocks.h: 1. The position you are in, and what the question is asking

blocks.p: As Chief Engineer of a UMS ship with central scanning and data logging, you have more measurements than any engineer has ever had and fewer people looking at the machinery than any engineer has ever had. The question follows directly from that trade, and it asks three things: which data deserves special attention and why; a chart you would formulate for condition monitoring; and the computer tools you would use to present it graphically and to analyse the trend. Answer them in that order and answer all three - the chart and the tools are as markable as the data.

blocks.h: 2. What a UMS ship gives you, and what it takes away

blocks.p: State this first, because every later choice is a consequence of it.

ul: What it takes away is the watchkeeper's senses. A manned engine room is monitored continuously by a human being who hears a knock, smells a hot bearing, sees a weep and feels a change in vibration long before any transducer registers a number outside its limit. On a UMS ship nothing is observed between rounds except what is instrumented.

What it gives you is a continuous, time-stamped, objective record of every instrumented point, taken at the same place, in the same way, at the same interval, without transcription error and without the drift of judgement that affects a hand-written log.

The consequence, and it is the whole answer in one sentence: the ship has exchanged continuous human observation for continuous instrumental observation, so the value of the instrumental record has to be actively extracted - which means the Chief Engineer's job is no longer to read the alarm printout but to interrogate the log.

blocks.p: Two further consequences shape the chart. An alarm is a failure of monitoring, not a success of it - by the time a point crosses an alarm setpoint the deterioration is complete and the only decision left is how to stop safely. And the arrangements the ship carries because she is unattended - the bridge and engineers' alarms, the fire and bilge detection, the machinery and boiler safeguards required of a periodically unattended machinery space under SOLAS chapter II-1 part E - are themselves equipment whose availability must be monitored, because their failure removes the ship's only substitute for a watchkeeper.

blocks.h: 3. The specific data that deserves special attention

blocks.p: The scanning system will log several hundred points. You cannot attend to all of them, and an answer that lists everything has made no engineering decision. Divide them into three groups by what the data is for, because that determines how it is treated.

Group A - slow-moving condition parameters. These change over weeks and months, they carry the deterioration signal, and they are the raw material of the chart. They matter as trends and are almost meaningless as single readings.

ul: Main engine cylinder performance - maximum and compression pressure per unit, exhaust gas temperature per unit and, more usefully, the deviation of each unit from the mean of all units. The deviation is the diagnostic quantity: it removes load, ambient and fuel-quality effects that move every cylinder together, and it is what identifies the one unit that is different.

Turbocharger condition - speed at given load, air inlet and outlet temperatures, scavenge air pressure and temperature, and the pressure drop across the air cooler and across the air filter. A charger fouling and a cooler fouling look similar in one reading and quite different in a trend.

Specific fuel consumption at reference load, and the shaft power against speed relationship normalised for displacement, trim and weather, which separates hull and propeller fouling from engine deterioration.

Lubricating oil condition - viscosity, base number against acid number, water content, insolubles, particle count and elemental spectrometric analysis. A single oil result is a data point; three with a slope are a diagnosis.
Cylinder liner wear and cylinder oil feed rate, and the scrape-down oil iron content where sampled.
Bearing temperatures - main, crankpin where measured, thrust and the stern tube - and shaft earthing where fitted.
Vibration on auxiliary engines, pumps, purifiers, compressors and fans, taken at fixed points in a fixed manner.
Differential pressures across every filter, strainer, cooler and purifier - the cheapest and most under-used deterioration signal on the ship.
Boiler water chemistry, exhaust gas boiler differential pressure and soot deposition indicators, and feed and condensate condition.
Auxiliary engine running hours, load sharing and specific consumption, which show up an engine that is doing more work than its share for the same fuel.

blocks.p: Group B - fast-moving safety and integrity parameters. These may be perfectly normal until the moment they are not. They are watched for the event rather than for the trend, and they are the parameters on which the ship's unattended status actually depends.

ul: Crankcase oil mist detector and bearing temperature high alarms, and scavenge space temperature - the three that precede a crankcase explosion or a scavenge fire.
Bilge level and bilge alarm status in every space, and any overboard discharge interlock.
Fire detection and the fixed extinguishing system's readiness.
Steering gear - hydraulic level, power availability and failure alarms.
Main engine safety system - slowdown and shutdown functions, and any override in force.
Electrical plant - generator availability, blackout and auto-start of the stand-by generator, preferential trips, and emergency generator readiness.
Starting air pressure and compressor availability, and control air.

The engineers' alarm, the dead-man alarm and the bridge alarm transfer - and the record that the duty engineer acknowledged, because an unacknowledged alarm on a UMS ship is a different event from an unacknowledged alarm on a manned one.

blocks.p: Group C - system-health parameters. Data about the monitoring itself, which nobody logs and which is the first thing to fail quietly.

ul: Sensors in fault, bypassed, inhibited or reading a frozen value, and the record of who inhibited what and when. An inhibited channel on a UMS ship is a blind spot in the only observation the ship has.

Alarm frequency and repeat-alarm analysis. A point that alarms thirty times a month is telling you something whether or not it is within limits; and a rising alarm count is itself a deterioration signal.
Calibration status and due dates of the instruments the chart depends on.
Data gaps in the log - periods where the scanner recorded nothing are periods where the ship was unobserved.

blocks.p: Before any chart is drawn, four disciplines have to be imposed, and stating them is what shows the examiner that you understand why most shipboard trending is worthless.

ol: Fix the operating condition. A parameter is only comparable with itself if it is taken at the same load, the same fuel, comparable ambient and comparable sea conditions. Either record at a defined reference condition - for example a fixed percentage of MCR at steady state - or normalise the reading to reference conditions before plotting it. Unnormalised data is the commonest reason a genuine trend is invisible.
Fix the method. Same instrument, same measurement point, same mounting, same operator procedure. A vibration reading taken 50 mm from where the last one was taken is a different reading.

Establish the baseline. The ship's own healthy values after commissioning, or after the last overhaul, at the reference condition - not the maker's shop-test figures. Without a baseline there is no such thing as an abnormal reading, which is why the first weeks of any monitoring regime produce nothing.

Distinguish three limits. The baseline, the alert limit at which you begin to plan, and the alarm or safe limit at which the machine must be stopped. The alert limit is derived from the parameter's own scatter about the baseline; the alarm limit comes from the maker. Confusing the two is why alert limits are usually set uselessly close to alarm limits.

blocks.p: The stem says formulate a chart, so give one, and give it a structure that could actually be issued as a shipboard document. Each row is one monitored parameter, and each row carries ten fields — parameter, measurement point and method, frequency, reference condition, baseline, alert, alarm or safe limit, trend rule, action on alert, and record. On a ship's own landscape form those are ten separate columns; below they are grouped three to a column so that the chart stays readable on a page. This is a specimen extract; the full chart would run to several pages.

headers: Alarm, trend rule, action and record
rows: M/E exhaust temp deviation from the mean of all units. Scanner channel per unit. Continuous, logged 4-hourly
At 75 % MCR steady, normalised for ambient. Baseline is the ship's own post-overhaul value. Alert on a deviation beyond the normal spread of the units
Alarm is the maker's high-temperature setpoint. Act on a rise over 3 consecutive logs: check fuel pump timing, injector and exhaust valve, and inspect through the scavenge ports. Record as a PMS job
Cylinder Pmax and Pcomp per unit. Indicator or online pressure sensor. Weekly
At fixed load, steady state. Baseline is the post-overhaul indicator card. Alert on falling Pcomp, or on the Pmax spread across units widening
Alarm is the maker's limit. Act on two successive sets moving the same way: check valve leakage, ring condition and fuel timing. File the indicator card set
Turbocharger air cooler differential pressure. DP across the cooler. Daily
At fixed load. Baseline is the clean-cooler value. Alert on a rise beyond the normal scatter
Alarm is the maker's limit. Act on a steady rise over 2 weeks: plan air-side cleaning at the next opportunity. Record in the log and the PMS
Shaft power at reference speed. Torsionmeter. Daily at noon
Normalised for displacement, trim and weather. Baseline is the post-docking clean-hull value. Alert when power demand exceeds baseline at the same speed
No safety alarm; this one is commercial. Act on a sustained rise over 30 days: assess hull and propeller cleaning. Record in the performance report
Lubricating oil base number against acid number. Sample to a shore laboratory. Monthly
In normal service. Baseline is the fresh charge value. Alert on approaching the condemning range
Alarm is the maker's condemning limit. Act on a slope across 3 consecutive samples: increase the renewal rate and investigate fuel sulphur and water ingress. File the laboratory report
Lubricating oil wear metals - iron, copper, chromium, lead. Spectrometric analysis. Monthly
In normal service. Baseline is the established running value. Alert on any element rising against its own history
No limit; this is diagnostic. Act on the rate of rise rather than the absolute value: identify the component the element points to. File the laboratory report
Auxiliary engine and pump vibration, overall level and spectrum. Fixed points, portable analyser. Monthly
At rated load, steady. Baseline is the post-overhaul signature. Alert on a rising overall level, or on a new frequency component appearing
Alarm is the maker's or the standard limit. Act on a rise over 2 readings or on any new component: diagnose from the spectrum and plan bearing renewal. Store the signature
Main and thrust bearing temperatures. Scanner channels. Continuous
At fixed load. Baseline is the ship's own normal. Alert on a rise relative to the other bearings and to sea temperature
Alarm is the maker's high alarm and slowdown. Act on divergence from the group of bearings: reduce load, investigate and prepare to stop. Record in the alarm log
Fuel oil filter differential pressure. DP across the filter. Daily
In normal service. Baseline is the clean-element value. Alert on a rise beyond the normal scatter
Alarm is the changeover DP. Act on a shortening interval between cleanings: investigate fuel quality and purifier performance. Record in the log
Purifier back-pressure and sludge discharge quantity. Gauge and discharge count. Daily
At normal throughput. Baseline is the commissioning value. Alert on any change against baseline
Alarm is the maker's limit. Act on a change over one week: check the bowl, the gravity disc, the throughput and the temperature. Record in the log
Cylinder liner wear. Measured at overhaul, with scrape-down iron monthly
No reference condition. Baseline is the as-new dimension. Alert when the wear rate exceeds the established rate per 1000 hours
Alarm is the maker's condemning wear. Act on the rate rather than the accumulated wear: review the cylinder oil feed rate and the base number grade. Record on the wear card
Alarm frequency and repeat alarms. Alarm history extract. Weekly
No reference condition. Baseline is the established normal count. Alert on any channel repeating abnormally
No limit. Act on a rising count on any channel: investigate the plant, and do NOT raise the setpoint. Record in the weekly review minute
Inhibited, bypassed or faulty channels. Scanner status report. Daily and at every handover
No reference condition. Baseline is zero. Alert on any channel inhibited without a raised defect
No limit. Act on any inhibit older than its authorised period: restore it, or record it with an authority and a time limit. Record in the inhibit register

blocks.p: Four things make this a chart and not a list, and each should be said in a sentence because each is a mark.

ul: Every row carries its reference condition and its baseline, so the reading is comparable with itself. A chart without those two fields produces numbers nobody can interpret.
Alert and alarm are separate fields. The alert is yours and is the one that creates work; the alarm is the maker's and is the one that stops the engine.
Every row has a trend rule, expressed as a number of consecutive readings or a rate, so that acting on a trend is a defined event and not a matter of opinion.

Every row has an action and a record, so the chart connects to the planned maintenance system and to the safety management system rather than sitting beside them. Under the ISM Code's maintenance element the ship must inspect at appropriate intervals, report and correct non-conformity with its possible cause, keep records, and identify the equipment whose sudden failure may result in a hazardous situation - and the chart is how that is done on a UMS ship.

blocks.h: 6. The computer tools for graphical representation

blocks.p: Answer this limb by what graphical form answers what question, not by naming software - a product list dates immediately and does not show engineering judgement. The tools sit in three layers: the scanning system's own historian, a general-purpose spreadsheet for the analysis you actually do at sea, and the planned maintenance and performance software that holds the history.

ul: Time-series line chart with the parameter on the vertical axis and date on the horizontal, and the baseline, alert and alarm limits drawn as horizontal reference lines. This is the workhorse: it shows position and direction in one picture and it is the only chart most parameters need.

Line chart with a fitted trend line and a moving average. The moving average suppresses scatter; the fitted line gives a slope, and the slope extrapolated to the alert or alarm line gives an estimated time to intervention - which is the number that lets you choose the port.

Multi-series line or column chart for per-unit comparison - all cylinder exhaust deviations on one chart, all bearing temperatures on one chart. The outlier is visible instantly and no calculation is needed.

Scatter plot with a regression for one parameter against another - shaft power against speed, exhaust temperature against load - which is how a reading is normalised and how a cause is separated from a symptom.

Control chart, plotting individual readings with the mean and control limits derived from the parameter's own scatter. Its value is that it flags a run of points on one side of the mean as a signal even though no single point has crossed a limit - which is precisely the case a limit-based alarm cannot detect.
Radar or spider chart for a multi-parameter snapshot of one machine against its own baseline profile, which is a good handover and superintendent's document.
Bar chart and Pareto for alarm counts by channel and for defects by system, which directs effort at the few causes producing most of the events.
Histogram for the distribution of a parameter, which shows whether scatter has widened even when the mean has not moved - often the first sign of an instability.

Vibration spectrum and waterfall plot - amplitude against frequency, and successive spectra stacked against time - which is the only presentation that identifies which component is deteriorating rather than merely that something is.

Conditional formatting and exception reporting, colouring cells that breach an alert and producing a one-page exception list. On a plant with several hundred points this is what makes a daily review possible at all.

blocks.p: Two practical points earn marks here. Automate the extraction: the scanner's log should be exported to the spreadsheet on a schedule rather than transcribed by hand, because manual transcription introduces error and stops the moment the ship gets busy. And pivot tables and lookup functions are what turn a raw export of several hundred thousand rows into the twenty charts that matter - which is a more useful skill for the engineer than any specialist package.
Graphing is presentation; trend analysis is the interpretation, and the stem asks for both. Six methods, in the order you would apply them.

ol: Normalisation. Correct the reading to the reference condition before anything else. This is the step that is usually omitted and it invalidates everything after it.

Smoothing. A moving average over an appropriate window separates the signal from the scatter. Choose the window from how fast the mechanism actually deteriorates - too short and you chase noise, too long and you hide the event.

Slope and rate of change. Fit a line and read the gradient. The rate matters more than the value: a wear metal at half the condemning limit and rising fast is a more urgent problem than one just below it and static for a year.

Extrapolation to the limit. Project the slope to the alert and alarm lines to estimate remaining useful life and therefore the intervention window. State the estimate with its uncertainty - it assumes the deterioration mechanism does not change, which is exactly what fails when a bearing begins to pick up.

Correlation and cross-checking. No single parameter should decide an intervention. A rising bearing temperature with rising vibration, rising oil iron and a falling oil film pressure is a diagnosis; any one of them alone is a suspicion. Correlating parameters is also how a sensor fault is distinguished from a plant fault - a genuine deterioration shows in more than one place.
Comparison. Against the ship's own history, against the sister ship, and against the maker's expected values. The sister-ship comparison is the strongest evidence available at sea and costs nothing.

blocks.p: Two failure modes should be named because the examiner will be listening for them. Do not adjust the baseline to accommodate deterioration - resetting the reference because the readings have drifted is the mechanism by which a plant declines invisibly for years. And do not raise an alarm setpoint to stop a nuisance alarm; investigate what the alarm is telling you and, if the setpoint really is wrong, change it through the management-of-change process with a recorded technical justification.

blocks.h: 8. What you do with what the trend tells you

blocks.p: Close on the management content, because the paper is Engineering Management and the data is worth nothing until it changes a decision.

ul: Convert the alert into a planned job in the PMS, with the spare identified, the port chosen and the manpower planned. A trend that generates no work order has achieved nothing.

Review formally and on a fixed cycle - a weekly engineers' review of the exception list and the alarm history, minuted, with actions owned. On a UMS ship this meeting replaces the watchkeeper's continuous observation and should be treated with the same seriousness.
Report to the office in the same format every month, so that a superintendent and a sister ship can be compared without re-working the data.

Feed back what was actually found on opening up. If the trend said a bearing was wiping and it was not, the interpretation was wrong and the limit or the method needs changing. A monitoring regime that is never corrected by findings becomes superstition.

Use the record in the survey. Recorded condition data accepted by the society can support a machinery planned maintenance scheme in place of an opened-up examination, so the chart has a value in the survey regime and not only in the maintenance budget.

Maintain the instrumentation as machinery. Calibration, correct siting and prompt repair of failed transducers are planned maintenance items. A neglected sensor is worse than no sensor, because it is believed.
Keep the manual competence alive. Indicator cards, sounding rods, a hand on a bearing and a look at the exhaust are the fallback when the system is down and the check on it when it is not.

blocks.p: End on the proposition that holds the whole answer together: on a UMS ship the log is the watchkeeper. Its value is not in the readings it contains but in the trends somebody extracts from it, and an alarm is the evidence that nobody did.

The stem is one unbroken paragraph with no limb labels, which is exactly why candidates lose marks on it - they write a general essay on condition monitoring and never produce the chart or the tools. The structure above splits the paragraph into its three actual tasks and signposts them: sections 2 and 3 answer 'the specific data', section 5 answers 'formulate a chart', sections 6 and 7 answer 'the tools for graphical representation and trend analysis'. A marker can find all three.

Section 3's division into three groups is the piece of thinking the question is really testing. A scanning system logs hundreds of points and an answer that lists them has made no decision. Grouping them by what the data is FOR - slow condition data that matters as a trend, fast safety data that matters as an event, and system-health data about the monitoring itself - shows the examiner a Chief Engineer's judgement rather than a memorised list. The third group in particular is what separates a strong answer: almost nobody mentions inhibited channels, alarm frequency or data gaps, and on a UMS ship they are the blind spots that matter most.

Section 4 exists because most shipboard trending is worthless for reasons that have nothing to do with the software. Unnormalised readings, an inconsistent method and no baseline will defeat any analysis, and putting those four disciplines before the chart makes the chart credible.

ul: Never producing a chart. The stem says FORMULATE a chart and it is one of three tasks. An answer without a tabulated chart has abandoned a third of the marks.
Listing every point the scanner logs. That is not special attention, it is a screenshot. Select, and say why you selected.

Naming software products instead of graphical forms. The question asks for tools in computer application for graphical representation and trend analysis - answer with what chart answers what question.
Treating exhaust temperature as an absolute value. The diagnostic quantity is the DEVIATION of each unit from the mean of all units, which removes load, ambient and fuel effects.
Forgetting normalisation. A parameter compared across different loads, drafts and sea states is not being compared at all.
Confusing the alert limit with the alarm limit. The alert comes from the parameter's own scatter and creates work; the alarm comes from the maker and stops the engine.
Deciding on one parameter. Correlate - rising temperature plus rising vibration plus rising wear metal is a diagnosis; one of them alone is a suspicion.
Omitting the UMS-specific dimension entirely and writing a generic condition monitoring answer. The question is set on a UMS ship for a reason.
An alarm is a failure of monitoring, not a success. By the time a point crosses its alarm setpoint the deterioration is complete. Say this and the examiner knows you understand what the log is for.
The rate of change matters more than the value. A wear metal at half the limit rising fast is more urgent than one just below the limit and static. Expect to be asked exactly this.

Never move the baseline to accommodate deterioration, and never raise an alarm setpoint to silence a nuisance alarm. Both are the classic ways a plant declines invisibly, and both are management-of-change failures.
An inhibited channel is a blind spot. On a UMS ship inhibiting a sensor removes the only observation the ship has of that point. It must be registered, authorised and time-limited.
A neglected sensor is worse than no sensor, because it is believed. Calibration is a planned maintenance item.

SOLAS chapter II-1 part E is the regulatory basis for a periodically unattended machinery space - the alarms, detection and safeguards that let the space be left unmanned. Do not attribute the UMS arrangements to the ISM Code; ISM element 10 is the maintenance obligation, which is a different thing.
Condition data can support a planned maintenance scheme in place of an opened-up survey - but only where the society has accepted the scheme. It is not automatic.
Your scanner logs six hundred points. Which twenty do you actually look at, and why those?
Why is exhaust temperature deviation more useful than exhaust temperature?
What is the difference between your alert limit and the alarm setpoint, and who sets each?
A bearing temperature has risen four degrees over three weeks and is well inside the alarm. What do you do?
The oil analysis shows iron rising steeply but still at half the condemning limit. Urgent or not?
One channel alarms twenty times a week. What do you do about it - and what do you NOT do?
How would you normalise shaft power so that you can compare last week with last year?
You open up the bearing the trend condemned and it is perfect. What now?
Show me how a chart entry becomes a job in the PMS.
The duty engineer inhibited a bilge alarm during a repair and went off watch. What is your position?

blocks.p: The route is POSITION - TRADE-OFF - DATA - DISCIPLINE - CHART - GRAPHS - TREND - ACTION. For the data hold three groups: SLOW CONDITION / FAST SAFETY / SYSTEM HEALTH. For the disciplines hold CONDITION - METHOD - BASELINE - LIMITS. For the chart fields hold PARAMETER - POINT - FREQUENCY - REFERENCE - BASELINE - ALERT - ALARM - RULE - ACTION - RECORD. For trend analysis hold NORMALISE - SMOOTH - SLOPE - EXTRAPOLATE - CORRELATE - COMPARE. And hold the closing line: on a UMS ship the log is the watchkeeper.

ul: SOLAS chapter II-1 part E - periodically unattended machinery spaces: fire and bilge detection and alarm, machinery and boiler safeguards, bridge and engineers' alarm arrangements, communications, and the requirement that the ship be as safe in all sailing conditions as one with the machinery space manned.

ISM Code element 10 - maintenance of the ship and equipment: inspection at appropriate intervals, reporting and correcting non-conformity with its possible cause, records, identification of equipment whose sudden operational failure may result in a hazardous situation, and regular testing of stand-by arrangements not in continuous use.

Classification society unattended machinery space notation, and the survey arrangements under which recorded condition data may support a machinery planned maintenance scheme. Described by function; no rule number is held or cited.
Statistical process control - individual and moving-range charts, control limits from the process's own variability, and the run rule. Industrial practice, not a maritime instrument.
Lubricating oil condition analysis - elemental spectrometric analysis, infrared spectroscopy, particle count, base number against acid number.
Hull and propeller performance normalisation - shaft power against speed corrected for displacement, trim and weather.

Every number in the chart is an example, not an authority. Alert and alarm limits belong to a particular engine, a particular maker's recommendation and a particular ship's baseline. The chart's STRUCTURE is the answer to the question; the figures illustrate it.
No maker's sampling interval or condemning limit is quoted. These differ between makers and engine types, and the answer directs the candidate to the manual.
we hold SOLAS at citation level and not as quotable text. Chapter II-1 part E is cited by identity and subject; no regulation below part level is asserted and nothing is quoted.
No class rule number is cited for the unattended notation or for the planned maintenance scheme survey arrangement. Both are described by function.
No software product is recommended. Tools are given by function because a product list dates immediately and answers nothing.

No earlier solved paper we hold sets this task. The engineering content is authored fresh from practice and corroborated against our own verified records for lubricating oil analysis, hull performance, preventive maintenance and data architecture. The grouping of parameters and the chart's field structure is the author's design and are recorded as engineering judgement.

notes: THIS QUESTION HAS NO DONOR, SO NOTHING CAN BE INHERITED AND NO REVERSAL IS REQUIRED. That is the whole temporal position and it is unusual on this paper. The risk on a fresh question runs the other way: not imported later law, but material drawn from present-day practice being written as though it were true in August 2023.

THE TWO REGULATORY ANCHORS ARE STABLE ACROSS THE WHOLE 2021-2026 CORPUS. SOLAS chapter II-1 part E has governed periodically unattended machinery spaces without relevant amendment, and the ISM Code's maintenance element stands as amended through MSC.353(92), in force 1 January 2015. Neither moved before or after this sitting.

NO GHG, ASSEMBLY OR DIGITAL-REGULATION MATERIAL IS ENGAGED, DELIBERATELY. The temptation on a data question is to reach for the 2023 GHG Strategy, EEXI and CII, or the cyber-risk instruments. None of them is what this stem asks about, and importing them would date an answer that otherwise has no date in it. The energy-efficiency and cyber material is where it belongs, on Q1 of this paper.
THE 33RD ASSEMBLY SET (6 December 2023) AND THE 34TH (3 December 2025) ARE BOTH FUTURE AND NEITHER IS NEEDED.

NOTHING IN THE ANSWER RESTS ON A TECHNOLOGY THAT POST-DATES THE SITTING. Spreadsheets, control charts, vibration spectra, waterfall plots, spectrometric oil analysis and shaft power meters were all long-established practice by 2023. Machine-learning anomaly detection and prescriptive maintenance are deliberately NOT presented as available shipboard tools; the answer's data architecture stops at what a scanning system and a spreadsheet could actually do on a ship at this sitting.
MERCHANT SHIPPING ACT, 1958 governs any Indian aspect; the 2025 Act commenced 15 March 2026. Nothing in this answer engages either.

questions.understand_first: A manned engine room is watched by a person, and a person is a remarkably good instrument. He hears a knock that was not there yesterday, smells a bearing before it is hot enough to alarm, sees a weep on a flange and notices that the note of a pump has changed. None of that is written down anywhere, and all of it is monitoring. When the space is left unattended, every bit of that disappears at once, and what you get in exchange is a machine that writes down a few hundred numbers, faithfully, at the same place and the same interval, for ever. So the trade is continuous human noticing swapped for continuous instrumental recording, and the whole of this question follows from that one exchange. The recording does not notice anything by itself - it just accumulates - so somebody has to go and look, deliberately and on a schedule, for the thing the watchkeeper would have spotted. That is why the answer is about selecting a small number of parameters rather than watching all of them, about comparing each reading with what that same machine did before rather than with a number in a book, and about acting when the direction changes rather than when a limit is crossed. Hold on to the sharpest version of it: an alarm is not the system working, it is the system telling you that you missed it - by the time a reading crosses a setpoint, the deterioration has already happened and the only choice left is how to stop safely. Everything else - the chart, the graphs, the statistics - is machinery for noticing early.
questions.memory_cue: POSITION - TRADE-OFF - DATA - DISCIPLINE - CHART - GRAPHS - TREND - ACTION (1 to 8). Inside step 3 hold SLOW CONDITION / FAST SAFETY / SYSTEM HEALTH. Inside step 4 hold CONDITION - METHOD - BASELINE - LIMITS. Inside step 7 hold NORMALISE - SMOOTH - SLOPE - EXTRAPOLATE - CORRELATE - COMPARE.

steps.title: The position you are in, and what the question is asking
points: More measurements than any engineer has had, and fewer people watching the machinery
Three tasks: which data deserves special attention, a chart to formulate, and the computer tools
All three are markable - an answer without the chart has abandoned a third of the marks

steps.title: What a UMS ship gives you, and what it takes away
points: It takes away the watchkeeper's senses - the knock, the smell, the weep, the change in note
It gives a continuous, time-stamped, objective record free of transcription error
The value of the record has to be actively extracted; the job is to interrogate the log, not read the printout
An alarm is a FAILURE of monitoring, not a success
The unattended-space arrangements under SOLAS II-1 part E are themselves equipment whose availability must be monitored

steps.title: The specific data that deserves special attention
points: Group A, slow condition data - exhaust deviation per unit, Pmax and Pcomp, turbocharger and cooler DP, normalised shaft power, oil condition and wear metals, liner wear, bearing temperatures, vibration, filter differentials, boiler chemistry, A/E load sharing
The diagnostic quantity for cylinders is the DEVIATION from the mean of all units, not the absolute temperature

Group B, fast safety data - oil mist detector, scavenge temperature, bilge levels, fire detection, steering gear, safety system and overrides, electrical availability, starting air, engineers' and dead-man alarms
Group C, system health - inhibited and faulty channels, alarm frequency and repeats, calibration status, data gaps
Group C is the group almost nobody mentions and the one that matters most on a UMS ship

steps.title: Telling a trend from noise
points: Fix the operating condition, or normalise to a reference condition before plotting
Fix the method - same instrument, same point, same mounting, same procedure
Establish the ship's OWN baseline after commissioning or overhaul, not the shop-test figure
Distinguish three limits: baseline, alert from the parameter's own scatter, alarm from the maker

steps.title: Formulating the condition monitoring chart
points: One row per monitored parameter, carrying ten fields, each answering a question somebody will ask
Parameter, point and method, frequency, reference condition, baseline, alert, alarm, trend rule, action, record
Reference condition and baseline are what make a reading interpretable
Alert and alarm are separate columns - one creates work, the other stops the engine
A trend rule makes acting on a trend a defined event and not an opinion
Action and record connect the chart to the PMS and to the ISM maintenance element

steps.title: The computer tools for graphical representation
points: Answer by what graphical form answers what question, not by product name
Time-series line chart with baseline, alert and alarm as reference lines - the workhorse
Trend line and moving average, and the slope extrapolated to give time to intervention
Multi-series comparison of like units; scatter with regression for normalisation
Control chart, which flags a RUN of points a limit-based alarm cannot detect
Radar for a machine profile; bar and Pareto for alarm counts; histogram for widening scatter
Vibration spectrum and waterfall - the only presentation that says WHICH component
Conditional formatting and exception reporting; automate the export; pivot tables do the reduction

steps.title: Trend analysis proper
points: Normalise first - the omitted step that invalidates everything after it
Smooth with a moving average whose window matches the deterioration rate
Slope and rate of change - the RATE matters more than the value
Extrapolate to the limit for remaining useful life, and state the assumption it rests on
Correlate across parameters - it is also how a sensor fault is told from a plant fault
Compare against own history, sister ship and maker's expectation
Never move the baseline to accommodate deterioration; never raise a setpoint to silence an alarm

steps.title: What you do with what the trend tells you
points: Convert the alert into a planned job with spare, port and manpower identified
A minuted weekly engineers' review of the exception list and alarm history
A monthly report in a fixed format so ships and superintendents can compare
Feed back what was actually found on opening up, or the regime becomes superstition
Recorded data can support a planned maintenance scheme in place of an opened-up survey
Maintain the instrumentation as machinery - a neglected sensor is believed
Keep the manual competence alive as fallback and as check

quick_revision.recall_15s: On a UMS ship the log is the watchkeeper. Select data in three groups: slow condition (exhaust DEVIATION per unit, Pmax, cooler DP, normalised shaft power, oil wear metals, vibration, filter DPs), fast safety (oil mist, bilge, fire, steering, safety system, electrical), system health (inhibited channels, alarm frequency, calibration, data gaps). Before plotting: normalise, fix method, baseline, three limits. Chart columns: parameter, point, frequency, reference, baseline, alert, alarm, trend rule, action, record. Trend: normalise - smooth - slope - extrapolate - correlate - compare. An alarm means you missed it.
quick_revision.critical_numbers: Three groups of data - slow condition, fast safety, system health. Four disciplines before plotting - condition, method, baseline, limits. Three limits - baseline, alert, alarm. Ten columns in the chart. Six trend-analysis steps. No engine figure in the chart is an authority: alert and alarm limits belong to the maker and to the ship's own baseline.
quick_revision.critical_regulation: SOLAS chapter II-1 part E - periodically unattended machinery spaces. If you remember one regulatory point, remember that it is part E which permits the space to be unmanned, by requiring the detection, alarm and safeguard arrangements that substitute for the watchkeeper - and that ISM Code element 10 is a separate obligation, about maintaining the ship and identifying the equipment whose sudden failure would be hazardous.
quick_revision.major_trap: Treating an alarm as the monitoring system working. It is the opposite: by the time a reading crosses its setpoint the deterioration is complete and the only decision left is how to stop safely. The related traps are moving the baseline to accommodate a drifting plant, and raising a setpoint to silence a nuisance alarm - both hide deterioration rather than manage it, and both are management-of-change failures.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the UMS condition monitoring question.
retrieval_cards.answer: 1 the position you are in and the three tasks; 2 what UMS gives and takes away; 3 the data in three groups; 4 the four disciplines that make a trend readable; 5 the condition monitoring chart; 6 the graphical tools; 7 trend analysis methods; 8 what you do with the result. Sections 2-3 answer the data limb, 5 answers the chart limb, 6-7 answer the computer tools limb.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How do you group the data on a UMS ship, and why in that way?
retrieval_cards.answer: By what the data is for. Group A slow condition parameters, which matter as trends and carry the deterioration signal. Group B fast safety parameters, which matter as events and on which the unattended status depends. Group C system-health parameters - inhibited channels, alarm frequency, calibration, data gaps - which are data about the monitoring itself. Grouping by purpose is what turns a list of hundreds of points into a decision.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Name the ten fields every row of a usable condition monitoring chart must carry.
retrieval_cards.answer: Parameter; measurement point and method; frequency; reference condition; baseline; alert limit; alarm or safe limit; trend rule; action on alert; record. Reference condition and baseline make the reading interpretable; alert and alarm are separate because one creates work and the other stops the engine; the trend rule makes acting a defined event; action and record connect the chart to the PMS.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Alert limit or alarm setpoint - what is the difference and who sets each?
retrieval_cards.answer: The alert limit is yours, derived from the parameter's own scatter about the ship's baseline, and crossing it creates planning and investigation. The alarm or safe limit is the maker's, derived from what the machine can withstand, and crossing it stops or slows the engine. Confusing them is why alert limits are usually set uselessly close to alarms, leaving no time to plan anything.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What four disciplines must be imposed before any trend is plotted?
retrieval_cards.answer: Fix the operating condition, or normalise the reading to a reference condition. Fix the method - same instrument, same point, same mounting, same procedure. Establish the ship's own baseline after commissioning or overhaul, not the maker's shop-test figure. And distinguish three limits: baseline, alert from the parameter's scatter, alarm from the maker. Unnormalised data is the commonest reason a genuine trend is invisible.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the six steps of trend analysis in order.
retrieval_cards.answer: Normalise to the reference condition; smooth with a moving average whose window matches how fast the mechanism deteriorates; fit a slope and read the rate of change; extrapolate to the alert and alarm lines for remaining useful life; correlate across parameters, which also distinguishes a sensor fault from a plant fault; and compare against own history, sister ship and the maker's expectation.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why is exhaust temperature deviation more useful than exhaust temperature?
retrieval_cards.answer: Because load, ambient temperature and fuel quality move every cylinder together, so an absolute temperature tells you mostly about the operating point. The deviation of each unit from the mean of all units cancels those common effects and isolates the one unit that is behaving differently - which is the unit with the fuel pump, injector or exhaust valve defect.

retrieval_cards.prompt: A channel nuisance-alarms twenty times a week. What do you do, and what must you not do?
retrieval_cards.answer: Investigate what the alarm is telling you about the plant, because a rising alarm count is itself a deterioration signal. Do NOT raise the setpoint to silence it, and do not inhibit it and forget. If the setpoint is genuinely wrong, change it through management of change with a recorded technical justification. An inhibited channel on a UMS ship is a blind spot in the only observation the ship has.

retrieval_cards.prompt: The trend condemned a bearing, you opened it up and it was perfect. What now?
retrieval_cards.answer: Record the finding and correct the interpretation - the limit, the measurement method or the diagnosis was wrong, and one of them must change. Feeding back what was actually found on opening up is what keeps a monitoring regime honest; a system never corrected by findings degrades into superstition, and the crew stop believing it long before the office does.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is the regulatory basis for leaving the machinery space unattended, and what is ISM element 10?
retrieval_cards.answer: SOLAS chapter II-1 part E governs periodically unattended machinery spaces - the fire and bilge detection and alarm, the machinery and boiler safeguards, and the bridge and engineers' alarm arrangements that substitute for a watchkeeper. ISM Code element 10 is separate: maintenance of the ship and equipment, inspection at intervals, records, and identification of equipment whose sudden failure may be hazardous.

decomposition_gate.question_intent: A scenario question set on the candidate's own ship, printed as one paragraph with three embedded tasks and no limb labels. The examiner is testing whether a Chief Engineer can turn an instrumentation system into a management regime: select from hundreds of points, design a document that could actually be issued, and present and interpret the result. The discriminator is the chart - most candidates can discuss condition monitoring and comparatively few produce a tabulated chart with reference conditions, baselines and separate alert and alarm columns. The second discriminator is whether the answer is UMS-specific at all, or a generic condition monitoring essay that would read the same on a manned ship.
decomposition_gate.mark_allocation: Sixteen marks with no printed split and no limb labels, so the split is adjudicated rather than read. The stem sets three tasks of visibly different size - 'explain the special attention you will pay to the specific data' is the largest, 'formulate a chart' is a single deliverable, and 'highlight the tools in computer application' covers both graphical representation and trend analysis. The answer allots sections 2 to 4 to the data and the disciplines, one section to the chart, and sections 6 and 7 to the tools, with a management close. The absence of any printed mark is the printed copy's and is not repaired.
decomposition_gate.examiner_expectation: That the answer is specific to an unattended machinery space and says what has been given up as well as gained. That the data is SELECTED with reasons rather than listed. That exhaust deviation, differential pressures and wear-metal rates appear, because they are the parameters an experienced engineer reaches for. That an actual chart is drawn, with reference condition and baseline in it. That tools are given as graphical forms answering questions rather than as software names. And that the answer ends in a work order and a review, because data that changes no decision is worth nothing.
decomposition_gate.primary_source_plan: There is no donor, so the plan is to build from marine engineering practice and corroborate against MIW's own verification records where they touch: QP2411 Q9 and QP2303 Q9 for lubricating oil analysis, QP2503 Q8 for the normalisation of shaft power, QP2401 Q4 for preventive maintenance and the survey link, QP2404 Q1 for the data architecture. Anchor the regulatory frame on SOLAS chapter II-1 part E and ISM element 10, both by identity. Deliberately NOT planned: any quotation of SOLAS text, which MIW holds at citation level only; any class rule number; any maker's setpoint or sampling interval; and any software product name.
decomposition_gate.freshness_risk: LOW - and the reason is that the question has no donor and no date. SOLAS chapter II-1 part E and the ISM maintenance element are stable across the whole corpus. The residual risk on a fresh question runs the other way from the usual one: present-day practice being written as though it were true in 2023. It is controlled by stopping the data architecture at what a scanning system and a spreadsheet could do at this sitting, and by not presenting machine-learning anomaly detection or prescriptive maintenance as available shipboard tools.
decomposition_gate.jurisdiction_risk: LOW to MEDIUM. Three levels must not be blurred: SOLAS chapter II-1 part E, which is what permits the space to be unattended; the ISM Code's maintenance element, which is a management-system obligation and a different thing; and the classification society's notation and survey arrangements, which are contractual and are what actually accepts recorded data in place of an opened-up examination. An answer that attributes the UMS arrangements to ISM, or that treats a planned maintenance scheme as automatically accepted, has the levels wrong.
decomposition_gate.technical_ambiguities: 'Formulate a chart' is genuinely ambiguous - it could mean a graph or a tabulated schedule. It is answered as a tabulated schedule, because the stem separately asks for graphical representation in the next sentence, so reading 'chart' as a graph would make the two requirements the same and leave the schedule unwritten. 'Tools in computer application' is likewise open between software products and analytical methods; it is answered as graphical forms and analytical methods, with an explicit statement of why a product list would not answer it. Neither reading is asserted as the only possible one.
decomposition_gate.target_answer_shape: Eight numbered sections. Bulleted lists for the three data groups, because each is a selection to be counted. A numbered list for the four disciplines, because they are sequential. A rendered TABLE for the chart itself - the deliverable the stem asks for, carrying ten fields per row in three grouped columns, with a specimen set of rows - followed by four bulleted propositions justifying its design. A bulleted list of graphical forms, each tied to the question it answers. A numbered list of six trend-analysis steps. A bulleted management close and a single-sentence closing proposition.

reverify_before_publication.claim: Every alert limit, alarm limit, frequency and reference condition appearing in the condition monitoring chart.
reverify_before_publication.why: These are ILLUSTRATIVE. They are properties of a particular engine, a particular maker's recommendation and a particular ship's baseline, and the answer says so in its own text. The chart's STRUCTURE is what answers the question. A reviewer must not read the specimen rows as MIW asserting a setpoint for any machine, and a candidate must not carry a figure from them into an oral.

reverify_before_publication.claim: That recorded condition monitoring data accepted by the classification society can support a machinery planned maintenance scheme in place of an opened-up examination.
reverify_before_publication.why: Described by function because MIW holds no class rule text. The proposition is well established across the MIW corpus - it appears in the QP2401 Q4 and QP2404 Q1 records - but no rule number is cited and the acceptance is not automatic. Stated as conditional on the society having accepted the scheme.

reverify_before_publication.claim: The regulatory frame - SOLAS chapter II-1 part E for periodically unattended machinery spaces, and ISM Code element 10 for maintenance.
reverify_before_publication.why: Both are cited by identity and subject rather than quoted, MIW holding SOLAS as a citation-level object. No regulation number below part level is asserted. Recorded because candidates routinely attribute the UMS arrangements to the ISM Code, and an answer that gets the attribution right should be protected from a reviewer who does not.

regulations: SOLAS chapter II-1 part E - periodically unattended machinery spaces: fire and bilge detection and alarm, machinery and boiler safeguards, bridge and engineers' alarm arrangements, and the requirement that the ship be as safe as one with the machinery space manned

ISM Code element 10 - maintenance of the ship and equipment: inspection at appropriate intervals, reporting and correction of non-conformity with its possible cause, records, identification of equipment whose sudden operational failure may result in a hazardous situation, and regular testing of stand-by arrangements

Classification society notation for periodically unattended machinery spaces, and the survey arrangements under which recorded condition data may support a machinery planned maintenance scheme. Described by function; no rule number held or cited
Statistical process control practice - individual and moving-range charts, control limits derived from the process's own variability, and the run rule. Industrial practice, not a maritime instrument

questions.short_title: Limitations of Recognized Organizations, and the Statutory Services Delegated
questions.text_verbatim: Classification societies as Recognized Organisations (RO) and play an important role in implementation of national and international regulations. State the limitations of the RO highlighting them with reasons. List the statutory services undertaken by a classification body on behalf of Administration.
questions.subpart_marks_note: ANOMALY: the source copy prints NO mark allocation for this question, and none for any question on the paper. Recorded at 16 marks under instruction 2 ("all questions carry equal marks"). GRAMMATICAL ANOMALY PRESERVED: the opening sentence has no main verb for its first clause - "Classification societies as Recognized Organisations (RO) and play an important role" does not parse. The intended sense is "act as Recognized Organisations and play an important role". The printed form is reproduced and is NOT repaired. The stem also prints "Organisations" with an s against "Recognized" with a z in the same phrase.

That is consistent with MIW's own finding: the RO family is heavily solved but NO solved question anywhere in the corpus asks for the LIMITATIONS of a Recognized Organization or for a LIST of the statutory services delegated to it. The absence of a chip row is therefore evidence in the same direction as the donor search, which is unusual and is recorded as such. The annotation is not MIW truth, it creates no family edge and it reaches no candidate-facing surface.
decomposition: What the question is really asking, and what it is not asking
The dual capacity - class and RO are two different things done by one body
Limitation one - the delegation is of function, never of responsibility
Limitation two - authority is specific, not general
Limitation three - the RO cannot make or waive the law
Limitation four - independence and the structural conflict of interest
Limitation five - jurisdictional and practical limits
The statutory services undertaken on behalf of the Administration
reuse_evidence: TIER C - FAMILY, NOT EXACT. The RO family is heavily solved, but every solved member asks a different question from this one. QP2309-Q2 (September 2023) asks what an RO is, what the RO Code contains and how Administrations monitor. QP2408-Q1 (August 2024) asks for the approval requirements and the oversight mechanisms. THIS EXAMINER ASKS TWO THINGS THAT ARE IN NONE OF THEM: the LIMITATIONS of an RO, with reasons; and a LIST of the statutory services a classification body performs on the Administration's behalf. Both halves are authored fresh.

NEAREST SITTING: QP2309-Q2 is one month later and supplies the instrument spine - the RO Code's adoption, structure and mandatory boundary - which is the same for both questions. QP2408-Q1 supplies the RO Code section-level depth. Both are INTEGRATED on main.
DIRECTION: the nearest donor is LATER by one month, and the depth donor by twelve. The single reversal is the Assembly obligations list; see temporal_review.

READ AND REJECTED, TOPICAL ONLY: QP2312-Q8, QP2304-Q9, QP2412-Q4, QP2509-Q9 and QP2606-Q8 are classification-society rule-formation and survey-type questions. They describe what class does under its OWN rules, which is the opposite side of the boundary this question is testing.

The RO Code's identity, adoption, three-part structure and mandatory boundary, and the conventional bases on which a delegation rests, are carried from the MIW verification records for QP2309 Q2 - the nearest sitting, one month later - and QP2408 Q1, which worked through the Code section by section. The stem asks for limitations 'highlighting them with reasons', so the reason attached to each head is the answer to the question and not commentary on it.

blocks.h: 1. The boundary the question turns on

blocks.p: The stem asserts that classification societies act as Recognized Organizations and play an important part in implementing national and international regulation, and then asks two things: what the limits of that role are, with reasons, and what statutory services a classification body actually performs on the Administration's behalf.
Both halves turn on one boundary, and stating it first makes the whole answer coherent: a classification society does two entirely different kinds of work, under two entirely different authorities.

ul: Classification is the society's own business, done under its own rules, for the owner who pays it, under a contract. Class rules are private standards. Condition of class, notations, periodical class surveys and the class certificate all belong here.

Statutory work is the flag State's business, done under convention and national law, on the Administration's behalf, because the Administration has delegated it. The certificates carry the flag State's name and authority, not the society's.

blocks.p: The society wears the second hat only where a flag State has handed it over, only to the extent handed over, and only for that flag's ships. Every limitation in this answer is a consequence of the statutory hat being borrowed rather than owned.

The instrument governing the arrangement is the Code for Recognized Organizations, adopted by resolutions MSC.349(92) of 21 June 2013 and MEPC.237(65), and made mandatory from 1 January 2015 through amendments to SOLAS, MARPOL Annexes I and II and the 1988 Load Line Protocol - the SOLAS hook being regulation XI-1/1. Parts 1 and 2 of the Code are mandatory; Part 3, the flag State oversight guidelines, is recommendatory. Note also the distinction the Code is built on and which candidates blur: recognition is the assessment of an organization against the Code, and authorization is the separate, later act of delegating specified functions. An organization can be recognized and still not authorized for a particular ship type or convention.

blocks.h: 2. Limitation one - the function is delegated, the responsibility is not

blocks.p: The limitation. The RO performs the survey and issues the certificate, but the Administration remains responsible for the statutory certification of its ships and for the ship's compliance. The RO cannot assume that responsibility and the flag State cannot shed it.

The reason. The obligation created by a convention is an obligation between Contracting Governments. A flag State promises the other parties that ships flying its flag comply; it cannot discharge a treaty obligation by contracting with a private company, and no other Government has any treaty relationship with the society. So when a ship is detained abroad, or a casualty is investigated, or the flag State's performance is audited, it is the flag State that answers - and it may not answer by pointing at its RO.

The consequence in practice. The Administration must run an oversight programme over its ROs; it retains the power to conduct its own additional inspections of ships its ROs have certified; and it can be, and is, audited on exactly this under the III Code and the IMO Member State Audit Scheme.

blocks.h: 3. Limitation two - the authority is specific, never general

blocks.p: The limitation. An RO may do only what the instrument of authorization says it may do. The Code requires the flag State to specify the functions conferred, function by function and convention by convention, and to record them in a formal written agreement. Anything not conferred has not been conferred.
The reasons, and there are three worth separating.

ul: Capability. The Code expressly forbids a flag State to authorize functions beyond the RO's capabilities, and an appendix breaks the survey and certification work into elementary modules precisely so that capability can be assessed module by module rather than once and for all. A society competent in ship structure is not thereby competent in gas carrier containment systems.

Transparency to third parties. A port State inspecting a foreign ship has to know what the certificate in front of it represents. That is why the flag State must deposit with the Secretary-General a list of its ROs together with the specific responsibilities and conditions of the delegated authority. A general authorization to 'act on our behalf' tells a port State nothing.

Controllability. A scope that is specified can be narrowed - by ship type, by convention, by function - as easily as it can be suspended or withdrawn. A general authorization can only be revoked entirely, which is a blunt instrument no Administration wants to use.

blocks.p: Three practical corollaries. The authority is flag by flag: the same society may be an RO for one flag and not another, with different scopes from each, and it may not survey a ship not entitled to fly the flag that authorized it. The authorization must cover the unglamorous end - corrective action and the withdrawal or cancellation of certificates - and a flag State that has not said who may withdraw a certificate has not finished authorizing. And the authority may be time-limited and is always revocable.

blocks.h: 4. Limitation three - the RO cannot make, waive or dispense with the law

blocks.p: The limitation. This is the sharpest limitation of the six and the one candidates most often miss. An RO applies the requirements; it cannot create them, relax them or excuse a ship from them.

ul: Exemptions - the power to exempt a ship from a convention requirement - belong to the Administration. So does the issue of an Exemption Certificate.

Equivalents - the acceptance of a fitting, material, appliance or arrangement other than that required, on the basis that it is at least as effective - is likewise the Administration's decision, and the Administration must communicate the particulars to the Organization.

Interpretation of national law is the flag State's. Where a national requirement goes beyond or differs from the convention, the RO must apply the flag's interpretation and, in doubt, refer the matter rather than decide it. The written agreement is required to deal expressly with interpretations, deviations and equivalent solutions.

Class rules are not statutory requirements. An RO cannot satisfy a convention requirement by pointing to compliance with its own rules, and it cannot amend its rules so as to change what a convention demands.

blocks.p: The reason. These are sovereign acts. Exempting a ship, or accepting something different from what a treaty requires, alters the bargain the flag State struck with the other Contracting Governments, and only the party to that bargain can alter it. Delegating survey work is delegating the finding of fact; delegating exemption would be delegating the law.

The practical form of this limitation is worth stating because it is what an engineer actually meets: the RO may recommend, and the Administration decides. A surveyor faced with an arrangement that does not meet the letter of the rule refers it to the flag, with a recommendation, and waits.

blocks.h: 5. Limitation four - independence, and the conflict the scheme is built around

blocks.p: The limitation. The Code requires the organization to be independent, to operate under a code of ethics, and not to engage in activities that could conflict with its independence. In particular it must not certify, as the flag State, a ship or an item it has itself designed, built, supplied, or is engaged to maintain; and its quality management system must be certified by a body accredited independently of the ROs and their associations.

The reason, and it is the structural weakness of the whole arrangement: the organization that surveys the ship is paid by the owner of the ship, and it competes commercially for that owner's business with other societies who also want it. Every independence rule in the Code is an answer to that single fact. The rule that the quality certifier must be independent of the ROs' own association exists because self-certification by the industry would defeat the object entirely.

Two related limits sit under this head. The society's dual capacity is itself a conflict to be managed - one surveyor attending one ship may be acting as class and as the flag State in the same visit, and the two roles have different masters and different consequences. And commercial pressure is a real limitation on what an RO will do: an owner dissatisfied with a society's rigour can change class, which is why oversight by the flag State, and the port State check that operates on the certificates, matter so much.

blocks.h: 6. Limitation five - the RO has no enforcement power

blocks.p: The limitation. An RO is not a policeman. It cannot detain a ship, it cannot prosecute, it cannot impose a penalty, and it cannot compel anybody to do anything. Its powers are those of a certifier: it may refuse to issue a certificate, suspend or withdraw one where its authorization allows, impose conditions and recommendations, and report.

The reason. Detention and prosecution are exercises of state power over persons and property. They belong to the flag Administration in respect of its own ships and to the port State in respect of ships in its ports, and neither is transferable to a commercial company by a contract.

What follows is the RO's reporting duty, and it should be stated as the counterpart of its lack of power. Because the RO cannot act, it must tell somebody who can. It is required to report to the flag State - and its authorization must say so - on matters including withdrawal or suspension of class, conditions the ship has not met, and deficiencies found; and it is required to co-operate with port State authorities in rectifying reported deficiencies. A failure to report is therefore a compliance failure and not merely poor service, because the reporting duty is what makes a body without enforcement power useful to a flag State at all.

blocks.h: 7. Limitation six - practical and jurisdictional limits

blocks.p: Collect the remaining limits, each with its reason, because they are separately markable and candidates rarely reach them.

ul: A survey is a sample at a moment in time. A surveyor sees the ship on one day, in one condition, in one port, and much of her is inaccessible. He certifies compliance as found at survey; he does not guarantee her condition for the certificate's whole validity. The reason is physical, not legal - and it is why the master's and Chief Engineer's obligation to maintain the ship between surveys is not displaced by the certificate.
The RO depends on the information it is given. Plan approval rests on the drawings submitted, survey on access provided and records produced. It has no investigatory powers to compel disclosure.
Recognition is not authorization and neither is universal: an organization recognized by twenty flags is an RO only for those twenty and only within each one's scope.

Subcontracting is constrained. Statutory work is performed by the RO's own exclusive surveyors under its control, and the Code regulates the control of subcontractors and service suppliers; an RO cannot simply hire out a statutory survey.
Some services are reserved to the Administration and are not delegable at all - see the closing part of section 8.
The RO cannot bind the flag State in its relations with other Governments, and it has no standing to answer to a port State or a coastal State for the flag's compliance.

blocks.h: 8. The statutory services undertaken on behalf of the Administration

blocks.p: Now the second limb. Note first the legal foundation, because the examiner will look for it: delegation is not a general power but rests on specific enabling provisions in the instruments themselves - SOLAS regulation I/6, Load Lines article 13, MARPOL Annex I regulation 6 and Annex II regulation 8, and Tonnage Convention article 6 - each of which permits the Administration to entrust surveys and inspections to nominated surveyors or recognized organizations.
What a classification body typically performs and issues on the Administration's behalf, by instrument:

blocks.p: Now the discriminating part of this limb - what a classification body does not do on the Administration's behalf, because knowing the boundary is worth more than lengthening the list.

ul: Registration of the ship, and issue of the Certificate of Registry. An act of the registry, not a technical service.
The Minimum Safe Manning Document, which is a determination by the Administration of what manning the ship needs.
Seafarer certification under STCW - certificates of competency, endorsements and their recognition are the Administration's.
Exemption Certificates and the acceptance of equivalents, for the reasons in section 4.

The Declaration of Maritime Labour Compliance Part I, which states the flag State's own national requirements - the RO may certify Part II, the shipowner's measures, but only the flag can declare its own law.

Insurance and financial-security certificates under CLC, the Bunkers Convention and the Nairobi Wreck Removal Convention, which are issued by the State on evidence of insurance and are not technical surveys at all.
Casualty investigation under the Casualty Investigation Code, which is a flag State function that must be independent of certification.
Detention, prosecution and penalty - for the reasons in section 6.

And, at the other end of the boundary, class survey and condition of class are the society's OWN work, not statutory work done for anybody. They are the first thing candidates put in this list and they do not belong in it.

blocks.p: Add one honest qualification, because it is true and it is a mark: exactly which of these an Administration delegates is that Administration's choice. Some flags delegate almost everything; others retain ISM, ISPS or MLC certification. The list above is what is commonly delegated, and the authoritative answer for any ship is the flag State's own instrument of authorization and the list it has deposited with the Secretary-General.

Close on the proposition that ties both limbs together: a Recognized Organization does the flag State's work, with the flag State's authority, within limits the flag State has written down - and every limitation on it exists because the certificate it issues carries somebody else's name.

The stem asks for limitations WITH REASONS and then for a list. That word 'reasons' is the whole design of this answer: each limitation is given as a proposition and then justified, because a bare list of limitations answers half of what was asked. Sections 2 to 7 therefore all follow the same shape - the limitation, the reason, the practical consequence - which also gives the candidate a template he can apply to a limitation he thought of himself.

Section 1 does the load-bearing work. Once the two hats are separated - class under the society's own rules for the owner, statutory under convention for the flag State - every limitation follows from the fact that the second hat is borrowed. A candidate who does not draw that distinction has no way to explain why any of the limits exist, and usually ends up listing them as arbitrary rules.

The table in section 8 is the answer to the second limb, but the bulleted list AFTER it is what separates a strong answer. Anyone can lengthen a certificate list; knowing that the Minimum Safe Manning Document, DMLC Part I, exemptions and CLC certificates are NOT delegated - and that condition of class is not statutory work at all - shows the examiner that the boundary is understood rather than the list memorised.

ul: Answering the RO Code question instead of this one. The corpus is full of questions asking what an RO is and how it is monitored; this examiner asks for LIMITATIONS and for a SERVICES LIST. Do not deliver a prepared RO Code answer.
Giving limitations with no reasons. The stem says 'highlighting them with reasons' and half the marks are in the justification.
Putting class survey, condition of class and class notations in the statutory services list. They are the society's own work under its own rules, not services performed for the Administration.
Saying the Administration delegates its responsibility. It delegates the function. This is the single proposition the examiner most wants to see.
Claiming an RO can grant exemptions or accept equivalents. Both are the Administration's, and this is the sharpest limitation of all.
Saying an RO can detain a ship. It cannot. It can refuse, suspend or withdraw a certificate and it must report.
Treating recognition and authorization as one act, or treating an authorization as universal. It is flag by flag and function by function.
Importing the 33rd Assembly resolution numbers. See the traps.

The Assembly obligations list at this sitting is A.1157(32), not A.1187(33). A.1187(33) was adopted 6 December 2023, four months AFTER this paper, and it revoked A.1157(32). Almost every piece of circulating material is written for a later sitting and carries the wrong number here.
The ISM implementation guidelines at this sitting are A.1118(30) of 2017, not A.1188(33). Same boundary, same date, same trap.
Exemptions and equivalents are the Administration's alone. Expect 'the arrangement does not meet the rule but is just as good - can your surveyor accept it?' No. He recommends; the flag decides.

The RO cannot detain. Expect 'you find the ship unfit - what can you actually do?' Refuse, suspend or withdraw the certificate within your authorization, impose conditions, and report to the flag State; detention is for the Administration or the port State.
The DMLC has two parts and only one of them is delegable. Part I states the flag State's national requirements and is the flag's; Part II is the shipowner's measures and can be certified by the RO.
Class rules are not statutory requirements, and compliance with class does not discharge a convention obligation.

Capability is a legal limit, not a commercial one. The Code forbids a flag State to authorize beyond the RO's capabilities, and an appendix breaks the work into modules so that capability is assessed module by module.

The list of ROs and the conditions of the delegated authority are deposited with the Secretary-General. That is why a port State can know what a certificate represents - and it is the answer to 'how would anyone else find out what your society is allowed to do?'
Your society is my flag's RO. Can your surveyor exempt my ship from a SOLAS requirement?
You find the ship unfit to proceed to sea. What can you actually do about it?
What is the difference between a class survey and a statutory survey, on the same ship, on the same day?
Who issues the Minimum Safe Manning Document, and why not the RO?
Which part of the DMLC can your society certify, and which can it not?
Is a society that is recognized by my flag automatically allowed to survey my gas carrier?
How would a port State officer find out what your society is authorized to do for my flag?
The owner threatens to change class if you write that deficiency. What protects the system from that?
The ship is detained abroad. Who answers to the port State - you or the flag?
Name three services a flag State typically does NOT delegate.

blocks.p: The route is TWO HATS - RESPONSIBILITY - SPECIFIC - CANNOT MAKE LAW - INDEPENDENCE - NO ENFORCEMENT - PRACTICAL - SERVICES. For the six limitations hold RESPONSIBILITY / SCOPE / SOVEREIGNTY / INDEPENDENCE / ENFORCEMENT / PRACTICAL, and for each of them hold the same three-part shape: LIMIT - REASON - CONSEQUENCE. For the services table, run the instruments in order: SOLAS - LOAD LINES - TONNAGE - MARPOL - AFS - BWM - MLC - POLAR. And hold the closing line: every limitation exists because the certificate carries somebody else's name.

ul: Code for Recognized Organizations - resolutions MSC.349(92) (21 June 2013) and MEPC.237(65); mandatory from 1 January 2015; Parts 1 and 2 mandatory, Part 3 recommendatory.
SOLAS regulation XI-1/1 - the provision giving the RO Code mandatory force.
RO Code Part 1 section 4 - the power to delegate, and the prohibition on authorizing beyond capability.
RO Code Part 1 section 5 - deposit with the Secretary-General of the list of ROs and the conditions of delegated authority.
RO Code Part 2 section 8 - the conventional bases for delegation, and the requirement to SPECIFY the functions, including withdrawal and cancellation.
RO Code Part 2 sections 2 and 7 - independence, ethics, and the independently accredited quality system.
RO Code appendices 2 and 3 - the elementary modules of survey and certification work, and the minimum elements of the written agreement.
SOLAS regulation I/6; Load Lines 1966 article 13; MARPOL Annex I regulation 6 and Annex II regulation 8; Tonnage 1969 article 6 - the enabling provisions for delegation.
SOLAS regulations I/4 and I/5 - exemptions and equivalents, powers of the ADMINISTRATION.
III Code, A.1070(28), mandatory 1 January 2016 - Part 2 requires an oversight programme for delegated authority.
A.1157(32) - the non-exhaustive list of obligations, operative at this sitting. A.1118(30) - ISM implementation guidelines, operative at this sitting.

Which services a flag actually delegates is that flag's choice. The table is the set that is COMMONLY delegated, not a statement of any Administration's instrument of authorization. The answer says so in its own text and no flag's authorization schedule is held.

The corpus copy of the RO Code has unverified edition and completeness (its edition and completeness are unverified in our source library). No section number rests on it alone; each is carried from our own verified records for two other sittings on this subject.
A.1157(32) and A.1118(30) are cited by identity only. We hold neither. Their identities, adopting sessions and revocation dates come from our own verified records; no clause of either is quoted.
we hold SOLAS at citation level and not as quotable text. Regulations I/4, I/5, I/6 and XI-1/1 are cited by identity and subject; nothing is quoted.

No certificate validity period is asserted. The stem asks for the services and the certificates, not for validity, and importing validity from an oil-tanker certificate register would import a tanker-specific set.

Three legal levels must be kept apart: the RO Code, an IMO instrument binding through the conventions; the authorization, an act of the flag State's national law; and classification, which is contractual and not statutory at all.

TWO CURRENCY POINTS WERE CHECKED: the MLC 2022 amendments are ADOPTED but NOT IN FORCE at this sitting - they enter into force 23 December 2024 - so nothing in the MLC row depends on them; and the Hong Kong Convention is NOT in force at this sitting (26 June 2025), so no ship recycling certificate appears in the table at all.
