questions.understand_first: A flag State promises the rest of the world that its ships meet the international rules, and then has to make that good on ships scattered across the planet that hardly ever come home. Almost no administration has surveyors everywhere its ships trade, so it hires organisations that already do - the classification societies, which have a global surveying network built for their own commercial work. And that is the point to hold on to: the society is doing somebody else's job, with somebody else's authority, and the certificate it hands over has somebody else's name on it. Every limit on what it may do follows from that one sentence. It cannot take on the responsibility, because the promise was made between governments and a government cannot discharge a promise by hiring a contractor. It cannot decide for itself what it is allowed to do, because the permission was written down job by job by the State that gave it. It cannot let a ship off a requirement or accept something different instead, because changing the rules is an act of the State that agreed them - the surveyor can recommend, but only the flag can decide. It cannot detain anybody, because seizing property is a power of government, not of a company; all it can do is refuse the certificate and tell the flag. And underneath all of it sits an uncomfortable fact the rules are mostly built around: the organisation doing the checking is paid by the owner being checked, and can be replaced by him. Notice too that the same society is wearing two hats. When it surveys under its own rules for the owner, that is its own private business and nothing to do with any government. When it surveys under a convention for the flag, it is borrowing public authority. The same surveyor may swap between the two in a single afternoon, and telling the two apart is most of this question.

quick_revision.critical_regulation: RO Code Part 2 section 8 - the conventional bases for delegation and the requirement that the authorization SPECIFY the functions conferred. If you remember one thing, remember the word specify: it is what makes every other limitation enforceable, because a scope that was written down function by function can be narrowed, suspended or withdrawn function by function.
quick_revision.major_trap: Citing A.1187(33) for the obligations list or A.1188(33) for the ISM implementation guidelines. Both were adopted 6 December 2023, four months after this sitting, and each revoked its 32nd or 30th Assembly predecessor. The operative instruments here are A.1157(32) and A.1118(30). Almost all circulating material is written for a later sitting and carries the wrong numbers.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the RO limitations question.
retrieval_cards.answer: 1 the two hats - class versus statutory; 2 responsibility is not delegated; 3 the authority is specific, never general; 4 the RO cannot make, waive or dispense with the law; 5 independence and the built-in conflict; 6 no enforcement power; 7 practical and jurisdictional limits; 8 the statutory services delegated, and the ones that are not. Every limitation is given as LIMIT - REASON - CONSEQUENCE, because the stem asks for reasons.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What are the two hats a classification society wears, and why does it matter?
retrieval_cards.answer: Classification is its own work, under its own rules, for the owner who pays it, by contract - class survey, notations and condition of class belong here. Statutory work is the flag State's work, under convention and national law, done only because the Administration delegated it, and the certificates carry the flag State's name. Every limitation on an RO follows from the statutory hat being borrowed rather than owned.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Can a Recognized Organization exempt a ship from a convention requirement, or accept an equivalent?
retrieval_cards.answer: No. Both are powers of the Administration, and the Exemption Certificate is the Administration's to issue. The reason is that they are sovereign acts: they alter the bargain the flag State struck with the other Contracting Governments, and only a party to that bargain can alter it. Delegating survey delegates the finding of fact; delegating exemption would delegate the law. The RO recommends and refers; the flag decides.

retrieval_cards.prompt: You are the RO surveyor and the ship is unfit to proceed to sea. What can you actually do?
retrieval_cards.answer: Refuse to issue, or suspend or withdraw, the certificate to the extent your authorization allows; impose conditions and recommendations; and report to the flag State. You cannot detain her, prosecute anyone or impose a penalty - those are exercises of state power belonging to the flag Administration and the port State, and are not transferable by contract. Because you cannot act, the reporting duty is what makes you useful.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why must an authorization SPECIFY the functions conferred?
retrieval_cards.answer: For three reasons. Capability - the Code forbids a flag State to authorize beyond an RO's capabilities, and capability is assessed by elementary module. Transparency - the flag deposits the list of its ROs and the conditions of delegated authority with the Secretary-General, so a port State knows what a certificate represents. And controllability - a specified scope can be narrowed by ship type, convention or function as easily as suspended or withdrawn.

retrieval_cards.prompt: On what provisions does a flag State's power to delegate statutory work rest?
retrieval_cards.answer: SOLAS regulation I/6, Load Lines 1966 article 13, MARPOL Annex I regulation 6, MARPOL Annex II regulation 8, and Tonnage Convention 1969 article 6 - each permitting the Administration to entrust surveys and inspections to nominated surveyors or recognized organizations. The RO Code itself is made mandatory through SOLAS regulation XI-1/1 and the corresponding MARPOL and Load Line Protocol amendments.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Name statutory services a flag State typically does NOT delegate.
retrieval_cards.answer: Registration of the ship and the Certificate of Registry; the Minimum Safe Manning Document; STCW seafarer certification and recognition; exemptions, Exemption Certificates and the acceptance of equivalents; DMLC Part I, which states the flag's own national requirements; CLC, Bunkers and wreck-removal financial security certificates; casualty investigation; and detention, prosecution and penalty. Class survey and condition of class are not statutory services at all.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which Assembly resolutions are operative at an August 2023 sitting for the obligations list and the ISM guidelines?
retrieval_cards.answer: A.1157(32) for the non-exhaustive list of obligations, and A.1118(30) of 2017 for the Guidelines on implementation of the ISM Code by Administrations. NOT A.1187(33) and A.1188(33) - both adopted 6 December 2023, four months after this sitting, each revoking its predecessor. Circulating material written for 2024 or later sittings carries the later numbers and is wrong here.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is the structural conflict the RO Code's independence rules answer?
retrieval_cards.answer: The organization surveying the ship is paid by the owner of the ship, and competes commercially with other societies for that owner's business - an owner dissatisfied with a society's rigour can change class. The Code answers with independence requirements, a code of ethics, a prohibition on certifying what the organization designed, supplied or maintains, and a quality system certified by a body accredited independently of the ROs and their own associations.

decomposition_gate.question_intent: Two tasks separated by a printed full stop, and the examiner is testing the BOUNDARY of delegated authority rather than knowledge of the RO Code. The first task is analytical and asks for reasons, not a list; the second is a register. The discriminator is the first: the corpus shows this examiner's colleagues asking repeatedly what an RO is and how it is monitored, and a candidate with a prepared RO Code answer will deliver it and score badly, because limitations are the one aspect that prepared answer does not contain. The second discriminator is inside the register - whether the candidate knows what is NOT delegated, and whether he keeps class work out of a statutory list.
decomposition_gate.mark_allocation: Sixteen marks with no printed split. The stem sets two tasks of comparable weight - 'state the limitations highlighting them with reasons' and 'list the statutory services' - and the phrase 'with reasons' roughly doubles the work in the first. The answer allots one framing section, six sections to the limitations, and one substantial section carrying both the register and the non-delegable boundary. That gives the limitations more space than the services, which is deliberate: a list can be written quickly and a reasoned limitation cannot.
decomposition_gate.examiner_expectation: That class and statutory work are separated before anything else. That each limitation carries its reason, because the stem says so. That the responsibility-versus-function proposition appears, and that exemptions and equivalents are correctly placed with the Administration. That the RO's lack of enforcement power is stated together with its reporting duty. That the services register is organised by instrument and names real certificates. And that the answer knows what is not delegable - which is the part that shows the boundary is understood rather than the list memorised.
decomposition_gate.primary_source_plan: Carry the RO Code spine from the MIW verification records for QP2309 Q2 and QP2408 Q1, which established Part 1 sections 4 and 5, Part 2 sections 2, 7 and 8 and appendices 2 and 3 against the Code text; corroborate against the corpus copy but rest no section number on it alone, its edition being unverified (RQ-25). Take the delegating provisions from Part 2 section 8. Build the services register from the certificate regime instrument by instrument, taking the structure but not the tanker-specific content or the validity periods from QP2406 Q1. Take the class-versus-statutory boundary from QP2312 Q8 and QP2509 Q9. Deliberately NOT planned: any quotation of SOLAS or RO Code text; any certificate validity; any flag's actual authorization schedule.
decomposition_gate.freshness_risk: MEDIUM - The RO Code, the enabling provisions and the certificate regime are all stable and need no reversal. The moving parts are two 33rd Assembly instruments: A.1187(33) and A.1188(33) were both adopted 6 December 2023, four months after this sitting, and each revoked the instrument that is operative here. They are small edits with a large consequence, because they are exactly the numbers a reviewer moving between papers would 'correct' forward. Two further currency points were checked and cleared: the MLC 2022 amendments are not in force at this sitting, and the Hong Kong Convention is not in force, so no recycling certificate enters the table.
decomposition_gate.jurisdiction_risk: HIGH, and it is the real subject of the question. Three levels must be kept apart: the RO Code, an IMO instrument binding through the conventions that refer to it; the authorization, which is an act of the flag State's national law and differs from flag to flag; and classification, which is contractual and not statutory at all. An answer that treats class rules or an IACS resolution as part of the statutory chain, or that presents a common delegation practice as a legal requirement, has the levels wrong. Where India is concerned the Administration is the Directorate General of Shipping under the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958.
decomposition_gate.technical_ambiguities: The printed stem's first sentence has no main verb for its first clause - 'Classification societies as Recognized Organisations (RO) and play an important role' does not parse - and the intended sense is 'act as Recognized Organisations and play an important role'. The answer answers the intended sense and the printed text is preserved unaltered. 'Limitations' is itself open: it could mean legal limits on authority, practical limits on what a survey can achieve, or the shortcomings of the delegation model as a policy. The answer covers all three rather than choosing, because each is separately markable, and orders them from the constitutional to the practical. 'Statutory services' is read as the services performed on the Administration's behalf, which excludes class work - the exclusion is stated rather than assumed.
decomposition_gate.target_answer_shape: Eight numbered sections. A short framing section with a two-item contrast. Six limitation sections, each in the same LIMIT - REASON - CONSEQUENCE shape so the reasons the stem asks for are visibly delivered and countable. A final section carrying the enabling provisions in prose, the services register as a rendered THREE-COLUMN TABLE by instrument, a bulleted list of what is NOT delegated, an honest qualification that delegation is the flag's choice, and a closing single-sentence proposition.

questions.text_verbatim: A. Describe the stages during which the power produced by the main engine of the ship is transformed into the effective power. B). Discuss the essential sea trial manoeuvres (navigation trials) conducted and typical objectives of each test.

blocks.h: 1. The power chain, as one idea

blocks.p: Before naming any stage, state the idea, because the stem asks for a transformation and a list of six powers is not one. Power is developed in the cylinder and is then reduced at every interface between there and the water. Each named power is the previous one less the loss at one interface, and the ratio between two adjacent powers is an efficiency. The last of them, effective power, is not power delivered to anything at all - it is the power that would be needed simply to tow the ship at that speed.
The chain, in order:
Indicated power → Brake power → Shaft power → Delivered power → Thrust power → Effective power.

Two remarks that repay a sentence each. Only three of these are directly measurable on a ship - indicated, brake and shaft power - and the rest are computed or inferred, which is why the propulsive coefficient is quoted rather than read off a gauge. And the losses are not all of the same kind: the first two are mechanical friction, and the last two are hydrodynamic and are far the largest.

blocks.h: 2. Indicated power - what the engine develops in the cylinder

blocks.p: Indicated power is the power developed by the gas on the piston, before anything is lost to friction. It is obtained from the indicator diagram - the pressure-volume diagram taken from the cylinder - and in the classical form is calculated from the mean indicated pressure, the piston area, the stroke and the number of working strokes per unit time, summed over all cylinders.

ul: Measured by mechanical indicator or, on a modern engine, by an electronic pressure transducer producing the same diagram continuously.

What it is used for: it is the only power that can be attributed to one cylinder, so it is the basis of load balancing between units and of combustion diagnosis. It is also the datum against which every later loss is expressed.

Where the loss begins: everything between the gas force on the piston and the flywheel - piston rings, gudgeon pin, crosshead, main and crankpin bearings, camshaft and valve gear drive, and the engine-driven pumps.

blocks.p: Brake power is the power actually available at the engine output coupling or flywheel - the power the engine delivers after its own friction and its own auxiliaries have been paid for. The name is historical: it was measured by a brake absorbing the output on a test bed.
The ratio joining the first two stages is the mechanical efficiency:

ul: Mechanical efficiency = brake power ÷ indicated power, and it is typically of the order of 0.85 to 0.92, being higher on a large slow-speed crosshead engine than on a medium-speed trunk-piston one.

The difference between the two is the friction power, which is very nearly constant with load. That has a practical consequence worth stating: mechanical efficiency falls sharply at low load, because a nearly constant friction loss is being taken from a much smaller indicated power - which is part of why prolonged low-load running is inefficient.
Measured on the test bed against a dynamometer; on board it is inferred rather than measured directly.

blocks.h: 4. Shaft power and delivered power - the transmission

blocks.p: Shaft power is the power transmitted along the shafting, measured where the torsionmeter is fitted - normally on the intermediate shaft in the shaft tunnel. It is obtained from the torque and the rotational speed, the torque being derived from the measured twist of a known length of shaft of known stiffness.

Delivered power is the power actually delivered to the propeller, at the propeller itself. It is shaft power less the losses in the bearings between the measuring point and the propeller - principally the stern tube bearing and the aftermost plummer blocks, and, where they lie between, the thrust block and any gearbox.

ul: The transmission or shafting efficiency is of the order of 0.97 to 0.99 for a direct-coupled diesel installation with a short shaft, and lower where a gearbox is interposed, a gearbox costing perhaps a further 2 to 3 per cent.

Note the practical point about the measuring position: the further forward the torsionmeter, the more bearing loss lies between it and the propeller. The difference between shaft power and delivered power depends on where you measured, not only on what the ship is.
Where no torsionmeter is fitted, shaft power is inferred from brake power and an assumed transmission efficiency - which is an assumption, and should be stated as one.

blocks.h: 5. Thrust power and effective power - the propeller and the hull

blocks.p: This is where the two largest losses occur and where candidates most often stop too early.

Thrust power is the useful power the propeller produces in the water: thrust multiplied by the speed of advance - and the speed of advance is not the ship's speed. The propeller works in the hull's wake, in water that is already being dragged along with the ship, so it advances through that water more slowly than the ship advances through the sea. The difference is described by the wake fraction.

Effective power is the power required to tow the hull at that speed against her total resistance: total resistance multiplied by ship speed. It is what the naval architect predicts from the model tank, and it is the true output of the whole installation.
Two separate effects sit between thrust power and effective power, and naming both is what completes the answer:

ul: Thrust deduction. The propeller working close astern of the hull lowers the pressure over the after body and so increases the hull's resistance. The thrust the propeller must produce is therefore greater than the resistance being overcome. This is described by the thrust deduction fraction.
Wake. The hull drags water with it, so the propeller advances into a slower stream, described by the wake fraction.

Together these two give the hull efficiency, which is the ratio of effective power to thrust power and is (1 minus the thrust deduction fraction) divided by (1 minus the wake fraction). On a conventional single-screw ship it is commonly greater than 1 - which surprises candidates and is worth explaining: it is not a violation of anything, but a statement that the propeller benefits more from working in the ship's own wake than it loses by increasing her resistance.

blocks.h: 6. The efficiencies that join the stages

blocks.p: Set the ratios out as a chain, because it makes the whole answer countable and shows where every watt went.

ul: Mechanical efficiency = brake ÷ indicated. Engine friction. Typically 0.85 to 0.92.
Transmission (shafting) efficiency = delivered ÷ brake. Bearings, thrust block, gearing. Typically 0.97 to 0.99 direct-coupled.

Propeller open-water efficiency = the propeller's efficiency measured alone in undisturbed water. Typically 0.60 to 0.70 for a conventional fixed-pitch propeller, and it is by far the largest single loss in the chain.
Relative rotative efficiency = the correction between the propeller's efficiency behind the hull and in open water, the wake being non-uniform. Close to 1, commonly 0.95 to 1.05.
Hull efficiency = effective ÷ thrust = (1 − t) ÷ (1 − w). Often greater than 1 on a single-screw ship.
Quasi-propulsive coefficient = effective ÷ delivered = hull × open-water × relative rotative. Typically 0.65 to 0.75.
Propulsive coefficient = effective ÷ brake (or effective ÷ shaft, if that is what is stated - and it should be stated). Typically 0.60 to 0.72.

blocks.p: Finish limb A with the proposition the chain exists to make: of the power developed in the cylinder, roughly two thirds reaches the water as useful towing power on a good conventional ship, and the great majority of what is lost is lost at the propeller and the hull, not in the machinery. That is why Q3's rudder devices and hull maintenance matter more to fuel consumption than any plausible improvement in mechanical efficiency.

blocks.h: 7. Sea trials - what a navigation trial is for, and the conditions it must be run in

blocks.p: Turning to limb B. A navigation or manoeuvring trial is conducted to demonstrate that the completed ship handles as she was designed to, to satisfy the international manoeuvring standard, and to produce the data that goes into the wheelhouse poster and the manoeuvring booklet so that the master knows what his ship will actually do. It is quite separate from the machinery trials, which prove the plant.

The governing instrument is the IMO Standards for Ship Manoeuvrability, resolution MSC.137(76), adopted 4 December 2002, which applies to ships of 100 m in length and over and to all chemical tankers and gas carriers regardless of length, constructed on or after 1 January 2004. Its explanatory notes set out the procedures.
The trial conditions are part of the answer, not a preamble. A manoeuvring result obtained in the wrong water or the wrong loading cannot be compared with the criterion it is being tested against.

ol: Deep, unrestricted water. Shallow water and bank effects change turning and stopping behaviour completely.
Calm environment - low wind and sea, and negligible current. Trials are run on reciprocal headings so that any residual current cancels.

Full load, even keel, or as near as practicable; where the ship cannot be trialled loaded - as with most tankers and bulk carriers, delivered in ballast - the trial is run in the ballast condition and the results are corrected or predicted to the loaded condition, and the correction is recorded.
Steady approach at the test speed and steady conditions throughout the measured run, with the engine at the specified setting.

blocks.h: 8. The essential manoeuvres, and the objective of each

blocks.p: Give the objective first and the procedure second, since the stem asks for objectives.

ul: Speed and power trial (progressive speed trial). Objective: to establish the relationship between shaft power, propeller revolutions and ship speed, to demonstrate the contract speed, and - on a modern newbuilding - to provide the measurement from which the ship's attained energy efficiency design index is verified. Procedure: runs at several engine settings on reciprocal headings over a measured distance, with the results corrected for wind, sea, current, water depth and displacement. This trial also fixes the datum against which the ship's whole service life is later judged - trial day is the best she will ever perform.

Turning circle test. Objective: to establish turning ability, and to measure the distances the master needs for collision avoidance and for planning a turn in confined water. Procedure: from a steady approach at test speed, the rudder is put over to the maximum design angle - normally 35 degrees - and held until the ship has turned at least 360 degrees, to port and to starboard. Measured: advance, transfer, tactical diameter, steady turning diameter, drift angle and the speed loss in the turn, which is substantial and surprises people. Criteria: the standard requires advance not to exceed 4.5 ship lengths and tactical diameter not to exceed 5 ship lengths.

Zig-zag test. Objective: to measure yaw-checking and course-keeping ability - how quickly the ship responds to helm and, more importantly, how quickly the swing can be stopped once she has started. This is the trial that matters most for course keeping in traffic. Procedure: the 10°/10° test - rudder to 10 degrees, held until the heading has changed 10 degrees, then reversed to 10 degrees the other way, and so on - and the 20°/20° test similarly. Measured: the first and second overshoot angles, and the initial turning time. Criteria: the standard sets limits on the overshoot angles that depend on the ratio of ship length to speed, recognising that a long slow ship must be allowed more overshoot than a short fast one; and it sets a separate limit for the 20°/20° first overshoot.

Initial turning test. Objective: to measure the promptness of the ship's initial response to helm, separately from her eventual turning circle. Procedure: rudder to 10 degrees from a steady approach. Criterion: the ship should not have travelled more than 2.5 ship lengths by the time her heading has changed by 10 degrees.

Stopping test (crash stop). Objective: to establish the distance and time to bring the ship to rest from full ahead using full astern power - the emergency the master will be asked about at every inquiry. Procedure: from full ahead at test speed, the engine is ordered full astern and held until the ship is stopped through the water. Measured: track reach, head reach, and the time; and note that the ship's heading is not controllable during the manoeuvre once steerage way is lost, which is itself a finding the master must know. Criterion: the standard requires the track reach not to exceed 15 ship lengths, with provision for the Administration to accept more for ships of large displacement where 15 is impracticable.

Spiral test - direct, and reverse. Objective: to establish whether the ship is directionally (course) stable, and if she is not, how unstable. Procedure: in the direct spiral, the rudder is set at a series of decreasing angles from one side through zero to the other, the steady rate of turn being recorded at each; in the reverse spiral, the ship is held at a series of rates of turn and the rudder angle required is recorded, which is quicker and works on an unstable ship. Result: a course-unstable ship produces a hysteresis loop around zero rudder, and the width of the loop measures the instability - meaning that within that band of rudder angles the ship will turn without being told to.

Pull-out test. Objective: a quick check of the same property. Procedure: after a steady turn, the rudder is returned to midships and the rate of turn recorded. Result: on a stable ship the rate of turn decays to zero; on an unstable ship a residual rate of turn persists, and the difference between the residual rates to port and to starboard indicates the size of the instability.

Astern and low-speed manoeuvring trials. Objective: to establish how the ship behaves going astern and at manoeuvring speeds, where the rudder is largely ineffective and transverse thrust dominates - which is what the master actually experiences berthing. Includes engine crash-astern and crash-ahead response times, steering gear tests including changeover to the second power unit and to emergency steering, and bow thruster performance where fitted.
Man-overboard and confined-water manoeuvres, where the trial programme includes them. Objective: to establish and record a recovery turn that will actually work in this ship.

blocks.p: Two closing points that turn a description into an answer. The results are not an academic record. They are reduced into the wheelhouse poster, the pilot card and the manoeuvring booklet, and their whole purpose is that the master and the pilot can predict the ship before they need to. And the manoeuvring performance is measured in ship lengths rather than in metres for a reason: it makes the criteria comparable between a coaster and a very large crude carrier, and it is why a large ship's alarming absolute stopping distance may still comfortably satisfy the standard.

End on the proposition that joins the two limbs: limb A accounts for where the engine's power goes, and limb B measures what the ship does with what is left. The trial is where the naval architect's prediction and the engineer's plant are checked against the sea for the first and best time.

Limb A is a chain and the marks are in the chain, not in the six nouns. The structure states the transformation in one sentence before naming any stage, then takes the stages in order, and then collects the efficiencies into a single list in section 6 - which is where a marker can count them. A candidate who writes six definitions in isolation has described the stages without describing the transformation the stem asked about.

Giving WHERE each power is measured is the discriminating detail in limb A. Only indicated, brake and shaft power are directly measurable on a ship; delivered, thrust and effective power are computed. That single observation explains why the propulsive coefficient is quoted from the trial rather than read from an instrument, and why the position of the torsionmeter changes the answer.

In limb B the objective is given before the procedure for every manoeuvre, because the stem asks for the typical objectives of each test and candidates reliably describe procedures instead. The trial CONDITIONS are given their own numbered section for the same reason: a result obtained in shallow water or the wrong loading cannot be compared with the criterion, and saying so shows the examiner that the standard is understood rather than listed.

ul: Stopping the chain at delivered power. The stem asks for the transformation into EFFECTIVE power, and the propeller and hull stages are where most of the loss is.
Confusing ship speed with speed of advance. Thrust power uses the speed of advance, which is lower because the propeller works in the hull's wake.

Omitting thrust deduction, or confusing it with wake. Wake is the propeller seeing slower water; thrust deduction is the propeller increasing the hull's resistance. Both are needed to get hull efficiency.
Saying hull efficiency cannot exceed 1. On a conventional single-screw ship it commonly does, and being able to explain why is worth a mark.
Quoting the propulsive coefficient without saying whether it is against brake or shaft power. Say which.
Describing sea trial procedures without giving the objectives. The stem asks for the objectives explicitly.
Forgetting the trial conditions - deep unrestricted water, calm, full load, reciprocal headings.
Running the turning circle one way only. It is done to port AND starboard, because a single-screw ship is not symmetrical.
Treating the zig-zag as a turning test. It measures yaw checking and course keeping - how the swing is STOPPED.
Mechanical efficiency falls at low load, because friction power is nearly constant while indicated power is not. Expect this as a follow-up on slow steaming.
The difference between shaft power and delivered power depends on where the torsionmeter is. The further forward it is, the more bearing loss lies between it and the propeller.

Hull efficiency = (1 − t) ÷ (1 − w), and it is usually greater than unity on a single-screw ship. The examiner will ask how a hull can have an efficiency above 100 per cent. It is a ratio of two powers, not a conversion.

Open-water propeller efficiency is the largest single loss in the chain - typically 0.60 to 0.70. Machinery improvements cannot compete with it, which is the whole justification for energy saving devices.

The manoeuvring criteria are expressed in SHIP LENGTHS, not metres, so that a coaster and a VLCC are judged on the same scale. A very large ship's frightening absolute stopping distance may satisfy the standard comfortably.
The 10°/10° zig-zag overshoot limits depend on the ratio of length to speed. A long slow ship is allowed more overshoot than a short fast one - the criterion is not a single number.
Heading is not controllable in a crash stop once steerage way is lost. The ship will usually swing, and which way she swings depends on her propeller.

Trials are usually run in ballast on tankers and bulk carriers and the results corrected or predicted to the loaded condition. Expect to be asked what you would do about that, and record the correction.
The reverse spiral works on a course-unstable ship and the direct spiral does not - which is the reason the reverse spiral exists.
Name the powers in order from the cylinder to the water, and tell me which of them you can actually measure.
What is the difference between ship speed and speed of advance, and which one does thrust power use?
How can hull efficiency be greater than one?
Where is the biggest loss in the whole chain, and what does that tell you about where to spend money?
Your torsionmeter reads shaft power. How do you get delivered power?
Why does mechanical efficiency get worse when you slow steam?
What does a zig-zag test tell you that a turning circle does not?
The ship was trialled in ballast. Is her manoeuvring booklet any use to you loaded?
You order full astern from full ahead. Which way will she go, and can you steer her?
What is a hysteresis loop in a spiral test, and what does its width mean for the man on the wheel?

blocks.p: For limb A hold the chain as six words in order: INDICATED - BRAKE - SHAFT - DELIVERED - THRUST - EFFECTIVE, and between them five efficiencies: MECHANICAL - TRANSMISSION - OPEN WATER - RELATIVE ROTATIVE - HULL. Remember that only the first three powers are measurable. For limb B hold the conditions as DEEP - CALM - LOADED - STEADY, and the manoeuvres as SPEED - TURNING - ZIG-ZAG - INITIAL TURN - STOPPING - SPIRAL - PULL-OUT - ASTERN. For the criteria hold three numbers in ship lengths: 4.5 advance, 5 tactical diameter, 15 track reach, and 2.5 for initial turning.

ul: IMO Standards for Ship Manoeuvrability, resolution MSC.137(76), adopted 4 December 2002 - ships of 100 m and over and all chemical tankers and gas carriers regardless of length, constructed on or after 1 January 2004.

Criteria under that standard - advance not more than 4.5 L; tactical diameter not more than 5 L; initial turning within 2.5 L for a 10-degree heading change; stopping track reach not more than 15 L, with provision for more on large displacement ships; and zig-zag overshoot limits expressed against the length-to-speed ratio.
The explanatory notes to that standard - the trial procedures and the treatment of trials in non-standard conditions.
SOLAS chapter V - the carriage of manoeuvring information on board, which is what the trial results become.
MARPOL Annex VI chapter 4 as revised by MEPC.328(76) - the speed trial as the measurement underlying the attained design index on a newbuilding. Cited as purpose only; no formula is asserted.
International towing tank practice for the conduct and correction of a speed and power trial. Cited generically; no procedure number or edition is held.

No efficiency figure here applies to a particular ship. Every value is a typical range for a conventional single-screw motor ship, and values differ with machinery type, shafting arrangement, hull form and loading.

We hold no copy of MSC.137(76) or of its explanatory notes. Application, conditions and criteria are cited by identity and by criterion from our own verified records. No paragraph is quoted, and the zig-zag overshoot limits are stated as depending on the length-to-speed ratio rather than reproduced as a table, because the table is not held.
No towing tank recommended procedure is held or cited by number or edition. Speed-trial conduct and correction are described by principle.

No shipyard or class trial programme is held. The set described is the standard manoeuvring set; an actual programme is agreed between builder, owner and society and contains items that are not manoeuvring trials at all.

The paper that prints the nearest version of this stem has not yet completed our own review, so its answer is deliberately not relied on. The power chain is re-derived here from principle and every relationship stated is checkable from its own definition.

notes: NO REVERSAL IS REQUIRED AND THE REASON IS TWOFOLD. The wording donor QP2303-Q5 is FIVE MONTHS EARLIER in the same year, so it cannot import later law; and the subject is naval architecture and a manoeuvring standard adopted in 2002, neither of which moves between sittings.

THE PROVENANCE POINT MATTERS MORE THAN THE TEMPORAL ONE ON THIS QUESTION. QP2303 is pushed but NOT INTEGRATED on main, so its ANSWER carries no governed authority. The power chain is therefore re-derived here from principle rather than carried, and QP2303-Q5 is used only to establish the printed stem and the two-word wording delta. No claim in this answer rests on an unreviewed paper.

MSC.137(76) IS STABLE ACROSS THE WHOLE CORPUS. Adopted 4 December 2002, applicable to ships constructed on or after 1 January 2004, and unamended in any way that changes the trials or the criteria. It is as true in August 2023 as at any other sitting in the 2021-2026 range.

THE ONE CURRENCY POINT IS THE EEDI CONTEXT AND IT IS STATED AT THIS SITTING'S POSITION. MARPOL Annex VI as revised by MEPC.328(76) entered into force 1 November 2022 from its own operative paragraph 3 - the corpus register's 2023-11-01 (correction request TSCR-3) is not consumed - and the speed trial is identified as the measurement underlying the attained design index. No index value, reduction factor or correction formula is asserted, so nothing here depends on the phase or reduction-factor state at any date.
NO ASSEMBLY MATERIAL IS ENGAGED. The 33rd Assembly set (6 December 2023) and the 34th (3 December 2025) are both future and neither touches this question.

NOTHING IN THE ANSWER RESTS ON A MEASUREMENT TECHNIQUE THAT POST-DATES THE SITTING. Electronic cylinder pressure measurement, shaft torsionmeters, satellite positioning for speed trials and reverse spiral testing were all long-established by 2023.
MERCHANT SHIPPING ACT, 1958 governs any Indian aspect; the 2025 Act commenced 15 March 2026. Nothing in this answer engages either.

questions.understand_first: Think of the engine's power leaking away through a series of gates on its journey from the cylinder to the sea. In the cylinder the gas pushes on the piston, and that is the most power that will ever exist - everything after it is less. Some is eaten getting the engine to turn itself: rings, bearings, its own pumps. What survives at the flywheel goes down the shaft, where the bearings and the stern tube take a little more. What arrives at the propeller is then handed to the water, and this is where most of it disappears, because a propeller is a fairly poor machine - it throws water backwards, and the water it throws is spinning as well as moving, which is energy the ship never sees. Right at the end there is a quantity that sounds odd until you see what it is for: the power you would need if you simply towed the ship along at that speed with a rope. That is the real output, because it is the only number that describes moving the hull rather than driving machinery. Two things about the last stage are worth holding, because they are what candidates lose marks on. The propeller is not swimming in clean water - it sits in the hull's wake, in water already being dragged along, so it is moving through that water more slowly than the ship is moving through the sea. And the propeller's own suction pulls back on the stern, so it makes the ship slightly harder to push than she would be if it were not there. The second limb is a different subject entirely. Once the ship is built, nobody actually knows how she will handle - the tank and the computer said one thing, and the sea has the final word. So before she is handed over she is taken out and made to do the things that will matter later: run at speed, turn hard both ways, be swung one way and then checked the other, and stopped from full speed. The point of every one of those is a number the master can rely on when he has thirty seconds to decide, and that is why the results end up on a poster in the wheelhouse rather than in a file.
questions.memory_cue: CHAIN - INDICATED - BRAKE - SHAFT AND DELIVERED - THRUST AND EFFECTIVE - EFFICIENCIES - TRIAL CONDITIONS - MANOEUVRES (1 to 8). Inside step 6 hold MECHANICAL - TRANSMISSION - OPEN WATER - RELATIVE ROTATIVE - HULL. Inside step 7 hold DEEP - CALM - LOADED - STEADY. Inside step 8 hold SPEED - TURNING - ZIG-ZAG - INITIAL TURN - STOPPING - SPIRAL - PULL-OUT - ASTERN.

steps.title: The power chain, as one idea
points: Each named power is the previous one less the loss at one interface; the ratio between two is an efficiency
Indicated - Brake - Shaft - Delivered - Thrust - Effective
Effective power is not delivered to anything: it is the power needed to TOW the ship at that speed
Only indicated, brake and shaft power are directly measurable on a ship
The first losses are mechanical friction; the last two are hydrodynamic and far the largest

steps.title: Indicated power - what the engine develops in the cylinder
points: Power developed by the gas on the piston, before any friction
From the indicator diagram - mean indicated pressure, piston area, stroke, working strokes per unit time, all cylinders
The only power attributable to ONE cylinder, so it is the basis of load balancing and combustion diagnosis
The loss begins at rings, gudgeon pin, crosshead, bearings, valve gear and engine-driven pumps

steps.title: Brake power, and mechanical efficiency
points: Power available at the output coupling or flywheel, after engine friction and engine-driven auxiliaries
Mechanical efficiency = brake / indicated, typically 0.85 to 0.92
Friction power is nearly constant with load, so mechanical efficiency FALLS sharply at low load
Measured on a test bed against a dynamometer; inferred rather than measured on board

steps.title: Shaft power and delivered power - the transmission
points: Shaft power is measured by torsionmeter from torque and revolutions, normally on the intermediate shaft
Delivered power is what actually reaches the propeller, after stern tube, plummer blocks, thrust block and any gearing
Transmission efficiency typically 0.97 to 0.99 direct coupled, lower with a gearbox
The difference depends on WHERE the torsionmeter is, not only on the ship
Without a torsionmeter, shaft power is inferred from brake power and an assumed efficiency - state the assumption

steps.title: Thrust power and effective power - the propeller and the hull
points: Thrust power = thrust x speed of advance, and speed of advance is NOT ship speed
The propeller works in the hull's wake, described by the wake fraction
Effective power = total resistance x ship speed - the power to tow the hull
Thrust deduction: the propeller lowers pressure over the after body and increases the hull's resistance
Hull efficiency = effective / thrust = (1 - t) / (1 - w), commonly GREATER than 1 on a single-screw ship

steps.title: The efficiencies that join the stages
points: Mechanical = brake / indicated, 0.85 to 0.92
Transmission = delivered / brake, 0.97 to 0.99 direct coupled
Propeller open-water efficiency 0.60 to 0.70 - by far the largest single loss
Relative rotative efficiency, close to unity, 0.95 to 1.05
Hull efficiency, often above 1
Quasi-propulsive coefficient = effective / delivered, 0.65 to 0.75; propulsive coefficient = effective / brake, 0.60 to 0.72
Roughly two thirds of cylinder power reaches the water, and most of the loss is at the propeller and hull

steps.title: Sea trials - what a navigation trial is for, and the conditions it must be run in
points: To demonstrate the ship handles as designed, satisfy the manoeuvring standard, and produce the wheelhouse poster and manoeuvring booklet
IMO Standards for Ship Manoeuvrability, MSC.137(76), adopted 4 December 2002
Applies to ships of 100 m and over and all chemical tankers and gas carriers, constructed on or after 1 January 2004
Condition one - deep, unrestricted water
Condition two - calm environment, negligible current, runs on reciprocal headings
Condition three - full load even keel, or trial in ballast with a recorded correction to the loaded condition
Condition four - steady approach and steady conditions through the measured run

steps.title: The essential manoeuvres, and the objective of each
points: Speed and power trial - the power/revolutions/speed relationship, contract speed, and the design index measurement; also the datum for the ship's whole service life
Turning circle both ways - advance, transfer, tactical diameter, drift angle and speed loss; advance not more than 4.5 L, tactical diameter not more than 5 L
Zig-zag 10/10 and 20/20 - yaw checking and course keeping; first and second overshoot angles, limits depending on the length-to-speed ratio
Initial turning - promptness of response; not more than 2.5 L travelled for a 10 degree heading change
Stopping test - track reach, head reach and time; not more than 15 L, and heading is not controllable
Spiral, direct and reverse - directional stability; a hysteresis loop measures the instability, and the reverse spiral works where the direct one cannot
Pull-out - a quick check of the same property by the residual rate of turn
Astern and low-speed trials, steering gear changeover and emergency steering, bow thruster; and man-overboard where programmed
Results become the wheelhouse poster, pilot card and manoeuvring booklet; criteria are in ship lengths so all sizes are judged alike

quick_revision.recall_15s: INDICATED - BRAKE - SHAFT - DELIVERED - THRUST - EFFECTIVE. Joined by mechanical, transmission, open-water, relative rotative and hull efficiencies. Only the first three are measurable. Effective power is the power to tow the ship; thrust power uses speed of advance, not ship speed; hull efficiency is (1−t)/(1−w) and is usually above 1. Trials: deep, calm, loaded, steady, reciprocal headings. Manoeuvres: speed, turning circle both ways, zig-zag 10/10 and 20/20, initial turn, crash stop, spiral, pull-out, astern. Criteria in ship lengths: 4.5 advance, 5 tactical diameter, 2.5 initial turn, 15 track reach.
quick_revision.critical_numbers: Mechanical efficiency 0.85-0.92; transmission 0.97-0.99; open water 0.60-0.70; relative rotative 0.95-1.05; QPC 0.65-0.75; propulsive coefficient 0.60-0.72 - all typical ranges, not values for any ship. Manoeuvring criteria in ship lengths: advance 4.5, tactical diameter 5, initial turning 2.5, stopping track reach 15. MSC.137(76), adopted 4 December 2002, ships of 100 m and over, constructed on or after 1 January 2004.
quick_revision.critical_regulation: IMO Standards for Ship Manoeuvrability, resolution MSC.137(76). If you remember one thing about it, remember that its criteria are expressed in ship lengths and not in metres - which is what allows a coaster and a very large crude carrier to be judged against the same standard, and why a large ship's alarming absolute stopping distance can still comply comfortably.
quick_revision.major_trap: Stopping the power chain at delivered power, or confusing ship speed with speed of advance. Thrust power is thrust times the speed of ADVANCE, which is lower than ship speed because the propeller works in the hull's wake. The related trap is treating wake and thrust deduction as the same thing: wake is the propeller seeing slower water, thrust deduction is the propeller making the hull harder to push, and you need both to reach hull efficiency.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the power transformation and sea trials question.
retrieval_cards.answer: Limb A: 1 the chain as one idea; 2 indicated power; 3 brake power and mechanical efficiency; 4 shaft and delivered power; 5 thrust and effective power; 6 the efficiencies collected. Limb B: 7 what a navigation trial is for and the conditions it must be run in; 8 the essential manoeuvres with the objective of each stated before the procedure.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Name the six powers in order and the five efficiencies between them.
retrieval_cards.answer: Indicated, brake, shaft, delivered, thrust, effective. Between them: mechanical efficiency (brake/indicated), transmission or shafting efficiency (delivered/brake), propeller open-water efficiency, relative rotative efficiency, and hull efficiency (effective/thrust). Quasi-propulsive coefficient is effective over delivered; propulsive coefficient is effective over brake or shaft - say which.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is effective power, and why is it not delivered to anything?
retrieval_cards.answer: Effective power is total resistance multiplied by ship speed - the power that would be needed simply to tow the hull at that speed. It is the true output of the whole installation, and it is not delivered to any component: it is the measure of moving the hull rather than of driving machinery. That is why it is the numerator of both the quasi-propulsive and the propulsive coefficient.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Wake fraction or thrust deduction - what is the difference?
retrieval_cards.answer: Wake is about the water the propeller sees: the hull drags water with it, so the propeller advances through that stream more slowly than the ship advances through the sea, which is why thrust power uses speed of advance. Thrust deduction is about the hull: the propeller lowers the pressure over the after body and so increases the hull's resistance, meaning the thrust required exceeds the resistance overcome. Hull efficiency combines both as (1−t)/(1−w).

retrieval_cards.prompt: How can hull efficiency be greater than one?
retrieval_cards.answer: Because it is a ratio of two powers, not a conversion, and nothing is being created. On a conventional single-screw ship the propeller gains more from working in the ship's own wake - advancing through slower water - than it loses by increasing her resistance through thrust deduction. So (1−t)/(1−w) commonly exceeds unity. It is not a violation of anything.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What conditions must a manoeuvring trial be run in, and why does it matter?
retrieval_cards.answer: Deep unrestricted water, because shallow water and bank effects change turning and stopping completely; a calm environment with negligible current, with runs on reciprocal headings so any residual current cancels; full load on even keel, or trial in ballast with a recorded correction to the loaded condition; and a steady approach with steady conditions through the run. A result obtained outside these conditions cannot be compared with the criterion it is tested against.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What does a zig-zag test tell you that a turning circle does not?
retrieval_cards.answer: Yaw-checking and course-keeping ability - how quickly the swing can be STOPPED once it has started, not how tightly the ship turns. The 10°/10° and 20°/20° tests measure the first and second overshoot angles, and the standard's limits depend on the ratio of ship length to speed, so a long slow ship is allowed more overshoot than a short fast one. It is the trial that matters most for course keeping in traffic.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the manoeuvring criteria and what each measures.
retrieval_cards.answer: Turning ability: advance not more than 4.5 ship lengths and tactical diameter not more than 5. Initial turning: not more than 2.5 lengths travelled by the time heading has changed 10 degrees. Stopping: track reach not more than 15 lengths, with provision for more on ships of large displacement. Yaw checking: overshoot limits in the zig-zag, depending on the length-to-speed ratio. All are in ship lengths so every size is judged alike.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What does a spiral test show, and why is there a reverse version?
retrieval_cards.answer: Whether the ship is directionally stable. The rudder is set at a series of decreasing angles from one side through zero to the other, and the steady rate of turn is recorded at each. A course-unstable ship produces a hysteresis loop around zero rudder, whose width measures the instability - within that band she will turn without being told to. The reverse spiral instead holds set rates of turn and records the rudder needed, which is quicker and works on an unstable ship where the direct spiral does not.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why does mechanical efficiency fall when you slow steam?
retrieval_cards.answer: Because friction power is very nearly constant with load while indicated power is not. The same friction loss is being taken from a much smaller indicated power, so brake divided by indicated falls. It is one of the reasons prolonged low-load running is inefficient, alongside poorer combustion, cooler components and turbocharger mismatch.

decomposition_gate.question_intent: Two unrelated halves printed as one question, which is itself the difficulty: candidates run out of time on limb A and give limb B four lines. Limb A tests whether the candidate understands propulsion as a chain of losses rather than as a set of definitions - the discriminator being whether he reaches thrust and effective power at all and can distinguish wake from thrust deduction. Limb B tests whether he knows what each manoeuvring trial is FOR, which is a different and less commonly prepared thing from knowing how each is conducted.
decomposition_gate.mark_allocation: Sixteen marks with no printed split and no printed limb marks on this copy or on the March 2023 sitting of the same stem. The two limbs are printed as equals and are treated as equals - six sections to limb A and two substantial sections to limb B, the second of which carries nine manoeuvres and is the longer of the two in words. Because there is no printed split, the proportions are adjudicated, and the adjudication is deliberately even: an answer that spends twelve minutes on the power chain and three on the trials has thrown away half the question.
decomposition_gate.examiner_expectation: That the chain is given in order and reaches EFFECTIVE power. That speed of advance is distinguished from ship speed. That wake and thrust deduction are both named and not confused. That the efficiencies are collected and can be counted. That the manoeuvring trial conditions are stated, because a result outside them is meaningless. That each manoeuvre is given with its OBJECTIVE. And that the criteria are known to be expressed in ship lengths.
decomposition_gate.primary_source_plan: Re-derive the power chain from principle rather than carrying it, the nearest donor QP2303-Q5 being pushed but NOT integrated and therefore of no governed authority; use it only to establish the printed stem and the two-word delta. Anchor limb B on the IMO Standards for Ship Manoeuvrability, MSC.137(76), and its explanatory notes, cited by identity and by criterion, MIW holding no copy. Corroborate manoeuvring vocabulary against QP2410 Q3 and speed-trial practice against QP2502 Q6. Deliberately NOT planned: any quotation of MSC.137(76); the zig-zag overshoot table, which is not held and is described by its dependence on the length-to-speed ratio instead; any towing tank procedure number; any EEDI correction formula.
decomposition_gate.freshness_risk: LOW - the lowest technical risk on the paper. The donor is five months earlier in the same year, the physics does not date, and MSC.137(76) was adopted in 2002 and is unamended in any way touching the trials or criteria. The one currency point is the EEDI context of a modern speed trial, and it is stated at this sitting's position with no index value or formula asserted, so nothing depends on the phase state at any date.
decomposition_gate.jurisdiction_risk: LOW. Three levels are kept apart: MSC.137(76), which is an IMO standard applying to ships of a stated size constructed on or after a stated date; SOLAS chapter V, under which the resulting manoeuvring information is carried on board; and the builder's and society's trial programme, which is contractual and contains items that are not manoeuvring trials at all. An answer that presents the whole trial programme as an IMO requirement has the levels wrong.
decomposition_gate.technical_ambiguities: 'The stages during which the power is transformed' does not say how many stages, and different textbooks divide the chain into five, six or seven by treating shaft and delivered power as one or two. The answer uses six and states explicitly where the boundary between shaft and delivered power lies and why it depends on the torsionmeter position, rather than asserting one division as correct. 'Essential sea trial manoeuvres (navigation trials)' is likewise open: read narrowly it is the manoeuvring set of MSC.137(76), read widely it takes in the whole builder's trial programme. The answer gives the manoeuvring set in full and names the wider programme items in one line, so the boundary is visible without the answer sprawling.
decomposition_gate.target_answer_shape: Eight numbered sections split visibly between the two printed limbs. For limb A: a one-sentence statement of the transformation, then five sections in chain order each saying what the power is, where it is measured and what is lost next, and a single bulleted list collecting all the efficiencies so they can be counted. For limb B: a short prose statement of purpose, a NUMBERED list of the four trial conditions, and a bulleted list of nine manoeuvres each stating objective, procedure, what is measured and, where the standard sets one, the criterion. A closing single-sentence proposition joining the two limbs.

blocks.h: 1. What an IMO convention is, and the four stages

blocks.p: The Organization has no power to make law. It is a forum in which States negotiate treaties and a secretariat that administers them; the binding force of every IMO convention comes from the consent of the States that become party to it, and from the national legislation each of them then enacts. Everything in this question follows from that, including the delay.
Name the four stages before explaining any of them:

ol: Proposal and development - a Member State or group of States raises the matter, and the technical work is done in the committee and sub-committee structure.
Adoption - the finished text is adopted, normally by a diplomatic conference convened for the purpose.
Acceptance - States individually express their consent to be bound, by ratification, acceptance, approval or accession, depositing an instrument with the Secretary-General as depositary.
Entry into force - when the conditions written into the convention itself have been satisfied, and the prescribed period after that has run.

blocks.p: What follows the fourth stage is implementation and enforcement - national legislation, administrative machinery, surveyors, certificates and penalties. That is not a fifth stage of the convention; it is what each Party must already have done before it could sensibly ratify, and it is one of the reasons the third stage takes so long.

Who may start it. A Member State, or a group of them, submits a proposal to the appropriate committee - the Maritime Safety Committee for safety, the Marine Environment Protection Committee for pollution, the Legal Committee for liability and compensation, the Facilitation Committee for documentary matters. In practice a proposal follows a casualty, a scientific finding or a commercial development; much of the modern instrument set can be traced to a specific disaster.

What happens. The committee decides whether the matter justifies a new instrument, and if so places it on its work programme with a target completion date. The detailed technical drafting is done in a sub-committee, over several sessions, with industry and non-governmental organisations in consultative status contributing expertise. The output returns to the parent committee, which settles the text.

Why this stage is slow, and legitimately so. The text must be technically sound, must work for every trade and every size of ship, and must be acceptable to States with radically different interests - large flags, coastal States with a pollution exposure, developing States with limited administrative capacity, and shipbuilding States. A text pushed through this stage against unresolved objections is a text that States will not later ratify, so speed here is a false economy.

Adoption fixes the text. A new convention is normally adopted by a diplomatic conference convened by the Organization, to which all States are invited - including States that are not Members of IMO, because a treaty is open to States generally. Amendments to an existing convention, and codes, are adopted by the relevant committee or by the Assembly, by resolution.
Three points that are commonly got wrong:

ul: Adoption creates no obligation on anybody. The text exists; nobody is bound by it. A State that voted for adoption is not thereby a Party.
Adoption is the date from which the delay is measured, and it is the date the stem's second limb is about.

Signature at the conference is usually 'subject to ratification' and is not consent to be bound - it is an indication of intent and an undertaking not to defeat the object of the treaty in the meantime. Consent comes later and separately.

blocks.h: 4. Stage three - acceptance, and the four ways of giving it

blocks.p: This is where the delay actually accumulates, so it is worth setting out precisely how a State becomes bound. The convention is opened for signature for a stated period, and thereafter remains open for accession.

ul: Signature subject to ratification, acceptance or approval. A two-step route. The State signs, indicating agreement with the text and an intention to proceed; it becomes bound only when it later deposits its instrument of ratification (or acceptance, or approval - the three differ in the internal constitutional process each State uses and not in their international effect). The gap between signature and ratification is where the national legislative work is done.
Definitive signature, where a convention permits it - signature not subject to ratification, which expresses consent in one step. Rare for technical conventions.

Accession. A single act by which a State that has not signed - typically because the signature period has closed - becomes a Party. It has exactly the same legal effect as ratification and is the route by which most States join an instrument that has been open for years.

Deposit with the depositary. In every case the instrument is deposited with the Secretary-General of the Organization, who is the depositary, keeps the count and informs all States. It is the date of deposit, not the date of the national law, that counts - which is a common examination point.

blocks.p: The essential proposition to state here is that ratification is not a formality but the end of a long domestic process. Before a State can responsibly deposit an instrument it must have enacted the enabling legislation, given itself the powers to survey, certify, detain and prosecute, provided or authorized the surveyors, and satisfied itself that its industry can comply.

Every convention contains its own entry-into-force article, and it is that article, not the Organization, that decides when the treaty becomes law. For a convention of important technical nature the condition is deliberately demanding and normally has two elements, sometimes three:

ul: a minimum number of Contracting States - typically between fifteen and thirty; and
those States between them representing a minimum percentage of world merchant shipping by gross tonnage - commonly 50 per cent, sometimes lower; and

occasionally a third, subject-specific criterion. The Hong Kong Convention is the standard example, requiring in addition a combined annual ship recycling capacity among the Contracting States - because a recycling convention ratified only by States that do no recycling would regulate nothing.

blocks.p: When the last condition is satisfied, the convention does not enter into force at once. A prescribed period runs - commonly twelve or twenty-four months - so that the newly bound States, the industry and the classification societies have time to prepare. Entry into force is general: the convention then binds all Parties. A State ratifying afterwards is bound a stated period after its own deposit.

State the purpose of the double condition, because it explains the delay rather than merely describing it: the numerical condition secures political legitimacy and the tonnage condition secures practical effect. A convention in force among thirty States owning two per cent of the world fleet would regulate almost no ships, and would put those States' owners at a competitive disadvantage against everybody else. The tonnage threshold is what prevents that - and it is also precisely what makes the wait so long, because it means the instrument cannot take effect until the major flag States have moved.
Separate the causes into three groups, because they have three different remedies.
Structural causes - built into the treaty system itself.

ul: The entry-into-force conditions are demanding by design, for the reason just given, and satisfying a tonnage threshold means waiting for a handful of large flag States whose own processes are not quick.
Unanimity of interest is impossible. The States that gain from an instrument and the States that pay for it are frequently different States.
The Organization cannot compel anybody. It can promote, assist and publish; it has no power to require ratification and no sanction for not ratifying.

blocks.p: National causes - inside each State.

ul: Enabling legislation takes parliamentary time, and maritime matters compete for it with everything else a government is doing. In many States the delay is simply that nobody has scheduled the Bill.

Administrative capacity. A State cannot honestly ratify until it can survey, certify, inspect, detain and prosecute under the new instrument - which means trained surveyors, revised forms, delegated authority to recognized organizations and a means of enforcement.
Legal and linguistic work - translation, reconciliation with existing national law, and the constitutional process each State's system requires.
Political change. A government that intended to ratify may be replaced by one with other priorities.

blocks.p: Industrial and economic causes - and this is the group candidates usually miss.

ul: The technology may not exist, or may not be affordable, at adoption. The Ballast Water Management Convention is the outstanding case: it required treatment systems that had to be developed, type-approved and manufactured at scale, and States were reasonably unwilling to bind their fleets to a requirement that could not yet be met.
Cost, and who bears it first. Compliance costs money, and an owner whose flag ratifies early bears it before his competitors do.

The free-rider problem, which is the economic root of the whole difficulty. Every State benefits if the instrument comes into force; each individual State benefits slightly more by being late. That is a rational calculation for each State and a bad outcome for all of them, and it is why the delay is a structural feature rather than mere inefficiency.

Uncertainty about interpretation. Where the guidelines needed to apply an instrument are still being written, States hold back rather than ratify into ambiguity - which is a very common and quite reasonable cause of delay.

blocks.p: Give examples with dates, because the stem asks for them, and be careful to state each as it stands at this sitting.

ul: SOLAS 1974 - adopted 1 November 1974, in force 25 May 1980. About five and a half years, and this is the quick end of the range for a major technical convention.

MARPOL - the 1973 Convention never entered into force on its own and had to be absorbed into the 1978 Protocol; Annexes I and II came into force on 2 October 1983, ten years after the original adoption. A good illustration that a stalled instrument is sometimes rescued by re-packaging rather than by waiting.
Bunkers Convention 2001 - adopted 23 March 2001, in force 21 November 2008. Nearly eight years, for a short liability convention with no technology requirement at all.
Maritime Liens and Mortgages 1993 - adopted 6 May 1993, in force 5 September 2004. Eleven years - and a reminder that a low-cost instrument can still wait a decade if no State feels urgency about it.
Nairobi Wreck Removal Convention 2007 - adopted 18 May 2007, in force 14 April 2015. Nearly eight years.

Ballast Water Management Convention 2004 - adopted 13 February 2004, in force 8 September 2017. Thirteen years, and the clearest case of technology and cost being the cause: the treatment systems and their type approval did not exist in usable form at adoption.

Hong Kong Convention 2009 - and this one is live as this paper is being sat. Adopted 15 May 2009. Its three-part condition - States, tonnage and recycling capacity - remained unsatisfied for fourteen years, because the tonnage and the recycling capacity are held by different groups of States. The conditions were satisfied in June 2023, two months before this examination, and the twenty-four-month period is now running, so the Convention will enter into force in June 2025. It is not in force today. Use it as the example of an instrument that has finally cleared the hurdle and is still waiting.

And the counter-examples that have not cleared it at all - the HNS regime and the Cape Town Agreement on fishing vessel safety, both adopted years ago and both still not in force. Some instruments never arrive.

blocks.p: The pattern is worth stating in a sentence: a technical convention typically takes between five and fifteen years, the length being driven by how much it costs the industry and how concentrated the tonnage is among States that are slow to move.

blocks.h: 8. What can be done to reduce the delay

blocks.p: Answer this limb in two halves - what the Organization has already done, which is the stronger half, and what more could be done.
Established measures that work.

ul: Tacit acceptance - the single most effective reform in the Organization's history. Under the classical explicit acceptance procedure an amendment entered into force only when a specified proportion of Parties had positively accepted it, which meant that amendments took as long as conventions and technical requirements could not be kept current. Under tacit acceptance, provided for in MARPOL article 16 and in the corresponding SOLAS provision, an adopted amendment is deemed accepted on a stated date unless a specified proportion of Parties objects, and enters into force a stated period later. The burden is reversed: silence now means yes. This is why SOLAS and MARPOL amendments enter into force on a predictable cycle of a few years while new conventions take a decade.

Make a new standard binding through an instrument already in force. Rather than negotiating a new convention, the Organization adopts the substance as a code and then makes it mandatory by amending SOLAS or MARPOL under tacit acceptance. The ISM Code, the ISPS Code, the RO Code and the III Code all arrived this way. It is the most powerful practical answer to the delay and it should be named.

Amend by protocol. Where a convention has stalled or needs substantial change, a protocol attached to it - as the 1978 Protocol rescued MARPOL, and the 1988 Protocols modernised SOLAS and Load Lines - can carry the new content with its own, more achievable entry-into-force conditions.

Technical co-operation and capacity building. The Organization's technical co-operation programme, model national legislation, regional workshops and the support given to developing Administrations directly attack the national-capacity cause, which is the largest single cause for the majority of States.
The Member State Audit Scheme and the III Code, which make each State's implementation performance visible and auditable, and so raise the capability that ratification depends on.

Publish the guidelines with the instrument, not years afterwards. The BWM experience showed that States will not ratify into interpretive uncertainty; producing unified interpretations and guidelines in parallel with the text removes a real and reasonable reason to wait.

blocks.p: What more could be done - stated as propositions rather than as settled policy.

ul: Set realistic entry-into-force conditions when drafting. A threshold designed to guarantee effectiveness can guarantee paralysis instead. The Hong Kong Convention's fourteen-year wait is the argument, and its third criterion is exactly the kind of condition that should be examined at drafting rather than regretted afterwards.
Phase the requirements and grandfather existing ships, so that the cost shock at entry into force is smaller and States are readier to bind themselves.

Allow, or encourage, voluntary early application by flags, owners, charterers and classification societies. Industry can and does apply a standard before it is law, and doing so removes the first-mover disadvantage by making the standard commercially normal in advance.

Keep the technology honest. Do not adopt a requirement that depends on equipment which has not been demonstrated and type-approved, because the instrument will then wait for the equipment rather than the other way round.
Targeted diplomacy with the major flag States, since the tonnage condition means a small number of registries can determine the date single-handedly.

Accept that regional and unilateral measures are part of the mechanism. Where a region legislates ahead of the international instrument, it creates commercial pressure that accelerates ratification - at the cost of a period of fragmented regulation, which is a real price and should be acknowledged as one.

blocks.p: Close on the proposition the whole question turns on: the delay is not administrative inefficiency. It is the price of a system in which no State can be bound without its own consent - and every serious remedy works either by lowering the cost of consenting or by removing the need to consent again.

Three tasks are printed as three sentences and they are not equal. The four stages are recall and can be written quickly; the delay with examples needs dates; and 'what can be done to reduce this delay' is an evaluative limb that most candidates have never prepared. The structure gives one section to naming the stages, four to explaining them, one to causes, one to examples and one to remedies - and the last two are where the answer is actually won.

Section 6's division into structural, national and industrial causes is the piece of thinking that makes section 8 possible. Once the causes are in three groups, the remedies fall out of them: tacit acceptance and the code-through-convention technique answer the structural group, technical co-operation and the Audit Scheme answer the national group, and phasing, early voluntary application and technology realism answer the industrial group. A candidate who lists causes at random cannot then produce a coherent remedy list.

Giving exactly four stages matters. The stem says four. Implementation and enforcement are named in section 1 as what FOLLOWS the fourth, which shows the examiner that the omission is deliberate rather than ignorant - and it also sets up the point in section 4 that domestic implementation must largely precede ratification, which is one of the answer's better observations.

ul: Giving five or six stages. The stem asks for four. Name implementation separately as what follows.
Saying IMO makes law. It does not. The binding force comes from States' consent and their national legislation, and this proposition explains the entire delay.
Treating signature as consent to be bound. Signature subject to ratification is an indication of intent; consent comes on deposit of the instrument.
Confusing ratification with accession. They have identical legal effect; accession is the route for a State that did not sign.
Giving no examples, or giving them without dates. The stem says 'with examples' and a date is what makes an example evidence.
Saying the Hong Kong Convention is in force. At this sitting it is not - see the traps.
Describing the delay as inefficiency. It is structural, and the free-rider problem is the reason.
Omitting tacit acceptance from the remedies. It is the single most effective answer the Organization has ever found and no answer to limb three is complete without it.
Forgetting that the tonnage threshold is what makes the wait long AND what makes the convention worth having.

The Hong Kong Convention is NOT in force at this sitting. Adopted 15 May 2009; its conditions were satisfied only in June 2023, two months before this paper, and the twenty-four-month period then began to run, so it enters into force in June 2025. The circulating solved answers are all written for a 2025 or 2026 sitting and treats it as a completed example. Here it is the live one - which is a better example, not a worse one.

Tacit acceptance applies to AMENDMENTS, not to new conventions. Expect to be asked why, if tacit acceptance works so well, new conventions still take a decade. Because a State cannot be deemed to have accepted a treaty it is not already party to.
Adoption creates no obligation on anyone. A State that voted for a text at the conference is not a Party.
It is the date of DEPOSIT of the instrument that counts, not the date of the national legislation.
Ratification, acceptance and approval differ only in each State's internal constitutional process, not in international effect.
The Hong Kong Convention's third criterion is recycling capacity - a subject-specific condition, and the standard example of a threshold that guarantees relevance and causes delay in equal measure.
MARPOL 1973 never entered into force on its own. It was absorbed into the 1978 Protocol. Expect this as a follow-up on why MARPOL is written '73/78'.
Some conventions never arrive at all - the HNS regime and the Cape Town Agreement are the current examples. An answer that implies every adopted convention eventually enters into force is wrong.
