blocks.p: The four stages are PROPOSE - ADOPT - ACCEPT - ENTER INTO FORCE, and implementation follows. For the four ways of consenting hold SIGN-THEN-RATIFY / DEFINITIVE SIGNATURE / ACCEPTANCE OR APPROVAL / ACCESSION, all deposited with the Secretary-General. For the causes hold three groups: STRUCTURAL / NATIONAL / INDUSTRIAL. For the examples hold four numbers - SOLAS 5½, Bunkers 8, Maritime Liens 11, BWM 13 - and one live case, the Hong Kong Convention at fourteen years and still waiting. For the remedies hold TACIT ACCEPTANCE - CODE THROUGH CONVENTION - PROTOCOL - CAPACITY - AUDIT - GUIDELINES WITH THE TEXT.

ul: The IMO Convention and the committee structure - Assembly, Council, MSC, MEPC, Legal, Facilitation and Technical Co-operation Committees, with sub-committees beneath MSC and MEPC.
MARPOL article 16 and the corresponding SOLAS provision - the tacit acceptance amendment procedure. Cited by identity and mechanism; no threshold figure or period is asserted.

Hong Kong Convention 2009 - adopted 15 May 2009; three-part entry-into-force condition of States, tonnage and recycling capacity; conditions satisfied June 2023; in force 26 June 2025 - FUTURE at this sitting.
SOLAS 1974 - adopted 1 November 1974, in force 25 May 1980.
MARPOL 73/78 - Annexes I and II in force 2 October 1983.
Bunkers Convention 2001 - adopted 23 March 2001, in force 21 November 2008.
Nairobi Wreck Removal Convention 2007 - adopted 18 May 2007, in force 14 April 2015.
Ballast Water Management Convention 2004 - adopted 13 February 2004, in force 8 September 2017.
Maritime Liens and Mortgages 1993 - adopted 6 May 1993, in force 5 September 2004.
III Code, A.1070(28), and the IMO Member State Audit Scheme - the implementation-capability half of the problem.
The Integrated Technical Cooperation Programme and model national legislation.

No treaty status figure is asserted for any instrument - no number of Contracting States and no percentage of world tonnage at this sitting. Such figures move continuously and we hold no treaty-status list. Thresholds are described as the instrument's own condition, never as the position reached.
We hold no copy of the Hong Kong Convention. Its adoption date, the shape of its three-part condition and the twenty-four-month period are carried from our own verified records; no article is quoted.
we hold MARPOL at citation level and not as quotable text. Article 16 is cited by identity and by mechanism; no objection threshold or period is stated as a figure.
The example dates are carried from our own verified records, not read at a depositary source for this paper. They are stable historical facts but they were not independently re-verified here.

The remedies are partly established practice and partly analysis, and the answer separates the two. Tacit acceptance, the code-through-convention technique, protocols, technical co-operation and the Audit Scheme are established; realistic thresholds, phasing, early voluntary application and the acceptance of regional pressure are propositions about what would help.

AT THIS SITTING IT IS NOT IN FORCE.

THE HONG KONG POSITION AT AUGUST 2023 IS UNUSUALLY PRECISE AND IS USED DELIBERATELY. Adopted 15 May 2009; its three-part condition was satisfied in JUNE 2023 - TWO MONTHS BEFORE THIS EXAMINATION - and the twenty-four-month period was then running, entry into force following on 26 June 2025. EVERY COMPLETED EXAMPLE USED HAD ALREADY ENTERED INTO FORCE BEFORE AUGUST 2023, AND EACH WAS CHECKED: SOLAS 1974 (25 May 1980), MARPOL Annexes I and II (2 October 1983), Maritime Liens and Mortgages 1993 (5 September 2004), Bunkers 2001 (21 November 2008), Nairobi WRC 2007 (14 April 2015) and BWM 2004 (8 September 2017). No example post-dates the sitting.

THE NOT-YET-IN-FORCE COUNTER-EXAMPLES WERE ALSO CHECKED AT THIS DATE: the HNS regime and the Cape Town Agreement on fishing vessel safety were both adopted and both not in force at August 2023, and neither had entered into force by the time this paper was authored.

THE TREATY MACHINERY ITSELF IS TEMPORALLY STABLE. Signature, ratification, acceptance, approval, accession, the depositary role of the Secretary-General, and tacit acceptance under MARPOL article 16 are unchanged across the whole 2021-2026 corpus and need no re-anchoring.

NO ASSEMBLY MATERIAL IS ENGAGED BEYOND A.1070(28), THE III CODE, WHICH IS MANDATORY FROM 1 JANUARY 2016 AND OPERATIVE. The 33rd Assembly set (6 December 2023) is four months future and none of it is needed; in particular no A.118x(33) resolution appears.

NO TREATY STATUS FIGURE IS ASSERTED AT ANY DATE, which removes the largest remaining currency risk on a question of this kind - a party count or tonnage percentage would date the answer to the week it was written.
MERCHANT SHIPPING ACT, 1958 governs any Indian aspect; the 2025 Act commenced 15 March 2026. Nothing in this answer engages either.

questions.understand_first: Start from the one fact that explains everything else: nobody can make a country obey a treaty it has not agreed to. The Organization is a place where governments negotiate and a secretariat that keeps the paperwork - it has no parliament and no police. So a rule only becomes law for a ship when her flag State has personally said yes and then written the rule into its own statute book. That single constraint produces the whole shape of the answer. First somebody has to propose the idea and the technical people have to argue it into a text everybody can live with. Then the text is fixed at a conference - and at that moment nobody at all is bound by it, which surprises people. Then each government goes home and does the slow part: passes a law, gives itself the power to inspect and prosecute, trains or hires surveyors, and only then formally lodges its agreement. And finally the treaty waits until enough governments have lodged - not just enough by headcount, but enough ships, because a rule agreed by thirty countries that own hardly any tonnage would regulate almost nothing and would simply penalise the owners of those thirty. That tonnage requirement is the clever part and the painful part at once. It is what makes the convention worth having, and it is exactly why it takes ten years, because it means waiting for a handful of very large registries. Underneath it all sits an awkward piece of arithmetic that no procedure can abolish: everyone is better off if the rule comes in, and each one individually is slightly better off going last, because whoever moves first pays for compliance while his competitors do not. Once you see that, the cures make sense - they all work either by making it cheaper to say yes, or by finding a way not to have to ask again.
questions.memory_cue: STAGES - PROPOSE - ADOPT - ACCEPT - ENTER INTO FORCE - CAUSES - EXAMPLES - REMEDIES (1 to 8). Inside step 6 hold STRUCTURAL / NATIONAL / INDUSTRIAL. Inside step 8 hold TACIT ACCEPTANCE - CODE THROUGH CONVENTION - PROTOCOL - CAPACITY - AUDIT - GUIDELINES WITH THE TEXT.

steps.title: What an IMO convention is, and the four stages
points: The Organization has no power to make law - binding force comes from States' consent and their national legislation
Stage 1 proposal and development; stage 2 adoption; stage 3 acceptance; stage 4 entry into force
Implementation and enforcement FOLLOW the fourth stage and are not a fifth
Much of what a State must do to implement has to be done BEFORE it can responsibly ratify

steps.title: Stage one - proposal and development
points: A Member State or group proposes to MSC, MEPC, the Legal Committee or the Facilitation Committee
Proposals commonly follow a casualty, a scientific finding or a commercial development
Technical drafting is done in a sub-committee over several sessions, with consultative organisations contributing
Slow legitimately: a text pushed through against unresolved objections is one States will not ratify

steps.title: Stage two - adoption
points: A new convention is normally adopted by a diplomatic conference open to all States, not only IMO Members
Amendments and codes are adopted by the relevant committee or by the Assembly, by resolution
Adoption creates NO obligation - the text exists and nobody is bound
Adoption is the date from which the delay is measured
Signature at the conference is usually subject to ratification and is not consent to be bound

steps.title: Stage three - acceptance, and the four ways of giving it
points: Signature subject to ratification, acceptance or approval - a two-step route; the gap is where national legislation is done
Definitive signature, where permitted - consent in one step; rare for technical conventions
Accession - a single act by a State that did not sign, with identical legal effect to ratification
In every case the instrument is DEPOSITED with the Secretary-General as depositary
It is the date of deposit, not the date of the national law, that counts
Ratification is the END of a long domestic process, not a formality

steps.title: Stage four - entry into force
points: Every convention contains its own entry-into-force article - that article decides, not the Organization
For an important technical convention: a minimum number of Contracting States, commonly 15 to 30
Plus a minimum percentage of world merchant shipping by gross tonnage, commonly 50 per cent
Occasionally a third subject-specific criterion - the Hong Kong Convention's recycling capacity
Then a prescribed period, commonly 12 or 24 months, before it takes effect
The numerical condition secures legitimacy; the tonnage condition secures practical effect - and causes the wait

steps.title: Why the delay happens
points: STRUCTURAL: demanding thresholds by design; conflicting national interests; the Organization cannot compel
NATIONAL: parliamentary time for enabling legislation; administrative capacity to survey, certify and prosecute; legal and linguistic work; political change
INDUSTRIAL: the technology may not exist or be affordable at adoption - the BWM case
INDUSTRIAL: cost, and the first mover bearing it before his competitors
INDUSTRIAL: the free-rider problem - each State gains slightly by going last, which is the economic root
INDUSTRIAL: uncertainty about interpretation where guidelines are still being written

steps.title: The delay, in worked examples
points: SOLAS 1974 - adopted 1 November 1974, in force 25 May 1980: about five and a half years
MARPOL - the 1973 Convention never entered into force alone; absorbed into the 1978 Protocol, Annexes I and II in force 2 October 1983
Bunkers 2001 - adopted 23 March 2001, in force 21 November 2008: nearly eight years, with no technology requirement
Maritime Liens and Mortgages 1993 - adopted 6 May 1993, in force 5 September 2004: eleven years
Nairobi Wreck Removal 2007 - adopted 18 May 2007, in force 14 April 2015: nearly eight years
Ballast Water Management 2004 - adopted 13 February 2004, in force 8 September 2017: thirteen years, technology and cost
Hong Kong Convention 2009 - adopted 15 May 2009, conditions satisfied June 2023, TWO MONTHS BEFORE THIS SITTING; twenty-four-month clock running; NOT IN FORCE today
And some never arrive - the HNS regime and the Cape Town Agreement
Typical range five to fifteen years, driven by cost to industry and by how concentrated tonnage is

steps.title: What can be done to reduce the delay
points: TACIT ACCEPTANCE - the burden reversed, silence means yes; MARPOL article 16 and the SOLAS equivalent. The single most effective reform
Make a standard binding through a convention already in force - the ISM, ISPS, RO and III Codes all arrived this way
Amend by protocol where an instrument has stalled - the 1978 Protocol rescued MARPOL; the 1988 Protocols modernised SOLAS and Load Lines
Technical co-operation, model national legislation and regional workshops, attacking the national-capacity cause
The Member State Audit Scheme and the III Code, raising the capability ratification depends on
Publish guidelines WITH the instrument - States will not ratify into interpretive uncertainty

Propositions: realistic thresholds at drafting; phasing and grandfathering; encourage early voluntary application; do not adopt requirements depending on undemonstrated technology; targeted diplomacy with major flags; accept regional pressure as part of the mechanism, at the cost of fragmentation

quick_revision.recall_15s: PROPOSE - ADOPT - ACCEPT - ENTER INTO FORCE. IMO makes no law; States consent and legislate. Adoption binds nobody. Consent is by ratification, acceptance, approval or accession, on deposit with the Secretary-General. Entry into force needs a number of States plus a tonnage percentage, then 12 or 24 months. Delay is structural, national and industrial, and its root is the free-rider problem. Examples: SOLAS 5½ years, Bunkers 8, Liens 11, BWM 13, Hong Kong 14 and still waiting. Cures: tacit acceptance, code-through-convention, protocol, capacity building, guidelines with the text.
quick_revision.critical_numbers: Four stages. Entry into force: commonly 15 to 30 States and about 50 per cent of world tonnage, then 12 or 24 months. Delays: SOLAS 1974 → 1980, 5½ years; MARPOL 1973 → 1983, 10 years; Bunkers 2001 → 2008, 8 years; Maritime Liens 1993 → 2004, 11 years; Nairobi 2007 → 2015, 8 years; BWM 2004 → 2017, 13 years; Hong Kong adopted 2009, conditions met June 2023, in force June 2025.
quick_revision.critical_regulation: MARPOL article 16 - tacit acceptance. If you remember one thing in limb three, remember what it changed: under explicit acceptance an amendment waited for positive acceptances and took as long as a convention, so technical requirements could not be kept current. Under tacit acceptance the amendment is deemed accepted unless enough Parties object. The burden is reversed and silence now means yes - and that is why SOLAS and MARPOL amendments arrive on a predictable few-year cycle while new conventions take a decade.
quick_revision.major_trap: Saying the Hong Kong Convention is in force, or that it 'took sixteen years'. At this sitting it is not in force: adopted 15 May 2009, its conditions were satisfied only in June 2023, two months before this paper, and it enters into force on 26 June 2025. The circulating solved answers are all written for a 2025 or 2026 sitting and treats it as completed. Here it is the live example - and it is a better illustration of the stem for exactly that reason.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the four main stages of an IMO convention, and say what follows them.
retrieval_cards.answer: Proposal and development in the committee and sub-committee structure; adoption, normally by a diplomatic conference; acceptance, by which individual States express consent to be bound; and entry into force, when the convention's own conditions are satisfied and the prescribed period has run. What follows is implementation and enforcement - national legislation, surveyors, certificates and penalties - which is not a fifth stage and must largely precede ratification anyway.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Ratification or accession - what is the difference, and does signature bind you?
retrieval_cards.answer: Ratification follows a signature already given, completing a two-step route; accession is a single act by a State that never signed, typically because the signature period closed. Their legal effect is identical. Signature subject to ratification does NOT bind the State - it indicates intent and an undertaking not to defeat the treaty's object. Consent takes effect on deposit of the instrument with the Secretary-General as depositary.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What conditions must be satisfied for a technical convention to enter into force, and why two of them?
retrieval_cards.answer: A minimum number of Contracting States, commonly fifteen to thirty, together with those States representing a minimum percentage of world merchant shipping by gross tonnage, commonly around fifty per cent; occasionally a third subject-specific criterion. Then a prescribed period of twelve or twenty-four months. The numerical condition secures political legitimacy; the tonnage condition secures practical effect, since a convention binding States with two per cent of the fleet would regulate almost nothing.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is the free-rider problem, and why does it explain the delay?
retrieval_cards.answer: Every State is better off if the convention comes into force, and each individual State is slightly better off being late, because whoever ratifies first imposes compliance costs on its own owners before their competitors bear them. That is a rational calculation for each State and a bad outcome for all of them. It is why the delay is a structural feature of a consent-based system rather than administrative inefficiency.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give four worked examples of the adoption-to-entry-into-force delay, with dates.
retrieval_cards.answer: SOLAS 1974 - adopted 1 November 1974, in force 25 May 1980, about five and a half years. Bunkers Convention 2001 - adopted 23 March 2001, in force 21 November 2008, nearly eight years, with no technology requirement at all. Maritime Liens and Mortgages 1993 - adopted 6 May 1993, in force 5 September 2004, eleven years. Ballast Water Management 2004 - adopted 13 February 2004, in force 8 September 2017, thirteen years.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Is the Hong Kong Convention in force at an August 2023 sitting?
retrieval_cards.answer: No. It was adopted 15 May 2009 and its three-part condition - States, tonnage and combined annual ship recycling capacity - remained unsatisfied for fourteen years. The conditions were met in June 2023, two months before this examination, and the twenty-four-month period then began to run, so it enters into force on 26 June 2025. It is the paper's best example of an instrument that has cleared its hurdle and is still waiting.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is tacit acceptance and what problem did it solve?
retrieval_cards.answer: Under explicit acceptance an amendment entered into force only when a specified proportion of Parties had positively accepted it, so amendments took as long as conventions and technical requirements could not be kept current. Under tacit acceptance - MARPOL article 16 and the corresponding SOLAS provision - an adopted amendment is deemed accepted on a stated date unless a specified proportion of Parties objects, and enters into force a stated period later. The burden is reversed: silence means yes.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How did the ISM Code become mandatory without a new convention, and why does that matter here?
retrieval_cards.answer: By being adopted as a code and then made mandatory through an amendment to SOLAS under the tacit acceptance procedure - the same route as the ISPS Code, the RO Code and the III Code. It matters because it is the most powerful practical answer to the delay: the substance takes effect through an instrument already in force and with near-universal participation, so no State has to be asked to ratify anything new.

retrieval_cards.prompt: If tacit acceptance works so well, why do new conventions still take a decade?
retrieval_cards.answer: Because tacit acceptance applies only to AMENDMENTS of an instrument a State is already party to. A State cannot be deemed to have accepted a treaty it has never joined - that would bind it without its consent, which is the one thing the system cannot do. New conventions therefore still require individual ratification or accession by enough States, and enough tonnage, one at a time.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Name three remedies for the delay that are established practice, and three that are proposals.
retrieval_cards.answer: Established: tacit acceptance for amendments; adopting a standard as a code and making it binding through a convention already in force; and amending by protocol where an instrument has stalled, as the 1978 Protocol rescued MARPOL. Also established are technical co-operation and the Member State Audit Scheme. Proposals: set realistic entry-into-force thresholds at drafting; phase requirements and grandfather existing ships; and encourage early voluntary application by flags, owners, charterers and class.

decomposition_gate.question_intent: Three tasks in three printed sentences, moving from recall to explanation to evaluation. The first is standard and every candidate has it. The second requires dates and is where most answers become vague - 'it takes a long time' is not an answer to a question that says 'with examples'. The third is evaluative and is the discriminator: the entry-into-force family is solved five times in the corpus and NOT ONE of those questions asks what could be done about the delay, so no prepared answer exists for it and the candidate must actually think. The examiner is testing whether he understands that the delay is a consequence of consent-based law rather than of bureaucracy.
decomposition_gate.mark_allocation: Sixteen marks with no printed split. The three tasks are visibly unequal in difficulty though not in length of stem: the four stages are recall, the delay with examples requires evidence, and the remedies limb requires analysis. The answer allots five sections to the stages - one naming them and four explaining them, since they are the framework everything else hangs on - one to causes, one to worked examples and one to remedies. Because there is no printed split the proportions are adjudicated, and the deliberate choice is to give the last two sections about a third of the answer between them, since that is where marks are won and lost.
decomposition_gate.examiner_expectation: That exactly four stages are given, because the stem says four. That adoption is correctly described as creating no obligation. That the four modes of consent are distinguished and the deposit rule stated. That the entry-into-force conditions are given with BOTH elements and the reason for each. That examples carry dates. That the Hong Kong Convention is correctly placed as not yet in force. That tacit acceptance appears in the remedies. And that the answer recognises the delay as structural rather than as inefficiency.
decomposition_gate.primary_source_plan: Carry the treaty machinery from the MIW verification records for QP2506 Q2 and QP2603 Q1, and the tacit acceptance material from QP2604 Q1 on MARPOL article 16. Take the committee structure from QP2309 Q4 and the code-through-convention technique from QP2408 Q1 and QP2309 Q2. Re-date every worked example for August 2023 and verify that each completed example had entered into force before the sitting. Deliberately NOT planned: any quotation of MARPOL article 16 or of the Hong Kong Convention, neither being held as quotable text; any treaty status figure - party count or tonnage percentage - at this or any date; any objection threshold stated as a number.
decomposition_gate.freshness_risk: HIGH - and it is concentrated entirely in the examples. Every donor in this family sits at least twenty-two months later and uses the Hong Kong Convention as a completed example, in force 26 June 2025. At this sitting it is not in force, and its conditions had been satisfied only two months earlier, which makes it the live example rather than the finished one. The completed examples were each checked to have entered into force before August 2023, and the not-yet-in-force counter-examples were checked to have been still waiting. No treaty status figure is asserted, which removes the remaining currency risk.
decomposition_gate.jurisdiction_risk: MEDIUM. Three levels must be kept apart: the international treaty, which binds only States that have consented; the national legislation by which a State gives it domestic effect and without which no ship can actually be prosecuted; and regional measures such as EU legislation, which are not IMO law at all and which the answer identifies as commercial pressure rather than as part of the treaty mechanism. An answer that says IMO 'passes' a regulation, or that treats a regional measure as international law, has the levels wrong.
decomposition_gate.technical_ambiguities: 'The four main stages' is not a term of art and is divided differently in different sources - some texts give proposal, adoption, ratification and entry into force; others fold proposal and drafting together and add implementation as a fourth. The answer takes the first division, gives exactly four as the stem requires, and names implementation expressly as what follows, so the choice is visible rather than asserted. 'Coming into force date' is read as entry into force generally, not as the date a particular State becomes bound, which is a separate and later date for a State ratifying after entry into force; the distinction is stated so it is not lost.
decomposition_gate.target_answer_shape: Eight numbered sections. A NUMBERED list of the four stages in section 1, because the stem says 'list and explain' and the list should be visibly delivered before the explanation begins. Four explanatory sections, each ending on why that stage takes the time it does, so the second limb is being built while the first is answered. A three-group bulleted analysis of causes. A bulleted list of worked examples, each with adoption date, entry-into-force date and elapsed years, with the Hong Kong Convention given at length as the live case. A remedies section split visibly into established measures and propositions. A closing single-sentence proposition.

It is not. The answer's whole third limb is stronger for having a live example, and a 'corrected' version would date the paper two years into its own future.

reuse_evidence: TIER C - LIMB-LEVEL REUSE FROM TWO DONORS, neither of which is this question. The stem is a composite of a survey-differentiation task and a certificate-register task.

LIMB (i), SURVEY TYPES: QP2310-Q2 (October 2023, PUSHED NOT INTEGRATED) supplies the purpose of the annual survey, the items examined and condition of class. QP2312-Q8(b) (December 2023) and QP2509-Q9(b) (September 2025), both INTEGRATED, supply the annual-versus-periodical distinction under the harmonized system. QP2503-Q2 and QP2507-Q7 (substantial corrosion at renewal survey) supply renewal-survey depth.

DAMAGE AND REPAIR SURVEYS ARE IN NONE OF THEM AND ARE AUTHORED FRESH. That is not an oversight in the donors - it is the discrimination this examiner is testing. Annual, intermediate and renewal are periodical surveys on a fixed cycle; damage and repair are OCCASIONAL surveys triggered by an event and are not part of the harmonized cycle at all. An answer that lists five surveys as though they were five stages of one cycle has failed the question.

blocks.h: 1. The distinction that organises the whole answer

blocks.p: The stem names five surveys in one breath, which invites the candidate to describe them as five stages of one cycle. They are not. Say so first, because it is the discrimination the question is really testing.

ul: Annual, intermediate and renewal are PERIODICAL surveys. They are calendar-driven, they recur on a fixed cycle anchored to the ship's anniversary date, they are what keep her certificates valid, and they are the surveys the harmonized system was built to co-ordinate.

Damage and repair surveys are OCCASIONAL surveys. They are event-driven. They are not part of the cycle, they appear in no schedule, and their timing is decided by what has happened to the ship rather than by the calendar.

blocks.p: A second distinction runs across all five and should be stated once rather than repeated: every one of them may be performed either as a statutory survey, on behalf of the flag Administration under a convention, or as a class survey, under the society's own rules - and in practice the two are carried out together by the same surveyor on the same visit. The findings, however, go to different places: a statutory finding affects a convention certificate, a class finding produces a condition of class.

ul: When. Every year, within a window of three months before or after the anniversary date of the certificate. It is the lightest and most frequent of the periodical surveys.

Purpose. To confirm that the ship, her equipment and her arrangements remain in a satisfactory condition and have not been altered without approval - in short, that nothing has changed for the worse since the last survey.

Scope. A general examination, largely visual and afloat, of the hull, closing appliances, freeboard marks, means of access, life-saving appliances, fire-fighting arrangements, machinery in operation, safety systems, pollution prevention arrangements and the ship's documentation. Selected equipment is tested in operation. It is deliberately not an opening-up survey.

What it produces. An endorsement on the existing certificate. The annual survey does not issue a certificate; it keeps one alive. An annual survey not completed within its window renders the certificate invalid, and that is the practical point that matters to a Chief Engineer.
When. Once in each five-year certificate period, taking the place of either the second or the third annual survey - so at roughly the mid-point of the cycle.

Purpose. To provide a deeper check part-way through the period, so that five years do not elapse between one thorough examination and the next. It exists because a purely visual annual survey cannot detect deterioration that develops inside tanks and structure.

Scope. Everything in an annual survey, plus additional examination - internal examination of selected ballast and cargo spaces, thickness measurement where the surveyor considers it necessary, more extensive testing of machinery and safety systems, and, on ships under the enhanced survey programme, a defined programme of tank examinations.
What it produces. An endorsement on the certificate in place of the annual endorsement. It does not produce a new certificate either.

When. At intervals not exceeding five years, completed before the certificate expires. It is also called the periodical or special survey, and in class practice it may be carried out progressively over the final years of the cycle rather than in one attendance.

Purpose. To establish that the ship is fit in every respect for the next five years of service. This is the only survey that asks that question. It is a complete re-examination, not a confirmation that nothing has changed.

Scope. The most extensive of the periodical surveys: examination of the structure inside and out, including drydocking or an approved in-water survey; internal examination of tanks and spaces; thickness measurement to establish wasted material, with substantial corrosion identified and the affected areas either renewed or brought under a defined monitoring regime; testing of tanks; opening up and examination of machinery, shafting and safety devices; overhaul or examination of boilers and pressure vessels; and full testing of the fire, life-saving and pollution prevention arrangements.
What it produces. A new certificate, valid for a further five years. It is the only one of the five surveys that does.

blocks.p: One practical point completes this section, because it is frequently examined: the bottom of the ship must be examined twice in every five-year period, one of those examinations being the renewal survey's docking, with a maximum interval between them - so drydocking is on a rhythm of its own within the cycle.

ul: When. Whenever the ship has suffered damage or a defect affecting her safety, her structural integrity, her class or the validity of a statutory certificate - grounding, contact, collision, fire, heavy weather damage, cargo or ballast tank failure, main engine or steering gear breakdown, shafting or rudder damage. It is not scheduled and there is no window.

Purpose. To establish what is damaged, how badly, and what must be done about it before the ship proceeds. It is a diagnostic survey: it determines the extent of the damage, its cause where that can be established, whether the ship remains fit to proceed and on what conditions, and what repair is required.

Scope. Confined to the damage and to anything the damage may have affected - and that qualification carries a mark, because grounding damage forward can affect tank boundaries, piping and structure well away from the visible dent.

Who calls it. The owner or master must report the damage - there is a standing duty to report a casualty or defect affecting the ship's safety or the efficiency or completeness of her equipment - and this is the survey candidates most often describe as though the surveyor turns up by himself. He does not; he is called.

What it produces. A survey report, a condition of class or a recommendation with a date by which the repair must be completed, and, where the damage is serious, a decision that the certificate is suspended or that the ship may proceed only to a repair port, in ballast, in fair weather, or under tow.

Insurance dimension. It also produces the technical evidence on which a hull and machinery claim will turn, and the surveyor's report is the document underwriters, average adjusters and, if it comes to it, a court will read.

When. During and after repair work - whether the repair follows a damage survey, is planned at a docking, or is the renewal of wasted structure found at a renewal survey. It commonly follows a damage survey but is a separate survey, and the difference between the two is the difference between diagnosis and treatment.

Purpose. To satisfy the society and the Administration that the repair has been carried out to an approved procedure, with approved materials, by qualified people, to the required standard, so that the ship is restored to the condition the certificate asserts.

Scope. Approval of the repair procedure before work begins; approval of materials and of welding procedures and welder qualifications; attendance during the work at agreed hold points; non-destructive examination of welds; and testing on completion - tank testing, pressure testing, operational testing of repaired machinery, and sea trials where the repair affects propulsion or steering.
What it produces. A report clearing the condition of class or recommendation that the damage survey raised, and the restoration or re-endorsement of the affected certificate.

The point that distinguishes a good answer. A repair carried out without the survey - even a technically excellent one - does not clear the condition, because what is being certified is not only that the steel is sound but that it was done under approval and witnessed. Emergency repairs at sea are accepted as temporary and must be reported and surveyed at the first opportunity.

blocks.h: 7. The harmonized system that ties the first three together

blocks.p: The three periodical surveys are not three independent regimes, and saying why earns marks. Before harmonization each convention ran its own survey cycle on its own dates, so a ship could face a Load Line survey in one port, a Safety Equipment survey two months later and an IOPP survey two months after that, with certificates of different lengths expiring at different times.
The Harmonized System of Survey and Certification, introduced by the 1988 Protocols to SOLAS and to the Load Line Convention and in force from 3 February 2000, fixed that:

ul: a common five-year period for the principal certificates;
a single anniversary date for the ship, to which every annual and intermediate survey is referred;
three-month windows either side of the anniversary date, so that surveys can be planned around the ship's trading pattern rather than dictating it;
a common vocabulary of initial, annual, intermediate, periodical, renewal and additional surveys across the instruments; and

provision for a certificate to be extended by a short period to allow a ship to complete a voyage to a port where the survey can be carried out - with the replacement certificate still dated from the original expiry, so that the extension does not buy extra time.

blocks.p: The operative survey guidance at this sitting is the Assembly's Survey Guidelines under the Harmonized System of Survey and Certification, resolution A.1156(32), which sets out for each certificate what the surveyor is to examine at each type of survey.

Damage and repair surveys sit entirely outside this scheme, which is why they have no windows, no anniversary and no guidelines of this kind - and that observation closes the first half of the question.

blocks.h: 8. The statutory certificates, their issuing authority and their convention

blocks.p: One standing note covers the whole register and saves repeating it in every line: the issuing authority is the flag State Administration in every case, and in practice most of these are issued by a Recognized Organization acting on the Administration's behalf under a specific delegation. Where a certificate is not delegable, or is not issued by the flag at all, the register says so.

blocks.p: Now the part that separates a strong answer. The stem asks for the IMO Convention under which they are issued - and several documents carried on board are not issued under an IMO convention at all. Name them and say what they are issued under:

ul: Certificate of Registry - issued by the flag State registry under national law, in India the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958. It is a document of nationality and title, not a technical certificate, and no IMO convention issues it.

Maritime Labour Certificate, and the Declaration of Maritime Labour Compliance Parts I and II - issued under MLC 2006, which is an International Labour Organization convention, not an IMO one. Part I states the flag State's own national requirements and is the flag's alone; Part II sets out the shipowner's measures and may be certified by an RO.

Ship Sanitation Control Certificate, or Ship Sanitation Control Exemption Certificate - issued by a port health authority under the International Health Regulations 2005, a World Health Organization instrument.

Certificates of competency, proficiency and endorsements - issued to seafarers by the Administration under STCW. An IMO convention, but the certificates are personal to the seafarer and are not ship certificates.

Certificate of Class - issued by the classification society under its own rules. It is not a statutory certificate at all, and it is the item most often wrongly included in this list. It is nonetheless indispensable, because most statutory certificates presuppose that the ship is in class.

blocks.p: Add the honest qualification: which certificates a particular ship carries depends on her type, size, trade and flag - a chemical tanker carries a Certificate of Fitness a bulk carrier does not, and a ship trading solely in domestic waters may carry national certificates in place of international ones.

Close on the proposition that connects the two halves of the question: a certificate is a statement that the ship was found to comply on a particular day. The periodical surveys keep that statement believable over five years; the occasional surveys are what happens when something occurs that makes it untrue.

The stem names five surveys as a list and the commonest failure is to describe them as five stages of one cycle. Section 1 refuses that in three lines - annual, intermediate and renewal are periodical and calendar-driven; damage and repair are occasional and event-driven - and that single distinction is worth more than any amount of detail about any one of them, because it is the discrimination the examiner set the question to test.

Sections 2 to 6 are deliberately parallel: when, purpose, scope, what it produces. The parallel structure lets a marker compare five surveys instantly, gives the candidate a template under time pressure, and makes one crucial fact visible - only the renewal survey produces a new certificate, while the annual and intermediate merely endorse one. That is a comparison an unstructured answer never quite makes.

In section 8 the table is the answer to the second limb, but the bulleted list after it is what earns the marks. The stem says 'the IMO Convention under which they are issued', and knowing that the Certificate of Registry is national, MLC is ILO, the Ship Sanitation Control Certificate is WHO and the Certificate of Class is not statutory at all is worth more than four more rows of the table.

ul: Presenting all five surveys as one cycle. Two of them are not in the cycle at all.
Saying the annual survey issues a certificate. It endorses one. Only the renewal survey issues a new certificate.
Putting the Certificate of Class in a list of statutory certificates. It is the society's own document under its own rules.
Forgetting the reporting duty in the damage survey. The surveyor is CALLED - the owner or master must report a casualty or defect. Candidates write as though he appears by himself.
Merging damage and repair surveys. One diagnoses, the other confirms the treatment; the repair survey is what clears the condition of class.
Saying a good repair clears the condition. It does not - the repair must be to an approved procedure and witnessed. That is what is being certified.
Omitting the harmonized system. The examiner named annual, intermediate and renewal in that order for a reason.
Listing certificates without their issuing authority or convention when the stem asks for all three columns.
Importing the 33rd Assembly resolution number for the survey guidelines. See the traps.

The Survey Guidelines under the HSSC at this sitting are A.1156(32), not A.1186(33). A.1186(33) was adopted 6 December 2023, four months AFTER this paper, and it revoked A.1156(32). Material written for any later sitting carries the later number.
The SOLAS Consolidated Edition current at this sitting is 2020, not 2024. The 2024 edition applies from 1 July 2024.
Only the renewal survey issues a certificate. Expect 'the surveyor has done your annual - what did you get?' An endorsement.
The intermediate survey REPLACES the second or third annual; it is not an extra survey on top of it.

An annual survey missed outside its window invalidates the certificate. Expect to be asked what happens if you cannot reach a surveyor - which is what the short extension provision is for, and the replacement certificate still runs from the original expiry, so the extension buys no time.
The bottom must be examined twice in five years, with a maximum interval between the two.
The Minimum Safe Manning Document, the Continuous Synopsis Record and Exemption Certificates are NOT delegable to a Recognized Organization.
MLC 2006 is an ILO convention, not IMO - and only Part II of the DMLC may be certified by an RO, Part I being the flag State's statement of its own law.
The Ship Sanitation Control Certificate is a WHO instrument issued by a port health authority under the International Health Regulations 2005.
CLC, Bunkers and wreck-removal certificates are financial security certificates issued by a State on evidence of insurance - they are not survey certificates and an RO does not issue them.

blocks.p: First hold the split: PERIODICAL - annual, intermediate, renewal; OCCASIONAL - damage, repair. For each survey hold the same four questions: WHEN - PURPOSE - SCOPE - WHAT IT PRODUCES. Hold one line for what each produces: ENDORSE - ENDORSE - NEW CERTIFICATE - CONDITION OF CLASS - CLEARS THE CONDITION. For the harmonized system hold FIVE YEARS - ANNIVERSARY DATE - THREE-MONTH WINDOWS - COMMON VOCABULARY - SHORT EXTENSION. For the certificate register run the instruments in order: SOLAS - LOAD LINES - TONNAGE - MARPOL - AFS - BWM - LIABILITY, then the four that are NOT IMO: REGISTRY, MLC, SANITATION, CLASS.

ul: SOLAS chapter I part B - surveys and certification: initial, annual, intermediate, periodical, renewal and additional surveys, and the duty to report a casualty or defect.

Harmonized System of Survey and Certification - introduced by the 1988 Protocols to SOLAS and to the Load Line Convention, in force 3 February 2000: five-year period, anniversary date, three-month windows, common survey vocabulary.

Tonnage Convention 1969 - the International Tonnage Certificate (1969).
MARPOL Annexes I, II, IV and VI - IOPP, NLS, ISPP, IAPP, EIAPP and IEE Certificates and the fuel oil consumption Statement of Compliance.
AFS 2001 and the BWM Convention 2004 - the anti-fouling and ballast water management certificates.
ISM Code (SOLAS IX) and ISPS Code (SOLAS XI-2) - the DOC, SMC and ISSC.
CLC 1992, Bunkers 2001, Nairobi WRC 2007 - financial security certificates issued by a State on evidence of insurance.

NOT IMO: Certificate of Registry (national law - in India the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958); MLC 2006 (ILO); Ship Sanitation Control Certificate (WHO, International Health Regulations 2005); Certificate of Class (the society's own rules).
No certificate validity period is asserted beyond the five-year harmonized period, which is stated because the harmonization cannot be explained without it. The stem does not ask for validity.
We hold no copy of A.1156(32). It is cited by identity, adopting session and revocation date only; no paragraph of the Survey Guidelines is quoted.
we hold SOLAS at citation level and not as quotable text. Chapter I part B is cited by identity and subject; no regulation number below part level is asserted for the survey scheme.
No class rule number is cited for damage survey, repair survey, the recording of a condition of class or the approval of a repair procedure. All four are described by function.

The register is the general set for a conventional cargo ship, with ship-type-specific certificates marked. What a particular ship carries depends on type, size, trade and flag, and the answer says so.
Damage and repair surveys have no MIW donor at all and are authored fresh from survey practice. They are the part of this answer with the least internal corroboration and the most examination value.

questions.understand_first: A certificate says one thing and only one thing: somebody competent looked at this ship and found her to comply. The difficulty is that the looking happened on a particular day and the certificate then has to stay believable for five years, during which the ship trades, corrodes, is loaded and unloaded and is sometimes damaged. Everything in this question is the machinery for keeping that statement honest. Most of it is a rhythm. Every year somebody comes and has a general look to see that nothing has gone backwards - quick, mostly visual, and it does not produce a certificate, it just keeps the existing one alive. Once in the middle of the five years the look goes deeper, because a walk round the deck will never find what is happening inside a ballast tank. And at the end of the five years the ship is examined properly from end to end, docked, measured for wasted steel, machinery opened up - and only that survey asks the real question, which is whether she is fit for the next five years. That is why only that one produces a new certificate. But two of the five surveys the examiner names have nothing to do with any of this rhythm, and noticing that is most of the question. When a ship hits something, catches fire, or breaks down, nobody waits for an anniversary. Somebody comes to find out what is broken and how bad it is - and then, separately, somebody comes to confirm that the fixing was done properly. Those two are called by events, not by the calendar. And there is a subtlety in the second of them worth holding: what is being approved is not just that the steel is now sound but that the repair was done to an agreed procedure and watched while it was done. A superb repair nobody witnessed does not clear anything, because the point of the whole system is not that the ship is good but that somebody accountable has said so.
questions.memory_cue: SPLIT - ANNUAL - INTERMEDIATE - RENEWAL - DAMAGE - REPAIR - HARMONIZED - CERTIFICATES (1 to 8). Inside steps 2 to 6 hold WHEN - PURPOSE - SCOPE - PRODUCES. What each produces: ENDORSE - ENDORSE - NEW CERTIFICATE - CONDITION OF CLASS - CLEARS THE CONDITION.

steps.title: The distinction that organises the whole answer
points: Annual, intermediate and renewal are PERIODICAL - calendar-driven, anchored to the anniversary date, and what keep certificates valid
Damage and repair are OCCASIONAL - event-driven, outside the cycle, with no window and no schedule
The stem names five as though they were one cycle; two of them are not in it
Any of the five may be done as a statutory survey or as a class survey, usually together
But the findings go to different places - a statutory finding affects a certificate, a class finding produces a condition of class

steps.title: Annual survey
points: WHEN: every year, within three months either side of the anniversary date
PURPOSE: to confirm the ship and equipment REMAIN satisfactory and have not been altered without approval
SCOPE: general, largely visual, afloat - hull, closing appliances, LSA, FFA, machinery running, documentation; selected items tested
PRODUCES: an ENDORSEMENT on the existing certificate, not a new one
Missed outside its window, the certificate is invalid

steps.title: Intermediate survey
points: WHEN: once per five-year period, in place of the second OR third annual survey
PURPOSE: a deeper check part-way through, because a visual annual cannot find deterioration inside tanks and structure
SCOPE: annual survey plus internal examination of selected spaces, thickness measurement where judged necessary, more extensive machinery and system testing, ESP programme where applicable
PRODUCES: an endorsement in place of the annual endorsement

steps.title: Renewal survey
points: WHEN: at intervals not exceeding five years, before the certificate expires; may be done progressively in class practice
PURPOSE: to establish fitness for the NEXT five years - the only survey that asks that question

SCOPE: structure inside and out with drydocking or approved in-water survey; tanks internally; thickness measurement and substantial corrosion identified and dealt with; machinery, shafting and safety devices opened up; boilers and pressure vessels; full system testing
PRODUCES: a NEW certificate - the only one of the five that does
The bottom must be examined twice in five years, with a maximum interval

steps.title: Damage survey
points: WHEN: whenever damage or a defect affects safety, structural integrity, class or certificate validity - unscheduled, no window
PURPOSE: to establish what is damaged, how badly, and what must be done before the ship proceeds
SCOPE: the damage and anything it may have affected - which reaches beyond the visible dent
The surveyor is CALLED: the owner or master must report a casualty or defect
PRODUCES: a report, a condition of class or recommendation with a date, and possibly suspension or a conditional voyage to a repair port
It also produces the technical evidence on which a hull and machinery claim turns

steps.title: Repair survey
points: WHEN: during and after repair - following damage, planned at docking, or renewing wasted structure found at renewal survey
PURPOSE: to confirm the repair was to an approved procedure, with approved materials, by qualified people, to standard

SCOPE: procedure approval BEFORE work begins; material, welding procedure and welder approval; attendance at hold points; NDT; testing on completion and sea trials where propulsion or steering is affected
PRODUCES: clearance of the condition of class and restoration of the affected certificate
A technically excellent unwitnessed repair does NOT clear the condition - approval and witness are what is certified
Emergency repairs at sea are temporary, and must be reported and surveyed at the first opportunity

steps.title: The harmonized system that ties the first three together
points: Before it, each convention ran its own cycle on its own dates with certificates of different lengths
Introduced by the 1988 Protocols to SOLAS and Load Lines, in force 3 February 2000
A common five-year period; a single anniversary date; three-month windows
A common vocabulary of initial, annual, intermediate, periodical, renewal and additional surveys
A short extension to complete a voyage - and the replacement certificate still runs from the ORIGINAL expiry
Survey guidance at this sitting is resolution A.1156(32)
Damage and repair surveys sit entirely outside this scheme, which is why they have no windows

steps.title: The statutory certificates, their issuing authority and their convention
points: Standing note: the issuing authority is the flag Administration, most often through an RO under a specific delegation

SOLAS - Safety Construction, Safety Equipment, Safety Radio or the combined Cargo Ship Safety Certificate; Passenger Ship Safety; DG document; Certificates of Fitness; DOC and SMC; ISSC; CSR; Safe Manning; Polar; grain authorization
Load Lines 1966 / 1988 Protocol - International Load Line Certificate
Tonnage 1969 - International Tonnage Certificate
MARPOL - IOPP, NLS, ISPP, IAPP, EIAPP, IEE and the fuel oil consumption Statement of Compliance
AFS 2001 and BWM 2004 - anti-fouling and ballast water certificates
CLC, Bunkers and Nairobi - financial security certificates issued by a State on evidence of insurance, not survey certificates
NOT delegable: Exemption Certificates, the Continuous Synopsis Record, the Minimum Safe Manning Document
NOT IMO at all: Certificate of Registry (national law), MLC 2006 (ILO), Ship Sanitation Control Certificate (WHO), and the Certificate of Class (the society's own rules)
What a ship carries depends on her type, size, trade and flag

quick_revision.recall_15s: Three periodical, two occasional. Annual - yearly within three months of the anniversary, general and visual, ENDORSES. Intermediate - replaces the second or third annual, goes inside tanks, ENDORSES. Renewal - five-yearly, drydocking, thickness measurement, machinery opened, issues a NEW certificate. Damage - event-driven, diagnoses, raises a condition of class; the surveyor is called. Repair - confirms the fix was to an approved procedure and witnessed, and CLEARS the condition. Harmonized system: 1988 Protocols, in force 3 February 2000 - five years, anniversary date, three-month windows. Guidelines at this sitting: A.1156(32).
quick_revision.critical_numbers: Five years - the harmonized certificate period and the renewal survey interval. Three months either side of the anniversary date - the annual survey window. The intermediate replaces the second or third annual. The bottom is examined twice in five years. 3 February 2000 - the harmonized system in force, from the 1988 Protocols. A.1156(32) - the operative Survey Guidelines. Three periodical surveys and two occasional ones.
quick_revision.critical_regulation: The Harmonized System of Survey and Certification, introduced by the 1988 Protocols to SOLAS and the Load Line Convention and in force from 3 February 2000. If you remember one thing about it, remember what it fixed: before it, each convention ran its own survey cycle on its own dates, so a ship met surveyors in three different ports for three different certificates. One anniversary date, one five-year period and three-month windows are what let a ship be surveyed around her trading pattern instead of despite it.
quick_revision.major_trap: Citing A.1186(33) for the HSSC Survey Guidelines. It was adopted 6 December 2023, four months after this sitting, and it revoked A.1156(32), which is the operative edition here. The related edition trap is the SOLAS Consolidated Edition: the current one at this sitting is 2020, not 2024. Circulating material written for a 2024 or later sitting carries both later references.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the surveys and certificates question.
retrieval_cards.answer: 1 the periodical-versus-occasional distinction; 2 annual; 3 intermediate; 4 renewal; 5 damage; 6 repair; 7 the harmonized system that ties the first three together; 8 the certificate register with issuing authority and convention, plus the documents that are not issued under an IMO convention at all. Each survey is given as when, purpose, scope and what it produces.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is the single distinction that organises the five surveys?
retrieval_cards.answer: Annual, intermediate and renewal are PERIODICAL: calendar-driven, anchored to the anniversary date, and what keep the certificates valid - they are what the harmonized system co-ordinates. Damage and repair are OCCASIONAL: event-driven, with no window, no anniversary and no place in any schedule. The stem names all five as though they were stages of one cycle, and two of them are not in the cycle at all.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which of the five surveys issues a certificate?
retrieval_cards.answer: Only the renewal survey. It is the only one that asks whether the ship is fit for the NEXT five years, and it produces a new certificate valid for a further five. Annual and intermediate surveys ENDORSE the existing certificate - the intermediate endorsement taking the place of the second or third annual. A damage survey produces a condition of class; a repair survey clears it.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is a damage survey for, and who calls it?
retrieval_cards.answer: To establish what is damaged, how badly, and what must be done before the ship proceeds - a diagnostic survey covering the damage and anything it may have affected, which reaches beyond the visible dent. The owner or master must report the casualty or defect: the surveyor is called, he does not appear by himself. It produces a report, a condition of class with a date, possibly a conditional voyage to a repair port, and the technical evidence for any insurance claim.

retrieval_cards.prompt: You made an excellent permanent repair with your own crew and no surveyor. Is the condition of class cleared?
retrieval_cards.answer: No. What the repair survey certifies is not only that the steel is sound but that the repair was carried out to an APPROVED PROCEDURE, with approved materials and qualified welders, and was WITNESSED. Procedure approval is required before work begins, with attendance at hold points, non-destructive examination and testing on completion. An unwitnessed repair, however good, clears nothing. Emergency repairs at sea are accepted as temporary and must be reported and surveyed at the first opportunity.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What did the Harmonized System of Survey and Certification change, and when did it come in?
retrieval_cards.answer: Before it, each convention ran its own survey cycle on its own dates with certificates of different lengths, so a ship met surveyors in different ports for different certificates. The 1988 Protocols to SOLAS and the Load Line Convention, in force 3 February 2000, gave a common five-year period, a single anniversary date, three-month windows either side of it, a common survey vocabulary, and a short extension to complete a voyage - with the replacement certificate still running from the original expiry.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which Survey Guidelines under the HSSC are operative at an August 2023 sitting?
retrieval_cards.answer: Resolution A.1156(32) of 2021. NOT A.1186(33), which was adopted 6 December 2023 - four months after this sitting - and revoked them. The parallel edition trap is the SOLAS Consolidated Edition: the current one here is 2020, the 2024 edition applying from 1 July 2024. Material written for a later sitting carries both later references.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Name documents carried on board that are NOT issued under an IMO convention.
retrieval_cards.answer: The Certificate of Registry, issued under national law - in India the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958. The Maritime Labour Certificate and DMLC, under MLC 2006, which is an ILO convention. The Ship Sanitation Control Certificate, issued by a port health authority under the International Health Regulations 2005, a WHO instrument. And the Certificate of Class, issued by the society under its own rules and not a statutory certificate at all.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Name three certificates a Recognized Organization cannot issue on the flag State's behalf.
retrieval_cards.answer: Exemption Certificates, because exempting a ship is a sovereign act belonging to the Administration; the Continuous Synopsis Record, which is the flag's own record of the ship's history; and the Minimum Safe Manning Document, which is the Administration's determination of what manning the ship needs. Also not delegable in practice are DMLC Part I, which states the flag's own national requirements, and the CLC, Bunkers and wreck-removal financial security certificates, which are issued by a State on evidence of insurance rather than after a survey.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Your Safety Equipment Certificate expires in a week and no surveyor is available where you are.
retrieval_cards.answer: The harmonized system provides for a short extension to allow the ship to complete her voyage to a port where the survey can be carried out - but the replacement certificate is still dated from the ORIGINAL expiry, so the extension buys no additional validity. Separately, an annual survey not completed within its three-month window renders the certificate invalid, which is a different and harsher rule from expiry.

decomposition_gate.question_intent: A composite question with two tasks and a hidden discrimination. The first task looks like recall - differentiate five named surveys - but the examiner has deliberately mixed three periodical surveys with two occasional ones, and the candidate who does not notice writes five paragraphs about one cycle. The second task is a register, and its own hidden discrimination is the phrase 'the IMO Convention under which they are issued', which is untrue of several documents every ship carries. The examiner is testing boundaries in both halves, not list length.
decomposition_gate.mark_allocation: Sixteen marks with no printed split. Three tasks are set - differentiate five surveys, give the purpose of each, and list the certificates with issuing authority and convention - and the first two are really one. The answer allots one framing section, five parallel survey sections, one section on the harmonized system that makes the first three intelligible as a system, and one substantial section carrying the register and the non-IMO documents. The proportions give slightly more to the surveys than to the register, because a list can be produced quickly under pressure and a differentiation cannot.
decomposition_gate.examiner_expectation: That the periodical and occasional surveys are separated. That the purpose of each is given, since the stem asks for purposes explicitly. That only the renewal survey is said to issue a certificate. That the damage survey is described as reported and called, not as spontaneous. That the repair survey is distinguished from it and that approval-and-witness is identified as what is being certified. That the certificate list gives all three columns the stem asks for. And that the Certificate of Class is kept out of a statutory list.
decomposition_gate.primary_source_plan: Carry the annual survey and condition of class from the MIW verification record for QP2310 Q2; the annual-versus-periodical distinction from QP2312 Q8 and QP2509 Q9; renewal depth, thickness measurement and substantial corrosion from QP2503 Q2 and QP2507 Q7; and the certificate register structure and the harmonization argument from QP2406 Q1, extended from its oil-tanker set to the general set. Author damage and repair surveys fresh from survey practice, no donor existing. Anchor the survey guidance on A.1156(32) by identity and reverse the donors' A.1186(33). Deliberately NOT planned: any quotation of SOLAS or of the Survey Guidelines; any certificate validity period beyond the five-year harmonized period; any class rule number; any ship recycling or MLC 2022 amendment content.
decomposition_gate.freshness_risk: MEDIUM - The survey scheme, the harmonized system and the certificate regime are all stable and need no reversal. The moving parts are two edition references: A.1156(32) is the operative Survey Guidelines here and every donor carries the 33rd Assembly successor adopted four months later; and the current SOLAS Consolidated Edition is 2020 rather than 2024. Two further currency points were checked and cleared by exclusion - the Hong Kong Convention is not in force so no recycling certificate belongs in the register, and the MLC 2022 amendments are not in force so nothing in the MLC entry depends on them.
decomposition_gate.jurisdiction_risk: HIGH, and it is concentrated in the register. Four legal orders appear in a list that looks homogeneous: IMO conventions, under which most of the certificates are issued; national law, under which the Certificate of Registry is issued; other United Nations agencies - the ILO for MLC 2006 and the WHO for the Ship Sanitation Control Certificate; and the classification society's own rules, under which the Certificate of Class is issued and which is not statutory at all. An answer that presents all of them as IMO certificates has the orders confused, and the stem's own wording invites exactly that error.
decomposition_gate.technical_ambiguities: 'Repair survey' is not a defined term in the conventions and is used in class practice for two related things - attendance during a repair following damage, and attendance during planned repair or steel renewal at a docking. The answer covers both and says so rather than choosing. 'Enlist ALL statutory certificates' is impossible to satisfy literally, since the set depends on ship type, size, trade and flag; the answer gives the general set for a conventional cargo ship, marks the ship-type-specific entries, and states the qualification explicitly rather than implying completeness it cannot have.
decomposition_gate.target_answer_shape: Eight numbered sections. A short bulleted framing section carrying the periodical-versus-occasional split. Five parallel survey sections, each a bulleted WHEN / PURPOSE / SCOPE / PRODUCES so that five surveys can be compared at a glance and the candidate has a template. A bulleted section on the harmonized system. A final section with a standing note on issuing authority, the register as a rendered THREE-COLUMN TABLE by instrument, a bulleted list of documents NOT issued under an IMO convention, an honest completeness qualification, and a closing single-sentence proposition joining the two halves.

reverify_before_publication.claim: That resolution A.1156(32) of 2021 is the operative Survey Guidelines under the Harmonized System of Survey and Certification at an August 2023 sitting, A.1186(33) having been adopted 6 December 2023 and having revoked them; and that the current SOLAS Consolidated Edition at this sitting is 2020, not 2024.
reverify_before_publication.why: This is the reversal on this question and it is the claim most at risk of being silently undone. Every donor read for this answer sits after 6 December 2023 and correctly carries the later resolution, so a reviewer moving between papers will read A.1156(32) as stale. It is not. MIW holds no copy of either resolution; identity and revocation dates come from its own read-at-source records.

reverify_before_publication.claim: That no ship recycling certificate, no International Certificate on Inventory of Hazardous Materials and no MLC 2022 amendment content belongs in the certificate register at this sitting.
reverify_before_publication.why: Checked rather than assumed. The Hong Kong Convention entered into force 26 June 2025 and the MLC 2022 amendments on 23 December 2024, both after this sitting. Recorded because a certificate register is precisely where a later-paper habit adds a row, and because the omission would otherwise look like an oversight rather than a decision.

reverify_before_publication.claim: The description of damage and repair surveys - their triggers, the reporting duty, the raising and clearing of a condition of class, and the requirement that a repair procedure be approved before work begins and the work witnessed.
reverify_before_publication.why: These have NO MIW donor anywhere in the corpus and are authored fresh from survey practice. No class rule number is cited, MIW holding no class rule text, and all four elements are described by function. This is the part of the answer with the least internal corroboration and it should be the first thing a reviewer with survey experience checks.

reverify_before_publication.claim: That the certificate register is the general set for a conventional cargo ship and cannot be complete, what a particular ship carries depending on her type, size, trade and flag.
reverify_before_publication.why: The stem says 'enlist ALL statutory certificates', which is not literally satisfiable. The answer states the qualification in its own text and marks ship-type-specific entries, but a reviewer could read the table as a claim of completeness. It is not, and no flag's certificate schedule is held by MIW.
