blocks.h: 1. The Code, and how a recommendatory text came to bind

blocks.p: The IMO Instruments Implementation Code - the III Code - was adopted by the Assembly as resolution A.1070(28) on 4 December 2013, its operative paragraph revoking A.1054(27), the 2011 Code that had supported the voluntary audit scheme.

Begin with the point that most answers miss, because it explains the instrument rather than summarising it. The Code is written in 'should' from beginning to end. It was never redrafted into obligation language. What binds is not the Code's own wording but the fact that the conventions were amended to require its use - by A.1083(28), A.1084(28) and A.1085(28) for Load Lines, Tonnage and COLREG; by MSC.366(93), MSC.373(93), MSC.374(93) and MSC.375(93) for SOLAS, STCW, the STCW Code and the 1988 Load Line Protocol; and by MEPC.246(66) and MEPC.247(66) for MARPOL and its 1997 Protocol. It became mandatory from 1 January 2016, and the IMO Member State Audit Scheme became mandatory with it, using the Code as its audit standard.

Recognise the technique, because it recurs across this paper: a standard is adopted as a code and then made binding by amending the conventions that refer to it - exactly as the ISM, ISPS and RO Codes were.

The Code has four parts: common areas, then flag States, coastal States and port States - and each of the three State parts closes on evaluation and review of its own performance, which is the Code's characteristic move and the reason limb (b) exists.
The objective is stated in the annex's first paragraph and it has two halves. The second half is routinely dropped and it is half the sentence:

ul: to enhance global maritime safety and protection of the marine environment; and
to assist States in the implementation of instruments of the Organization.

blocks.p: The assisting half matters because it fixes the Code's character. It is not a new set of technical requirements. It is a statement of what a State has to be able to do in order to make instruments it has already ratified actually work - which is the gap between ratification and effect that Q7 of this paper is about.
Three further propositions from the common part complete the objective:

ul: A State is bound only in respect of instruments to which it is a Contracting Government or Party. The Code creates no obligation under a treaty a State has not joined.

Which role dominates is decided by geography and circumstance. A large flag with little coastline is engaged mainly as a flag State; an archipelagic State with few ships is engaged mainly as a coastal State. The Code addresses all three roles because most States occupy all three.

The State is to promulgate laws and take all other steps necessary to give the instruments full and complete effect - and, in a provision worth quoting in substance, is not to transfer damage or hazards from one area to another, or transform one type of pollution into another.

blocks.h: 3. The strategy recommended to the flag State

blocks.p: The Code's strategy paragraph has three limbs and they are a cycle, not a document:

ol: Develop an overall strategy to ensure that the State's international obligations are met, covering its flag, port and coastal roles together rather than separately.
Establish a methodology to monitor and assess that the strategy is in fact delivering implementation and enforcement - so the strategy has to be measurable.
Continuously review it in order to achieve, maintain and improve overall performance and capability.

blocks.p: Develop - monitor - review. That is the answer to 'the strategy recommended to flag state', and it should be given in those terms rather than as a list of good intentions.

The Code then says what the strategy must be built on. National legislation and administrative procedures must address the whole field the instruments cover, and the State must be able to communicate the strategy and the legislation to everybody concerned. Most usefully for an examination answer, the Code identifies three initial actions a State must take before anything else is possible:

ul: the ability to promulgate laws giving the instruments effect;
a legal basis for enforcement and verification - the power to inspect, detain, penalise and prosecute; and
sufficient personnel with maritime expertise to do the work.

blocks.p: That third item is why the Code exists at all: a State that has ratified a convention and has no surveyors has implemented nothing.

blocks.h: 4. Which IMO instruments the Code covers

blocks.p: The printed question - 'Which all IMO instruments covered in the code' - is ambiguous, and there are two correct answers. Give both and say why they differ; that is what a careful candidate does.
First answer - the six subject areas. The Code's own scope paragraph names six areas and names no convention at all:

ul: safety of life at sea;
prevention of pollution from ships;
standards of training, certification and watchkeeping;
load lines;
tonnage measurement of ships; and
preventing collisions at sea.

blocks.p: Note carefully what is not there: maritime security is not one of the six, although the preamble refers to security. That is a favourite examination point.

Second answer - the treaty instruments under which the Code is actually mandatory. These are the conventions that were amended to require it, and the Assembly maintains a non-exhaustive list of obligations under instruments relevant to the Code. At this sitting that list is resolution A.1157(32). The instruments are SOLAS 1974 with its 1978 and 1988 Protocols; MARPOL and its 1997 Protocol; STCW 1978 and the STCW Code; the Load Line Convention 1966 and its 1988 Protocol; the Tonnage Convention 1969; and COLREG 1972.
Do not lead with a count. Neither the Code nor the list states a number, and both nine and ten circulate depending on how the Protocols are counted. List the instruments.

blocks.h: 5. Key performance indicators for flag State performance

blocks.p: This is limb (b), and it is short, factual and heavily marked. The Code requires the flag State to evaluate its own performance on a periodic basis, in respect of its processes, procedures and resources, and it offers indicators for doing so.

ul: Port State control detention rates.
Flag State inspection results.
Casualty statistics.
Communication and information processes.
Annual loss statistics - excluding constructive total losses.

blocks.p: Two propositions about these indicators separate a good answer from a list.

ul: Their stated purpose is diagnostic. They exist so the State can determine whether its staffing, resources and procedures are adequate to meet its obligations - not to produce a league table.

They are for the State's own self-evaluation, not a return to the Organization. The Code is not a reporting regime; the external check is the Member State Audit Scheme, which is a different mechanism.

blocks.p: The Code then lists further areas for regular review, and naming several of them shows depth: detentions in relation to the size of the fleet; incompetence or misconduct of individuals holding certificates the State has issued; the State's responses to port State control deficiency reports; serious casualty investigations and the lessons taken from them; pollution violations; and the suspension or withdrawal of certificates and of delegations.
Notice the shape of the list: it is designed to catch a flag State that issues certificates freely and does nothing when the ships carrying them are detained abroad.
Limb (c) has three parts and the flag State's is the largest. Give it under six heads.

ul: Implementation. Establish and maintain a safety and environmental protection programme, with minimum elements including policy and instructions, resources, an audit and inspection programme independent of any body issuing the certificates, and defined responsibilities. That independence requirement is the same principle as the RO Code's and is worth naming.
Manning. Ensure ships are sufficiently and efficiently manned, applying the Organization's Principles of Safe Manning, and issue the manning document.

Delegation. Where survey and certification are delegated to a recognized organization, do so under a formal written agreement, give specific instructions on what is to happen when a ship is found unfit to proceed to sea, and maintain an oversight programme with supplementary surveys and competent supervising staff. This limb connects directly to Q5 of this paper.

Enforcement. Prohibit a ship from sailing until she complies; inspect periodically; provide penalties of adequate severity to discourage violation; and institute proceedings after investigation irrespective of where the violation occurred - which is the provision that makes flag State jurisdiction real rather than territorial.
Surveyors. Ensure surveyors and investigators are qualified, trained and carry identification documents, whether they are the State's own staff or an RO's.
Casualty investigation. Investigate impartially and objectively, with a view to prevention rather than blame, and report to the Organization.

blocks.p: And the part closes, as every State part does, on evaluation and review - which is limb (b) above.

This is the limb candidates most often leave empty, and the reason is that they look for controls over ships and find none. The coastal State's obligations under the Code are overwhelmingly SERVICES TO SHIPPING, not controls over it. Say that first and the limb writes itself.

The Code opens the part with a general proposition that applies to coastal and port States alike: exercising a right conferred by an instrument incurs the additional obligations that go with it. A State that claims jurisdiction over its waters accepts the duty to service them.
The service areas are:

ul: radiocommunication services;
meteorological services and warnings;
search and rescue services;
hydrographic services - surveying and charting;
ships' routeing systems;
ship reporting systems;
vessel traffic services; and
aids to navigation.

blocks.p: Beyond the services, the coastal State should operate a control and monitoring programme within its waters, be able to respond in a timely way to pollution incidents, and co-operate in casualty investigation where a casualty occurs in its waters or involves its interests. And it too must periodically evaluate its own performance.

blocks.h: 8. Port State responsibilities, and how the three roles interlock

blocks.p: The port State part is short and has three obligations at its centre:

ul: provide adequate reception facilities for ship-generated waste - the obligation whose absence undermines MARPOL more than any other single failure;
operate port State control; and
maintain a register of local fuel oil suppliers, which is the enforcement handle for fuel quality.

blocks.p: Three further propositions carry the marks:

ul: No more favourable treatment. A ship flying the flag of a State that is not party to an instrument is not to receive more favourable treatment than a ship of a Party. Without this the whole convention system could be evaded by re-flagging.

The port State control programme should be consistent with the Assembly's Procedures for Port State Control - at this sitting, resolution A.1155(32) - and in practice with the regional memorandum of understanding to which the State belongs.

Port State control officers must be free of commercial pressure, and must not be employed by, or undertake work on behalf of, recognized organizations or classification societies. The reason is exact: a PSCO checking a certificate issued by his own employer is checking his employer's work, and the whole value of port State control is that it is an independent second look at what the flag State and its RO have certified.

blocks.p: And the port State part, like the others, ends on periodic evaluation of its own performance.

Close by joining the three roles, because that is what the limb is really asking and it converts a list into an understanding. The flag State certifies its own ships wherever they are; the coastal State provides the services and monitors the waters it claims; the port State takes an independent second look at ships that come to it. The three overlap deliberately, so that a failure by one is caught by another - a flag that certifies too easily is exposed by detentions abroad, and those detention rates come back to it as the first of its own performance indicators. The Code's real subject is not any of the three roles but the closing of the loop between them - and above all three sits the Member State Audit Scheme, under which the State is itself audited against this Code.

The stem prints three lettered limbs, and the later sittings of this identical question print (6), (4) and (6) against them - a split that is not printed here but is a fair guide to the examiner's intent. The structure follows it: sections 2 to 4 answer limb (a), section 5 answers limb (b), and sections 6 to 8 answer limb (c), with section 1 supplying the framing that makes all three intelligible.

Section 1 is not preamble. The single most valuable observation about the III Code is that it is written in 'should' throughout and binds only because the conventions were amended to require it. A candidate who says that has explained an instrument; one who does not has summarised a document. It also sets up the technique - code adopted, then made mandatory through the conventions - which appears twice more on this paper, at Q5 and Q7.

Section 7 is where the marks are quietly available. Almost every candidate writes a long flag State section and a reasonable port State section, and then produces two vague lines on coastal States. The reason is that they are looking for controls over ships. Once you see that the coastal State's obligations are SERVICES - radio, weather, search and rescue, charts, routeing, reporting, VTS, lights - the limb becomes a list you can actually write.

ul: Giving only the first half of the objective. It is to enhance safety and environmental protection AND to assist States in implementation. The second half is what the Code is actually for.
Answering 'which instruments' with only one of the two possible answers. The six subject areas and the treaty instruments are different answers to an ambiguous question - give both.
Including maritime security in the six subject areas. It is not one of them.
Leading with a count of instruments. Neither the Code nor the Assembly's list states a number, and both nine and ten circulate.
Writing the coastal State limb as controls over shipping. It is services TO shipping.
Treating the performance indicators as a report to IMO. They are the State's own self-evaluation; the external check is the Audit Scheme.
Forgetting that annual loss statistics EXCLUDE constructive total losses.
Omitting the port State's reception facility obligation, which is the one whose absence does most damage in practice.
Citing the 33rd Assembly resolution numbers. See the traps - this is the single largest risk on this question.
The list of obligations at this sitting is A.1157(32), NOT A.1187(33). A.1187(33) was adopted 6 December 2023 - four months after this paper - and revoked it.

The Procedures for Port State Control at this sitting are A.1155(32), NOT A.1185(33). Same date, same boundary, same trap. Circulating material written for any later sitting carries both later numbers.
The Code itself is A.1070(28) of 4 December 2013 and is unaffected. It was the LISTS that were replaced, not the Code - and confusing the two is the error the reversal invites.
The Code reads in 'should'. Expect 'if it only says should, how is it mandatory?' Because the conventions were amended to require its use, from 1 January 2016.
Maritime security is not one of the six subject areas.
The flag State's audit and inspection programme must be independent of any body issuing the certificates. Same principle as the RO Code's independence requirement.

Port State control officers must not be employed by, or work for, recognized organizations or classification societies. A PSCO checking his own employer's certificate is not an independent second look.
Proceedings are instituted irrespective of where the violation occurred. That is what makes flag State jurisdiction real.
Constructive total losses are excluded from the annual loss statistic. A small point that is asked because it shows whether the candidate has read the indicator or recited it.
The III Code says 'should' everywhere. So is it mandatory, and how?
What are the two halves of the Code's objective?
Name the six subject areas. Is security one of them?
How many instruments is the Code mandatory under?
Give me the flag State performance indicators. Who are they for?
Your flag has a high detention rate abroad. What does the Code expect it to do about that?
What does a coastal State actually have to provide?
Why must a port State control officer not work for a classification society?
What is no more favourable treatment, and what would happen without it?
Who audits the flag State, and against what standard?

blocks.p: The route is HOW IT BINDS - OBJECTIVE - STRATEGY - INSTRUMENTS - INDICATORS - FLAG - COASTAL - PORT, which maps onto framing, limb (a) in three parts, limb (b), and limb (c) in three parts. For the strategy hold DEVELOP - MONITOR - REVIEW. For the six areas hold SAFETY - POLLUTION - TRAINING - LOAD LINES - TONNAGE - COLLISIONS. For the indicators hold DETENTIONS - INSPECTIONS - CASUALTIES - COMMUNICATION - LOSSES. For the coastal State hold RADIO - WEATHER - SAR - CHARTS - ROUTEING - REPORTING - VTS - LIGHTS. For the port State hold RECEPTION - CONTROL - FUEL REGISTER. And hold the closing idea: the Code's subject is the closing of the loop between the three roles.

questions.understand_first: A country can sign a treaty in the morning and change nothing at all. Signing is a promise; keeping it needs laws on the statute book, inspectors who exist and are trained, an office that answers letters, and courts that will actually fine somebody. For years the uncomfortable truth was that some States had ratified everything and implemented almost nothing, and there was no polite way of saying so. The III Code is the answer to that - not a new set of technical rules about ships, but a description of what a State has to be able to do before its ratifications mean anything. Notice the shape of it. A State meets shipping wearing three different hats and the Code takes them one at a time. As a flag, it is responsible for its own ships wherever in the world they are - certifying them, manning them, and going after them when they misbehave abroad. As a coastal State, its duties are mostly the opposite of policing: it has to provide things - charts, weather, radio, search and rescue, buoys, traffic services - because claiming authority over a stretch of sea comes with the job of making it safe to cross. And as a port State, it takes an independent second look at foreign ships that visit, which is the check on the first hat being worn carelessly by somebody else. The clever part, and the thing to carry away, is that each part ends by telling the State to measure itself. A flag State is told to watch how often its ships are detained in other people's ports - which is exactly the evidence that a foreign inspector, not itself, has produced. So the three roles are deliberately overlapped, the failures of one showing up in the records of another, and the whole thing is then audited from outside against this same Code.

quick_revision.recall_15s: A.1070(28), 4 December 2013, mandatory 1 January 2016 - and it binds only because the conventions were amended to require it, since the Code itself says 'should'. Objective has two halves: enhance safety and environmental protection, AND assist States to implement. Strategy is develop - monitor - review. Six areas: safety, pollution, training, load lines, tonnage, collisions - security is NOT one. Indicators: detentions, inspections, casualties, communication, losses (excluding CTLs). Flag certifies, coastal SERVICES, port takes the second look. At this sitting: A.1157(32) and A.1155(32), not the 33rd Assembly numbers.
quick_revision.critical_numbers: A.1070(28), adopted 4 December 2013, mandatory 1 January 2016; revoked A.1054(27). Four parts. Six subject areas. Three initial actions. Five performance indicators. Eight coastal State service areas. Three port State obligations. Flag State part at paragraphs 15 to 44, coastal at 45 to 51, port at 52 to 63. Operative Assembly instruments at this sitting: A.1157(32) and A.1155(32).
quick_revision.critical_regulation: Resolution A.1070(28) - the III Code itself. If you remember one thing, remember why a document that says 'should' on every page is nonetheless mandatory: the conventions were amended to require its use, from 1 January 2016, by a chain of Assembly, MSC and MEPC resolutions. The same technique made the ISM, ISPS and RO Codes binding, and recognising it is worth a mark in the oral.
quick_revision.major_trap: Citing A.1187(33) for the list of obligations or A.1185(33) for the Procedures for Port State Control. Both were adopted 6 December 2023 - four months after this sitting - and each revoked its 32nd Assembly predecessor. The operative instruments here are A.1157(32) and A.1155(32). All three integrated sittings of this identical question sit after that boundary and correctly carry the later numbers, so every piece of circulating material is wrong for this paper. Note that the Code itself, A.1070(28), is NOT reversed - it was the lists that were replaced, not the Code.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the III Code question.
retrieval_cards.answer: 1 how a text written in 'should' came to bind; 2 the objective; 3 the strategy; 4 which instruments are covered - both answers; 5 the performance indicators; 6 flag State responsibilities; 7 coastal State responsibilities; 8 port State responsibilities and how the three interlock. Sections 2-4 are limb (a), section 5 is limb (b), sections 6-8 are limb (c).

retrieval_cards.prompt: The III Code says 'should' throughout. How is it mandatory?
retrieval_cards.answer: Because the conventions were amended to require its use. The Code, resolution A.1070(28) of 4 December 2013, was never redrafted into obligation language; instead A.1083(28), A.1084(28) and A.1085(28) amended Load Lines, Tonnage and COLREG, MSC.366(93) and MSC.373-375(93) amended SOLAS, STCW, the STCW Code and the 1988 Load Line Protocol, and MEPC.246(66) and MEPC.247(66) amended MARPOL and its 1997 Protocol. Mandatory from 1 January 2016.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What are the two halves of the Code's objective?
retrieval_cards.answer: To enhance global maritime safety and protection of the marine environment, AND to assist States in the implementation of instruments of the Organization. The second half is routinely dropped and it is what fixes the Code's character: it is not a new set of technical requirements about ships but a statement of what a State must be able to do to make instruments it has already ratified actually work.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Name the six subject areas the Code covers - and the one that is not there.
retrieval_cards.answer: Safety of life at sea; prevention of pollution from ships; standards of training, certification and watchkeeping; load lines; tonnage measurement of ships; and preventing collisions at sea. MARITIME SECURITY IS NOT ONE OF THEM, although the preamble refers to security. Note that this is one of two correct answers to 'which instruments' - the other is the list of treaty instruments under which the Code is mandatory.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the flag State performance indicators, and say who they are for.
retrieval_cards.answer: Port State control detention rates; flag State inspection results; casualty statistics; communication and information processes; and annual loss statistics excluding constructive total losses. Their purpose is diagnostic - to let the State determine whether its staffing, resources and procedures are adequate - and they are for the State's own periodic self-evaluation, not a return to IMO. The external check is the Member State Audit Scheme.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What does a coastal State actually have to do under the Code?
retrieval_cards.answer: Provide services, not controls. Radiocommunication services; meteorological services and warnings; search and rescue; hydrographic services; ships' routeing systems; ship reporting systems; vessel traffic services; and aids to navigation. Beyond those, a control and monitoring programme in its waters, timely response to pollution incidents, cooperation in casualty investigation, and periodic self-evaluation. Candidates leave this limb empty because they look for controls over ships and find none.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the port State's three central obligations, and the independence rule.
retrieval_cards.answer: Adequate reception facilities for ship-generated waste; port State control; and a register of local fuel oil suppliers. Plus no more favourable treatment for ships of non-parties, and a PSC programme consistent with the Assembly's Procedures and the regional MOU. Port State control officers must be free of commercial pressure and must not be employed by, or work for, recognized organizations or classification societies - a PSCO checking his own employer's certificate is not an independent second look.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which Assembly resolutions are operative at an August 2023 sitting for the obligations list and for port State control procedures?
retrieval_cards.answer: A.1157(32) for the non-exhaustive list of obligations, and A.1155(32) for the Procedures for Port State Control, 2021. NOT A.1187(33) and A.1185(33), both adopted 6 December 2023 - four months after this paper - each revoking its predecessor. Note that the Code itself, A.1070(28), is NOT reversed: it was the lists that were replaced, not the Code.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How do the three State roles interlock, and why does that matter?
retrieval_cards.answer: The flag State certifies its own ships wherever they are; the coastal State provides services and monitors the waters it claims; the port State takes an independent second look at visiting ships. They overlap deliberately, so a failure by one is caught by another - a flag that certifies too easily is exposed by detentions abroad, and those detention rates come back as the first of its own performance indicators. Above all three sits the Member State Audit Scheme.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How many IMO instruments is the III Code mandatory under?
retrieval_cards.answer: Do not give a number. Neither A.1070(28) nor the Assembly's list of obligations states one. Nine circulates because it counts SOLAS 1974, SOLAS PROT 1988, MARPOL, MARPOL PROT 1997, STCW 1978, LL 1966, LL PROT 1988, TONNAGE 1969 and COLREG 1972; ten circulates because the list also carries a SOLAS PROT 1978 column. List the instruments instead of counting them.

decomposition_gate.question_intent: Three printed limbs testing three different things: knowledge of an instrument, knowledge of a short factual list, and understanding of how the three State roles fit together. The examiner is testing whether the candidate grasps that the III Code is about STATE CAPABILITY rather than about ships. Two discriminators: limb (b) is short, factual and either known or not; and within limb (c) the coastal State part is where most answers collapse, because candidates search for controls over shipping and the Code's coastal obligations are services to it.
decomposition_gate.mark_allocation: Sixteen marks with no printed split on this copy. The three integrated sittings of this identical stem print (6), (4) and (6) against the limbs, and while those marks are DELIBERATELY NOT IMPORTED as printed truth for this copy, they are a fair guide to the examiner's intent and are used as such. The answer allots framing plus three sections to limb (a), one section to limb (b), and three sections to limb (c) - matching the 6/4/6 shape without asserting it.
decomposition_gate.examiner_expectation: That the Code is named with its resolution number and date, and that its mandatory route is explained rather than assumed. That BOTH halves of the objective are given. That the strategy is given as a cycle. That the ambiguity in 'which all IMO instruments' is noticed and both answers supplied. That the five indicators are produced accurately, including the exclusion of constructive total losses. That the coastal State limb is answered as services. And that the answer closes by connecting the three roles rather than listing them.
decomposition_gate.primary_source_plan: Carry the paragraph-level content of A.1070(28) from the INTEGRATED MIW verification records for QP2401 Q9, QP2403 Q7 and QP2412 Q9, which read the resolution in full. Read QP2302-Q2 for the printed stem only, that paper being pushed but not integrated. Take the port State control material from QP2309 Q9 and QP2312 Q2, and the coastal State jurisdictional framing from QP2309 Q8. Reverse both 33rd Assembly citations to A.1157(32) and A.1155(32). Deliberately NOT planned: any quotation of A.1070(28); any count of instruments; any content of A.1157(32) or A.1155(32) beyond their identity, neither being held; any claim about the Audit Scheme's periodicity or procedural rules.
decomposition_gate.freshness_risk: HIGH - this question carries more reversal risk than any other on the paper. Two Assembly instruments must be reversed, both adopted on the same day four months after the sitting, and all three integrated depth donors sit after that boundary and carry the later numbers correctly for themselves. The trap is compounded because the Code's OWN number, A.1070(28), is not reversed - so a reviewer applying a blanket correction in either direction gets it wrong. The mandating chain and the Audit Scheme are stable and need nothing.
decomposition_gate.jurisdiction_risk: MEDIUM to HIGH. The whole question is about the boundary between three State roles, and the commonest error is to attribute a port State power to a coastal State or a coastal State service to a flag State. Two further boundaries matter: the Code is an IMO instrument that binds through the conventions, while the national legislation it demands is domestic law; and the Code's obligations attach only in respect of instruments the State has actually joined. Where India is concerned the Administration is the Directorate General of Shipping under the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958.
decomposition_gate.technical_ambiguities: The printed limb 'Which all IMO instruments covered in the code.' is genuinely ambiguous - it can mean the Code's six subject areas, which name no convention, or the treaty instruments under which the Code is mandatory. The two answers are different and the answer gives both with an explanation of why, rather than choosing one and risking the other. The stem is also printed as a statement with a full stop rather than as a question; that is preserved and answered as the question it plainly is. 'Strategy recommended to flag state' is read as the Code's strategy paragraph, which addresses the State in all three roles rather than the flag role alone, and the answer says so.
decomposition_gate.target_answer_shape: Eight numbered sections mapped onto the three printed limbs. Prose for the framing section, because how the Code binds is an argument. A bulleted two-part objective. A NUMBERED three-step strategy, because it is a cycle and the order matters. Two clearly separated bulleted answers to the instruments question. A bulleted list of five indicators followed by two propositions about what they are for. Three bulleted sections for the three State roles, the coastal one led by the services proposition. A closing paragraph joining the roles and naming the Audit Scheme above them.

reverify_before_publication.claim: That resolution A.1157(32) is the non-exhaustive list of obligations under instruments relevant to the III Code, and A.1155(32) the Procedures for Port State Control, operative at an August 2023 sitting - A.1187(33) and A.1185(33) having been adopted 6 December 2023 and having revoked them.
reverify_before_publication.why: THE SINGLE MOST IMPORTANT FLAG ON THIS PAPER. All three integrated depth donors - QP2401 Q9, QP2403 Q7 and QP2412 Q9 - sit after 6 December 2023 and correctly carry the later numbers for their own sittings, so a reviewer moving between papers will read both citations here as stale and be tempted to 'correct' them forward, which would date the answer four months into its own future. It must survive editing. MIW holds no copy of either resolution; identity and revocation dates come from its own read-at-source records.

reverify_before_publication.claim: That the Code itself, resolution A.1070(28) of 4 December 2013, is NOT affected by the 33rd Assembly and is cited unchanged.
reverify_before_publication.why: Recorded because the reversal above invites the opposite error. A reviewer who understands that two citations on this question were reversed backwards may apply the same correction to the Code's own number. It was the LISTS that were replaced, not the Code, which stands unrevoked and mandatory from 1 January 2016.

reverify_before_publication.claim: The paragraph-level content of the III Code relied on - the objective, the strategy, the six subject areas, the three initial actions, the flag State part, the performance indicators, and the coastal and port State parts.
reverify_before_publication.why: The text of A.1070(28) was NOT re-read for this paper. It is carried from the integrated MIW verification records for QP2401 Q9, QP2403 Q7 and QP2412 Q9, whose material reads the resolution in full, and is stated at the level that verification established rather than extended. This is authoritative internal reuse, not fresh primary verification.

reverify_before_publication.claim: That no count of the instruments under which the Code is mandatory is asserted.
reverify_before_publication.why: Neither the Code nor the Assembly's list states a number, and both nine and ten circulate depending on whether the SOLAS 1978 Protocol column is counted. The answer lists the instruments instead. Recorded so that a reviewer does not add a count for tidiness, and so a candidate is not caught out by an examiner who has seen the other figure.
